23166-who-was-she-from-the-atlantic-mont:
Bayard Taylor sets a storytelling trap in Who Was She?, from the Atlantic Monthly for September 1874. The host sets his terms before telling. A full glass, another cigar, and silence from his guest until the ghastly tale reaches its lamentable end. The papers at the story's center may be examined afterward, as much as the listener likes.

Taylor, the era's most famous American travel writer, turns here to a mystery of identity told over cigars. A woman glimpsed, pursued, and never quite named gives the tale its ache. The frame, a host binding his guest to silence, was the period's favorite way to raise a story's stakes. Who was she? The question outlasts the evening, which is the design. Taylor's polish keeps the ghost of an answer always one page away.
alarcon-three-cornered-hat-1874:
Pedro Antonio de Alarcon published The Three-Cornered Hat in 1874, a Spanish tale set in a small Andalusian town. Lucas is a miller whose wife, Frasquita, is admired by the town's mayor, or corregidor. The corregidor, named for his three-cornered hat, plots to have Lucas sent away for a night. He hopes to visit Frasquita alone.

Frasquita outwits him, and a chain of mix-ups in the dark follows. Husbands, wives, and officials trade places and chase each other through the night. Alarcon based the story on an old folk ballad. Its humor and pace later inspired a famous ballet with music by Manuel de Falla.
allen-encyclopedia-pure-materia-medica-v:
Timothy Field Allen aimed at completeness, and his Encyclopaedia of Pure Materia Medica began in 1874. Volume I opens a record meant to hold every symptom from every prover, sorted by remedy. Allen, a New York doctor and botanist, gathered reports from across the homeopathic world.

Nothing is summed up or sharpened here; the raw proving record stands as reported. That choice made the set the largest homeopathic materia medica ever compiled, a quarry for later, shorter books. Kent and others mined these pages. The first volume sets the scale: exact, vast, and meant for reference, not reading through.

Volume II of Allen's Encyclopaedia, also from 1874, keeps the great proving record moving at full pace. Timothy Field Allen collected symptoms from every source he trusted, then filed each one under its remedy. The order within an entry runs through the body, region by region, so nothing hides.

Allen prints what provers said, in their own plain terms, with sources named beside the reports. A reader can watch one drug act across dozens of people, dose by dose and day by day. As the second of ten volumes, it deepens the archive that made the Encyclopaedia the school's fullest store of drug effects.
arxiv-2511-20074:
Almenara, Leleu, Guillot, and a large team confirm three giant planets around a Sun-like star. Their 2025 paper characterizes the TOI-7510 system. The star is a solar analog watched by the TESS telescope. A machine-learning search first flagged two candidate planets. Follow-up observations corrected that early picture substantially.

One transit had been credited to the wrong planet. Three transiting giants actually circle the star. Their orbital periods run about eleven, twenty-three, and forty-nine days. Radii measure roughly two-thirds to nearly one Jupiter radius. Together they form the largest known transiting trio. Their periods sit near a 4:2:1 resonance chain. That near-resonance makes transit times wobble strongly. Photodynamical modeling pinned down the planet masses. Estimates run from very light to six-tenths of Jupiter. Orbits look nearly circular and closely aligned. CHEOPS, ASTEP, and EulerCam supplied follow-up photometry.
arxiv-2511-20174:
Grossman, Herman, Shushan Alshochat, and colleagues give ion pumps the flashing action theory promised. Their 2025 paper advances ratchet-based ion pumps, called RBIPs. Sorting ions of the same charge is hard. Water treatment and battery recycling both need it. Ratchets can push ions opposite ways.

Direction depends on each ion's diffusion speed. Current reversal with signal frequency is the ratchet signature. Earlier pump demos missed that flip entirely. A bipotentiostat now drives both device contacts independently. Matched signals unlock genuine flashing ratchet behavior. Performance jumped by an order of magnitude. That is up to one thousand percent improvement overall. Current and voltage flipped with frequency as hoped. Adding a voltage offset tunes the output asymmetry. Surface potentials are controlled precisely at both contacts. Ion sorting moves closer to practical devices. Resource recovery applications stand to gain most.
arxiv-2511-20274:
Sinha, Atreya, A, Ali, and Das teach vision-language models to read whole scenes, relations included. Their 2025 paper presents ScenarioCLIP for natural scene analysis. CLIP-style models match images with short captions well. Real scenes hold many objects acting and relating. Class lists alone miss that compositional structure.

ScenarioCLIP feeds text, grounded relations, and images together. Separate encoders handle global, object, and relation levels. Focused regions spotlight where relations happen. Contrastive cross-alignment ties the levels across modalities. An EMA teacher distills global knowledge downward steadily. The companion Action-Genome dataset supplies training material. It extends several public indoor and outdoor collections. Language models generated action and relation annotations. Manual and automatic curation cleaned the result. Benchmarks covered retrieval and fine-grained understanding tasks. Zero-shot and fine-tuned results beat prior methods. Scene-level reasoning moves beyond object naming. Robotics and surveillance both need such reading.
arxiv-2511-20474:
Anchan, Thomas, and Roy build three small perception modules for assistive technology. Their 2025 paper tests a modular deep learning framework inspired by Smart Eye systems. One module judges eye state, open or closed. Another reads facial expressions for emotion. A third identifies speakers from voice recordings.

Each module is a separate, lightweight neural network. A convolutional network handles eye images and drowsiness cues. A deeper convolutional network classifies expressions on the FER2013 dataset. A recurrent LSTM network identifies speakers from custom audio. Eye state detection reached ninety-three percent accuracy in testing. Expression recognition scored highest at 97.8 percent accuracy. Speaker identification reached 96.89 percent accuracy. The results validate specialized models for constrained assistive devices. Merging the modules into one real-time system remains future work. Latency and efficiency on embedded hardware are the next hurdles.
arxiv-2511-21174:
Magnetic monopoles, isolated north poles, have been hunted since Dirac, and the Standard Model hides one: the Cho-Maison electroweak monopole, a hybrid of the Dirac and 't Hooft-Polyakov types. Y. M. Cho argues in 2025 that the model should contain a neutral cousin, the Z monopole. It carries no electric magnetic charge, so electromagnetism ignores it, but it bears the neutral magnetic charge tied to the Z boson sector. Cho shows how to construct the object and explains the topology that allows it.

The neutral charge involved is about 1.83 times the electric charge, and the Z monopole's mass could be around 3.28 TeV, lighter than the Cho-Maison monopole's mass. That is closer to collider reach. Cho discusses what the new monopole would imply if found: a fresh window on force unification. The paper is a construction and argument, not an experimental report, and closes by inviting searches.
arxiv-2511-21674:
Agnes Korcsak-Gorzo and eight coauthors make a brain-like learning rule efficient enough for millions of simulated neurons, in 2025. Eligibility propagation, or e-prop, trains recurrent spiking networks with a local, biologically plausible rule, but its original form updates on a clock tick, wasting computation on silent neurons. Their version is event-driven: updates happen only when spikes occur.

Built into a large-scale spiking network simulator, the rule keeps prominent biological features: continuous dynamics and weight updates, strict locality of information, and sparse connectivity. Tested on neuromorphic MNIST, a handwritten-digit task in spikes, the system learns without the performance loss such constraints might suggest. The network scales to millions of neurons, showing that biological realism, often treated as a tax on efficiency, can instead shape it. The work bridges machine learning and computational neuroscience toward sustainable, brain-inspired AI.
arxiv-2511-21774:
Single author Pete Rigas characterizes when quantum strategies are optimal in the Odd-Cycle game, a two-player game hinging on whether a cycle can be two-colored, in 2025. Alice and Bob answer questions about a shared cycle without communicating; quantum entanglement can raise their winning chances. Rigas connects this game to an unlikely partner, the physics of foam.

Repeating the game in parallel mirrors minimizing foam surface area. The paper introduces new machinery for the link: a topological odd-blocker, marked components of a giant graph, and structures called pearls. These tie the giant component's properties to the maximum quantum winning probability. Concretely, the analysis frames how Alice and Bob can win about 11 percent more often with quantum strategies than classical ones. Error bounds from other quantum games, including XOR variants, locate where the advantage comes from.
arxiv-2511-21974:
Rivière and Trott probe how attention heads in Transformer language models learn to resolve ambiguous words during training. Using Pythia training checkpoints, they found when disambiguation jumps, then hunted heads whose attention to the cue rose in step.

They studied a small 14 million parameter model and a larger 410 million parameter one. In the small 14 million parameter model, the candidate heads were fragile, sensitive to the cue's position and part of speech, though deleting them demonstrably hurt disambiguation in causal ablation tests. The larger 410 million parameter model told a different developmental story. In the larger model, by contrast, several identified heads behaved surprisingly robustly and generalized well across perturbed stimuli. Repeating the small-model analysis across all its random seeds confirmed the pattern. Watching mechanisms develop, they argue, reveals how fragile and robust parts share the work.
arxiv-2512-00974:
Aradhya Chakrabarti designs a small processor for cheap FPGAs in a 2025 paper. FPGAs are chips whose hardware can be rewired after manufacture, and soft-core processors are CPUs built inside them. On low-cost boards, such processors often suffer from low code density and depend on proprietary toolchains.

Chakrabarti built a 32-bit dual-stack processor on a Gowin Tang Nano board, using open-source design flows. Its instruction set borrows a subset of the WebAssembly specification, which packs instructions tightly. The paper details the design, implementation, and evaluation. Dense code and open tools could make tiny custom processors easier to teach, share, and deploy.
arxiv-2512-01174:
Hyunjun Kim and Sooyoung Ryu present DrawingBench in a 2025 paper on evaluating AI agents. As agentic systems act more autonomously, trust needs verifiable evaluation, proof that an agent behaves reliably. Existing benchmarks often lack the transparency and auditability to supply that proof.

DrawingBench evaluates agentic language models through mouse-based drawing tasks. The model must produce sequences of low-level GUI actions, moving and clicking a mouse to draw. Those tasks test spatial reasoning and interface control together, and every action can be checked. A verifiable drawing test gives auditors a concrete record of what the agent actually did.
arxiv-2512-01274:
Zehua Zhao and a large team built a hard test for chemistry skill in AI models. Past tests were too easy and too narrow. They used simple tasks and scored just the final answer. That left out the steps an expert would take.

Their test, SUPERChem, holds hundreds of expert-made problems. Each problem needs deep thought, not just recall. Problems span many branches of chemistry. Each comes in both text form and a form with images. Scoring the full path of thought shows where a model truly grasps chemistry and where it just guesses.
arxiv-2512-01474:
Alexandra Lehtmets and co-authors study how starlight pushes gas around planets and discs. Star rays and gravity shape planet atmospheres. They also shape gas-rich debris discs. How that gas acts can tint the star's own surface.

By reading that tint, teams can infer what gas is present. The work tracks radiation-driven motion of atoms near stars. Those motions set how fast gas leaves a planet or disc. Knowing the rates helps judge which planets can hold their air over long ages. Rates for gas loss feed straight into planet habitability models, where air loss over billions of years can strip a world bare.
arxiv-2512-01674:
Zhizhen Chen and co-authors propose a pairing route that skips pair-wise attraction. Pair condensates in bosons are prized quantum states. Past routes need direct attraction between pairs. Their route uses periodic driving instead, called Floquet engineering.

Starting from hard-core bosons with modulated hopping, they derive an effective model. Three-site terms in that model drive odd pairing between neighbors. The result is a condensate with a twisted pair form. Driven pairing opens a new path to exotic states in cold atom labs. Cold atom tests can tune the drive live, so the predicted pair state can be hunted by sweeping frequency rather than rebuilding samples.
arxiv-2512-01874:
Entangled photons, particles of light linked at the quantum level, are usually made by splitting one photon into two. A 2025 paper by Dmitry Skachkov, Dirk R. Englund, and Michael N. Leuenberger tackles the much harder task of producing larger entangled groups of photons directly on a chip.

Ordinary materials respond too weakly at these higher orders, which has blocked the direct approach. The team turns to a layered material, niobium chloride, an excitonic Mott insulator whose strong response may clear that hurdle. If it works, programmable multiphoton entangled states could become a practical building block for quantum light sources and quantum computing hardware.
arxiv-2512-02474:
Haofeng Huang and Ling Gai study how online shops guess what a user will pick next. Sequential recommendation drives personal picks on shopping, ad, and streaming sites. Strong recent systems, such as BERT4Rec, lean on plain item numbers that carry no meaning, and they ignore text and images.

Their 2025 study, called Q-BERT4Rec, gives each item a compact code built from its meaning instead. Text and image details feed into that code, so similar items sit close together. Richer item codes could help shops suggest goods that fit taste, even for new or rare items. Good codes save shops from blind guesses when a user has odd taste in goods.
arxiv-2512-02874:
Haonan Wang and three co-authors merge several draft answers into one for open ended questions. Majority voting works when answers are short and can match exactly. Open ended reasoning, like code generation or web research, has no well defined majority across whole solutions.

Their logit averaging method runs reasoning in parallel, then blends the models' scores token by token into a single answer. One voice emerges from several lines of thought. Blending at the score level could lift quality on hard open tasks without training a bigger model. One voice from many drafts reads clean to the user, who need not see the clash of drafts that went into the blend.
arxiv-2512-03474:
Mistakes in a task often show in the result, not the motion. Wenliang Guo, Yujiang Pu, and Yu Kong present a mistake detection method in this 2025 work. Procedural tasks, like assembly or cooking, need systems that support learning and execution.

Most past methods analyze how an action is performed. The authors instead model the action effect, what the action produces. Wrong object states or layouts can reveal an error that motion alone hides. Effect-based checks could make tutoring and safety systems more helpful. Effects are often easier to verify than motions, since outcomes can be checked by sensors.
arxiv-2512-03774:
Motion planning for self-driving cars often relies on model predictive control, which optimises a short stretch of driving again and again. Johannes Fischer and colleagues note a flaw in a 2025 robotics preprint. Real-time planning uses convex approximations, and the best solution may lie outside the simplified region being searched. Their fix lets learning widen the search without giving up safety.

The proposed method, Safety Reinforced Model Predictive Control, uses safe reinforcement learning to propose a fresh reference trajectory for the controller. A constrained learning setup keeps that proposal inside safe regions, defined through a handcrafted energy-based index. A multiplier that adapts with the state is learned alongside the policy, enforcing the safety constraint during training. In a highway scenario, the combined planner beat both plain predictive control and learning alone on safety and performance measures.
arxiv-2512-03974:
Machine-learned force fields promise fast simulations with near-quantum quality, yet they often miss the temperatures at which real materials change phase. Paul Fuchs and Julija Zavadlav propose a repair strategy in a 2025 computational physics preprint. Their complaint is specific: biased training data can shift predicted transition points by several hundred kelvin, far too much for practical design work.

Instead of retraining on more reference data, the method learns top-down from experiment. A differentiable trajectory reweighting algorithm adjusts the model until the free energy difference between phases vanishes at the true pressure and temperature. On pure titanium, the corrected model matched the true transition points within tenths of a kelvin up to five gigapascals, and liquid diffusion improved too. The method is model-blind, extends to systems with several elements, and can target other known properties.
arxiv-2512-04074:
A landmark of graph theory says the minor relation is a well-quasi-order. In any infinite list of graphs, some earlier one sits inside a later one. Corentin Lunel and Clément Maria ask whether that order survives when graphs come embedded in the plane, in a 2025 preprint. Embedded versions matter for knot diagrams and surfaces, where the drawing is part of the data.

The authors prove the embedded immersion relation is a well-quasi-order on plane graphs of bounded carving-width. Their tools are structured tree decompositions and an argument about forests. Through directed medial graphs, they extend the result to the embedded minor relation at bounded branch-width. The unbounded case falls to classical grid theorems. Together the pieces show the embedded graph minor relation well-quasi-orders all plane graphs, carrying the landmark theorem into the topological setting where embeddings carry information.
arxiv-2512-04274:
Leonardo Furuta, Renan Magalhães, Haroldo Lima Junior, and Luís Crispino ask what changes when matter surrounds a wormhole. Real black holes sit inside disks of gas and dust. A wormhole could sit inside such a disk too. The group treats wormholes as stand-ins for black holes. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies how the matter nearby shifts the waves and light the object takes in.

The team traced the paths that light rays follow around these dirty wormholes. A thick shell of matter can create new rings of light. Those rings can trap waves for a long time. The trapped waves then leave clear marks on the bands of energy the wormhole absorbs. Most marks stayed near their old spots even when the shell was heavy. That steadiness hints at a trait that future observations could test.
arxiv-2512-04874:
James Tian develops a dynamic that steadily erases one chosen feature direction from an operator while keeping as much of everything else as possible. The endpoint of that erasure is the classical shorted operator, known from electrical network theory. His 2025 arXiv paper builds the path itself: a monotone sequence of positive operators with an exact decomposition of what has been removed at each step, converging to the shorted limit.

Carried into reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, the dynamic yields a family of kernels that settles on the largest kernel below the original and blind to the chosen subspace. On finite samples, the matching Gram operators inherit the same neat split. That split gives a canonical form of kernel ridge regression and a principled way to enforce invariance to nuisance traits. Data analysts gain one unified frame for building kernels that ignore what should not matter.
arxiv-2512-04974:
Armand Kassaï Koupaï, Lise Le Boudec, and Patrick Gallinari introduce ECHO, a system for generating the solutions of partial differential equations on grids of a million points. Such equations govern fluids, heat, and waves, but learning-based solvers have stumbled on dense grids, on drifting errors over long runs, and on designs tied to a single task. ECHO attacks all three problems at once with a fresh architecture.

A layered convolutional design squeezes the data a hundredfold while keeping the detail at each mesh point, and a training scheme lets the system produce fine-grained solutions from coarse inputs. Instead of stepping one frame at a time, ECHO learns whole stretches of a trajectory, which curbs long-run drift. It handles forward and inverse problems, filling-in tasks, and both guided and free generation, and it tops prior methods on million-point tests with tangled shapes and fast-changing dynamics.
arxiv-2512-05074:
Laetitia Bettmann, Artur Lacerda, Mark Mitchison, and John Goold study what happens when an open quantum system is driven across a phase transition in finite time. Such systems leak energy to their surroundings, and quick driving produces extra disorder beyond what slow driving would. The authors ask whether that extra disorder follows universal rules near the transition, the way the famous Kibble-Zurek mechanism governs defects in closed systems.

They show it does: the excess entropy grows as a power law in the driving time, with exponents set by the transition itself, not on details. For a broad class of systems whose states stay Gaussian, the laws predict something stranger — the leading excess does not depend on driving speed at all. The team checks the predictions on two models, a driven-dissipative Dicke model and an open Kerr model. The results frame how dissipation behaves in critical open quantum systems.
arxiv-2512-05174:
Marco Vallone presents a unified quantum theory of lossy plasmonic cavities — tiny structures where light and collective electron waves merge into hybrid particles called polaritons. In such cavities, coherent behaviour, relaxation, fading phase, and outright absorption all act at once, and a consistent account has to treat them on equal footing. Vallone builds that account as an open-system framework, since the cavity trades energy with its surroundings.

Starting from the photon's propagator, he derives a self-energy that captures both the shifting and the damping of the hybrid modes. Tracing out the surroundings yields evolution equations for the upper and lower polariton branches, including leakage, scattering between branches, and dephasing, plus closed-form steady states and line shapes. The theory holds at low polariton density while covering even ultrastrong coupling, and it speaks directly to measured spectra, time-domain tests, and the design of dissipation in nanophotonics.
arxiv-2512-05274:
Iryna Karpenko and Dmitry Shepelsky solve a boundary-value problem for the modified Camassa-Holm equation, a model of shallow-water waves that can form peaked crests. They work on the half line — a shoreline geometry — where the wave field is prescribed both at the start and at the boundary, a harder setting than the whole line. Their tool is the Riemann-Hilbert approach, which recasts the evolution as a factorization problem for matrices in the complex plane.

They characterize the solution entirely through that factorization. The data of the problem are spectral functions built from the initial and boundary values. The compatibility of those functions is itself expressed in spectral terms. Such characterizations open the door to long-time asymptotics and explicit formulas for this class of nonlinear wave equations. The paper extends inverse-scattering machinery for this equation to the half-line setting physical boundaries demand.
arxiv-2512-05374:
Charlie Summers, Haneen Mohammed, and Eugene Wu argue that language-model agents need the same upgrade databases once gave applications: moving enforcement out of hand-written code and into the system itself. Agents that perform complex, stateful tasks produce flows of data between tools and steps. Today nobody has good visibility into those flows. Policy violations, corrupted processes, and security flaws all grow in that blind spot, while each workflow improvises its ad hoc checks.

The authors propose Data Flow Controls: policies about where data may travel, enforced natively by the system the way access controls and validation are enforced inside a database engine. They describe work on a portable implementation of such controls for database systems, and lay out a research agenda toward flow control for whole agent ecosystems. The position is that agent safety will not scale as application-level discipline; it has to become infrastructure.
arxiv-2512-05674:
Gargi Panda, Soumitra Kundu, Saumik Bhattacharya, and Aurobinda Routray work on unmixing hyperspectral images. Every pixel in such an image blends light from several pure materials, called endmembers. The task is to name those materials and say how much of each sits in every pixel. Their 2025 network, 3D-CSCNet, is built by unrolling an optimization method into a learned model.

The core block learns sparse codes that respect structure in all three dimensions of the data cube at once, so space and spectrum inform each other. The estimated abundances pass into a decoder that rebuilds the image, and the decoder's weights then give the endmembers. A second algorithm, which stretches a projected simplex to cover the data, supplies a smart starting point for those endmembers. On three real datasets and one simulated set, at several noise levels, the network beat leading methods.
arxiv-2512-05774:
Ziyang Wang leads a nine author team arguing that software watching long videos should behave less like a captioning machine and more like a detective. Answering questions about hours of footage usually hinges on a few scattered moments. Standard pipelines caption everything first, wasting effort and blurring fine timing. Their framework, Active Video Perception, treats the video as an environment to interrogate.

Three model agents loop in rounds: plan, observe, reflect. The planner proposes a targeted look: a span of time, a region, a closer view. The observer returns time stamped evidence from the pixels. The reflector judges whether the evidence gathered so far can answer the query, and either stops or sends the loop out again. Across five long video benchmarks, the method took the best accuracy. It beat the strongest rival while using under a fifth of the inference time and about an eighth of the input tokens.
arxiv-2512-05974:
Xiaoyu Chen, Haibin Liu, and Jianming Cai ask whether nature's presumed quantum compass is genuinely a good design, or merely the one evolution happened to find. The radical pair mechanism is the leading candidate for how birds sense Earth's magnetic field: light born molecule pairs whose chemistry the field nudges. Laboratories sense fields with Ramsey protocols on diamond defects instead.

Both models run under both conditions, laboratory and in vivo. With precise timing control and decent prior knowledge of the field's direction, the Ramsey approach wins. Remove that knowledge and control, as the body must, and the radical pair model stands out. It trades raw accuracy for practicality: a sensor that works with no setup, no calibration, and no advance information. The verdict rehabilitates the biological design. Evolution optimizes fitness under mess. Working blind in warm, noisy tissue, it is not a crude compass. It is the appropriate technology.
arxiv-2512-06174:
Shilin Hu and four co-authors teach a diffusion model the physics of shadows before letting it paint them. Inserted objects fail when their shadows point the wrong way. The team's approach builds the shadow twice. First, geometry and light direction yield a coarse, correctly placed shadow.

Confidence scores govern how strongly the cues steer generation. The diffusion model then refines the anchored estimate into a realistic shadow. Errors fell roughly thirty percent against the previous best. Tests used the standard DESOBA outdoor benchmark. A physical scaffold beats hallucinated physics.
arxiv-2512-06274:
Hanmo Zhang, Zenghui Sun, and Kai Wang extend a classic decision tool to cases where people's choices sway each other. The tool, the restless bandit model, helps planners split scarce help among many people whose needs shift over time, even when no help is given. It shines in public health, but the classic form treats each person as an island.

The authors add a spread model, so a nudge to one person can ripple to friends and contacts. That change makes the planning problem huge, since every joint state and action must be weighed. They show the core update has a shape that lets a greedy climb reach a strong, provable share of the best result, and that repeated updates settle down. A learning method built on these ideas beat both short sighted and network blind plans on real graph data.
arxiv-2512-06874:
Ziyun Yu, Yiru Zhou, Chen Zhao, and Hongyi Wen ask whether large language models can stand in for real people in opinion surveys. The worry is bias: models tuned with human feedback lean toward majority views, which may erase the voices of smaller groups. The authors test direct prompting and step-by-step prompting on survey questions spanning many topics. They also try a method called CLAIMSIM, which first draws out varied claims from the model's own knowledge.

CLAIMSIM did produce a wider spread of answers, yet neither approach matched real users well. Models tended to hold one fixed stance no matter which demographic profile they were given. They also produced claims from a single viewpoint. When handed clashing claims, they struggled to weigh the fine differences between groups. The study warns that simulated respondents, as things stand, are a shaky substitute for asking actual people.
arxiv-2512-07074:
Huanbiao Zhu and co-authors extend a machine-learning method that corrects particle physics measurements for the distortions of the detector itself. The correction, called unfolding, is an inverse problem: from smeared readings, recover the true distribution. A celebrated algorithm, OmniFold, does this with classifiers in a loop resembling expectation-maximization, and it has already served real experiments. Its weakness is trust in the simulator: the forward model is only approximate, with the slack carried by nuisance parameters.

The new algorithm, Profile OmniFold, folds those nuisance parameters into the learning itself, letting the data discipline the simulation's uncertain knobs. The authors demonstrate it first on a simple Gaussian example, where the truth is known exactly. They then run a case study on simulated data from the CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider.
arxiv-2512-07374:
Yezi Liu and co-authors teach large language models to forget on the cheap. Unlearning, removing specific knowledge to honor deletion rights, fix errors, or update facts, usually means retraining or fine-tuning the whole model, or demanding the original training data. Their framework, Recover-to-Forget, works from the small adapter modules that practitioners already use to steer big models, the low-rank LoRA updates.

From many paraphrased prompts, the method reads the adapter's gradients, then a trained decoder reconstructs the direction the full model's gradient would have taken. Following that reconstructed direction unlearns the target while sparing general skill. The decoder is trained on a smaller proxy model and transferred to the real target, so the scheme reaches large or even black-box systems. Theory addresses how well the trick crosses between models, and experiments show effective forgetting with general performance preserved.
arxiv-2512-07474:
Yifei Huang, Tianyu Yan, Sitong Gong, Xiwei Gao, and four co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on living books. Their system, Living Novel, turns a novel into a chat with its characters. Readers can talk with several figures from the story.

Two problems plague such systems. Generic language models drift out of character as a chat goes on. They also leak spoilers and use knowledge the story world forbids. The team answers with a two-stage training pipeline. Deep Persona Alignment uses reinforcement fine-tuning with no added data to lock in character. A second stage adds a story-time knowledge graph and retrieval. That stage enforces what each character can know at each point in the plot. The test case is Jules Verne's Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea. Lab tests and a five-day diary study followed. Their model beat a flagship model on character fidelity.
arxiv-2512-07674:
Mehmet Yigit Avci and six co-authors wrote this 2025 medical imaging paper on a stubborn problem. MRI scans differ from machine to machine and protocol to protocol. Those shifts can bury the biology a doctor actually needs to see.

Harmonization methods try to iron out such scanner differences. Image-based ones need example target scans, which are not always available. Text-guided ones lean on simple labels that miss fine acquisition detail. The authors propose DIST-CLIP, a framework with a more flexible guide. It accepts either a target image or the scan's own DICOM metadata. The design splits each scan into anatomy and contrast as separate parts. A pretrained CLIP encoder reads the contrast side of that split. An adaptive style transfer module then pours the contrast into the anatomy. On varied real clinical datasets, the method beats leading rivals. It wins on fidelity while keeping anatomy intact.
arxiv-2512-07774:
Andrew Kalish, Pedro Fittipaldi de Castro, and Wladimir Benalcazar wrote this 2025 physics paper on order inside chaos. A lattice equation called the discrete nonlinear Schrödinger equation governs waves in many systems. It can behave ergodically, exploring everything, or trap energy in breathers.

Breathers are localized packets that hoard energy instead of sharing it. The switch between the two regimes had no precise marker before. The authors sample many equivalent starting conditions for the system. They watch the spread of the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy across that ensemble.  Its ensemble variance works as a dynamical order parameter. In the ergodic phase the variance vanishes, exactly as an order parameter should. Once ergodicity breaks, the variance turns finite and stays so. The time the ensemble takes to settle shows a sharp singularity at the switch. The method needs no special trajectory.
arxiv-2512-07974:
Christian Northe and Paolo Rossi wrote this 2025 theoretical physics paper on a mismatch. Topological defects are seams in a quantum system that store exotic information. Theory predicts how much entanglement survives across such a seam.

Numerical simulations have refused to match those predictions. Something in the standard calculation, not the simulations, must be off. The authors shift how reduced density matrices are prepared with defects present. Defect networks dress the state, and that dressing changes the accounting. Two kinds of defect get detailed treatment in the Ising model. Group-like defects are the simpler, symmetry-like case to handle. Duality defects, which swap order and disorder, are the subtler one. With the new preparation, theory and numerics agree across the board. The fix works at the level of the density matrix itself. Other entanglement measures beyond entropy inherit the correction automatically.
arxiv-2512-08074:
Simen Jacobs, Julian Voits, Nikita Frolov, Ulrich S Schwarz, and Lendert Gelens, biophysicists, posted a review on arXiv in December 2025. It is the first part of a two part survey on how biological systems respond to temperature. Nearly every biological rate depends on temperature, yet the observed curves often stray far from the simple Arrhenius law taught in chemistry.

Part one surveys the descriptive models used across scales, from single enzymes to whole organism performance. The authors discuss thermal performance curves, in symmetric and asymmetric forms, plus extensions of the Arrhenius law. They explain practical quantities these models define, such as optimal temperatures, thermal breadths, and thermal limits. They also review microscopic models of temperature effects, noting that those miss cooperative effects. Part two will take up how full system responses emerge from many interacting reactions.
arxiv-2512-08674:
Rongzhao Zhang and a large team present a multi agent system to support team decisions in gut and bowel cancer care. Good care in this field needs joint reading of endoscopy images, scans, and lab markers, which is hard for a single model to handle well. Single large models can lose context or invent details when cases grow complex.

The proposed system splits the work among agents that mimic a human multidisciplinary team, each handling part of the evidence before a joint view is formed. Expert review gave the system a high composite score, well above a single model baseline. The biggest gains came in reasoning quality and medical accuracy. The authors argue that team style agent design offers a more clear, robust, and scalable path for clinical decision support.
arxiv-2512-09074:
Shangqing Xu and coauthors present DeepTherm, a modular deep learning system for early warning of deadly heatwaves. Severe urban heat threatens public health, yet predicting an incoming deadly heatwave is hard. A central difficulty is defining and estimating heat related mortality, and a warning system also needs available data, robustness across space and time, and clear decision costs.

DeepTherm avoids any need for past heat mortality records. Its dual prediction pipeline separates baseline mortality, in the absence of heatwaves and other irregular events, from total mortality. That split lets the system flag excess risk tied to heat. Evaluation on real data across Spain shows consistent, robust, and accurate performance across groups. The design also allows a trade off between missed alarms and false alarms to be set explicitly. The authors argue that modular deep learning can meet the practical demands of a public health warning system.
arxiv-2512-09174:
Sabrina Stierwalt and coauthors report the neutral hydrogen content of a compact dwarf group. Gas maps show multiple bridges between members, indicating the group is gravitationally bound. The maps also reveal two new dwarf satellites that are easy to see in gas yet barely visible in optical images,.

The previously known members have similar stellar and gas masses, while the new satellites are far smaller in stars yet still gas rich. New optical spectra confirm the link between the gas detections and their faint optical counterparts. The group velocity spread, mass to light ratio, size, and gas fraction all match compact dwarf groups in a leading simulation. Its satellite pattern suggests two groups merging. The group sits in a tendril between cosmic filaments,.
arxiv-2512-09274:
Garvit Grover and colleagues study nulling, a strange habit of pulsars in which their radio pulses switch off for a while and then return. Nulling is common in slow pulsars and matters for understanding how their emission works. Measuring it is hard because single pulses from faint pulsars blur into background noise.

The team built a new method, the N-sum algorithm, which adds pulses together so real emission stands out from noise more clearly. That gives a firmer measure of the nulling fraction, the share of time a pulsar spends off, even for weak sources with few recorded pulses. Checked against simulations, real data, and a recent Gaussian mixture method, the algorithm agrees well. The authors also measure repeating on-off rhythms in five pulsars, three of them for the first time, and compare how that rhythm relates to each pulsar's spin-down energy loss.
arxiv-2512-09374:
V. Arvind, Srijan Chakraborty, and Samir Datta study catalytic computation, an unusual model of computing with very little clean memory. A catalytic machine works in logarithmic space but also gets a large tape already filled with arbitrary data. It may use that tape as scratch space only if it restores the contents when finished. The model was introduced in 2014 and has surprising power.

The authors derandomize isolation inside this model. Their first result gives a catalytic algorithm that finds a minimum-weight solution to a search problem, given oracle access to the matching decision problem. That yields catalytic algorithms for planar matching problems and weighted arborescences. Their second set of results places several classes, including search SAT and classes based on randomness, inside a two-round oracle version of catalytic space. A third part locates reachability inside an unambiguous catalytic class, with a tradeoff between oracle workspace and catalytic space.
arxiv-2512-09674:
Yufeng Shen and colleagues investigate the topology of neighborhood complexes for a family of graphs called induced k-independent graphs. A neighborhood complex is built from a graph by taking sets of nodes that share a neighbor, and its shape, studied through algebraic topology, encodes information about the graph. Their interest comes from a correspondence found earlier between cut complexes of cycles and neighborhood complexes of stable Kneser graphs.

That correspondence suggests the homotopy type of total cut complexes may be related to neighborhood complexes of these induced graphs more broadly. The authors work out the homotopy types of some total cut complexes and of neighborhood complexes of other graphs. Their tools come from algebraic topology and discrete Morse theory, which simplifies complexes by canceling cells in pairs without changing their shape. The paper adds to topological combinatorics, mapping how these graph-derived spaces are put together.
arxiv-2512-09774:
Richard Evan Schwartz offers a new, cleaner proof of Mostow rigidity, a famous theorem in geometry. The theorem says, roughly, that the shape of certain higher dimensional spaces is fixed completely by their basic algebraic structure. Schwartz stresses that the article contains no new research. Its value lies in the route: a self contained argument that asks little more of the reader than undergraduate real analysis.

The proof is written for graduate students interested in geometry and topology who may find older accounts heavy going. Schwartz calls it unusually clean and analytically light compared with standard treatments. The article was prepared for the Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society, a venue known for readable surveys and expositions. Students who want to understand why rigidity holds, without first mastering a large technical apparatus, are the intended audience for this streamlined presentation.
arxiv-2512-10074:
Peyman Moeini and Mark Coates ask why small and medium sized firms rarely adopt real time location systems. These systems track assets and people indoors, feeding the data that Industry 4.0 workflows, warehouse and manufacturing software, and digital twins depend on. Large enterprises deploy them increasingly; smaller firms lag. The authors review the literature on technical, financial, and organizational constraints, from infrastructure and calibration effort to legacy integration and human factors. They then survey sixteen manufacturing and technology professionals in Canada and the United States.

The blockers were upfront cost, installation effort, integration difficulty, and the need for many anchor nodes. Most would accept only modest upfront investment, well under ten thousand dollars, and preferred low infrastructure deployments. The authors draw design directions: wireless modular architectures, cloud managed self calibrating systems, standard integration interfaces, and methods that minimize or eliminate anchors. Adoption, they conclude, fails on fit rather than value.
arxiv-2512-10274: David Ayala and John Francis prove a stronger, space-level version of the Pontryagin-Thom theorem, a classic result in topology. In plain terms, their paper shows that the space of maps from a manifold into a Thom space can be matched with a moduli space of submanifolds. So questions about maps can be recast as questions about shapes sitting inside other shapes. The proof runs to sixty-two pages of mathematics.
arxiv-2512-10474:
L Panier and co-authors use starquakes of light, the oscillations measured by space telescopes, to peer inside red giant stars that are burning helium in their cores. Missions such as Kepler and TESS made these mixed-mode patterns rich and precise. But models still miss parts of what is observed, mostly because mixing inside the star is uncertain.

With an updated Liège evolution code, the team computed oscillation patterns for a range of models and traced how inner features shape the seismic signal. Sharp chemical gradients and the amount of central overshooting proved decisive, shifting the semi-convective layers and the local buoyancy frequency. Oddly, the changes nearly cancel in total core size. So a star evolves much the same while its seismic fingerprint changes a lot, which is exactly what makes the signal a sharp tool.
arxiv-2512-10574:
Amy Attwater and a large team caught a galaxy in the act of shutting down its own star formation. NGC 4064 is a satellite of the Virgo cluster that already lost most of its cold gas to environmental stripping as it ploughed through the cluster. Stripping alone, the authors note, struggles to clear the dense gas in a galaxy's centre, where stars are still being born.

Using the MUSE instrument under the MAUVE survey, they found a two-sided outflow of ionised gas. The outflow is driven by the galaxy's remaining star formation, concentrated in its centre. This happens even though the galaxy's overall birth rate sits below the usual main sequence. The outflow carries mass away fast enough to remove the leftover gas sooner than star formation alone would burn it. Modest feedback, they conclude, can finish the quenching that stripping started.
arxiv-2512-10674:
Javier Villena Toro and Mehdi Tarkian estimate where an object sits in space, its full six-degree-of-freedom pose, without any training for that object. Recent zero-shot methods lean on huge models and cloud computing, which brings delay, energy cost, and data governance worries that real robots, with modest onboard hardware, cannot accept. Their pipeline, Geo6DPose, trades model scale for geometric reliability and runs fully on the device.

It matches features from a foundation vision model between prepared object templates and the live scene, then filters matches geometrically. Scene points are lifted into three dimensions and template features into the object's own coordinates, and only mutual correspondences survive. A RANSAC step recovers candidate poses, ranked by a score mixing reprojection consistency and spatial support. The system answers in under a second on one ordinary graphics card, matching far larger baselines.
arxiv-2512-11074:
Christopher Driggers-Ellis and colleagues extend a widely used dataset for multimodal machine translation, where systems translate text linked to images. The original Multi30k covers only four European languages, all in Latin script, which has narrowed research toward those languages. Earlier extensions added only a few more languages and scripts.

Their MultiScript30k translates the English sentences into Arabic, Spanish, Ukrainian, and both simplified and traditional Chinese using a large multilingual translation model. Similarity checks show the new versions track the source closely and compare well with earlier hand built extensions. Quality scores from an automatic judge were mixed across languages. The release aims to open multimodal translation research to a wider range of language families and writing systems.
arxiv-2512-11174:
A study of mixed quantum standard motion finds that a widely used approximation can produce impossible probability spreads. The Liouville equation approach treats part of a system quantum mechanically and part classically, preserving total population, energy, and purity, and often matching exact quantum results for averages. Its density, though, comes from a partial transform that can turn negative.

Comparing exact evolution with the approximate one from pure starting states, the authors show the off diagonal parts of the density behave differently in resonance effects, especially for low energy states. In simple models they prove the approximation can make marginal phase space densities negative, something no physical system allows, and that this failure is generic rather than accidental. The violations fade as the starting energy grows relative to the gap between states. They propose a negativity index to warn users when the approximation is misbehaving.
arxiv-2512-11374:
Tomáš Koref and fellow authors mine the arguments inside court judgments to test whether Central and Eastern European judges really reason as formalists, as common narratives claim. Courts must justify choices, but reading reasoning at scale needs automation. The team built methods to detect and classify judicial argument in choices of the Czech supreme courts.

Their MADON data set contains hundreds of choices with thousands of paragraphs labelled by experts into eight argument types, plus whole decision formalism labels. Training on a corpus of hundreds of thousands of Czech choices, they adapted transformer language models to the legal domain and handled class imbalance with special losses. The best models identified argumentative paragraphs, sorted argument types, and classified choices as formalistic or not with strong balanced scores. A three stage process mixing modern transformers with standard methods kept costs down while staying explainable.
arxiv-2601-06674:
C. Gallesco and two co-authors sort chains of states for data in fixed classes in 2026. Such data, like words or gene codes, change step by step in time. Most models for them are chains whose next step rests on the past few steps.

Work in the past dwelt most on chains with just one step of past. Yet the traits of longer chains can be read through the short ones. One maps a long chain to a short one on a blown-up set of states. The paper works out that map and sorts the chains by what they share. This tells those who model such data which chains act the same at heart. The scope runs from gene codes to speech and far past both. A clear sort saves time when a new chain must be picked.
arxiv-2601-06874:
Changli Wu and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with MVGGT. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Most existing 3D referring expression segmentation methods rely on dense, high-quality point clouds. While real-world agents such as robots and mobile phones operate with only a few sparse RGB views and strict latency constraints.

The authors introduce Multi-view 3D Referring Expression Segmentation. Where the model must recover scene structure and segment the referred object directly from sparse multi-view images. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-06974: Research by Quoc-An Nguyen and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with UETQuintet at BioCreative IX - MedHopQA. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Biomedical Question Answering systems play a critical role in processing complex medical queries. Yet they often struggle with the intricate nature of medical data and the demand for multi-hop reasoning. The authors propose a model designed to effectively address both direct and sequential questions. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07074:
Pedro Abdalla and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers robust mean estimation under quantization. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. The authors consider the problem of mean estimation under quantization and adversarial corruption. The authors construct multivariate robust estimators that are optimal up to logarithmic factors in two different settings.

The first is a one-bit setting, where each bit depends only on a single sample, and the second is a partial quantization setting. In which the estimator may use a small fraction of unquantized data. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07374:
Andrea Ferrara and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers possible evidence for a pair-instability supernova nature of ultra-early JWST sources. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Recent JWST observations have revealed a population of unexpectedly bright sources at ultra-high redshift , challenging current models of early galaxy formation. One extreme example is Capotauro.

An F356W-dropout identified in the CEERS survey and initially interpreted as a luminous galaxy at z 30 z 30. But subsequently found to be variable over an 800 800 day baseline. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07674:
Xingran Chen and colleagues defend decentralized learning against a playful-sounding but serious attack. Random walk algorithms are popular in distributed systems for their low overhead and scalability. They now support decentralized learning, where data stays on local devices. Their weakness is reliance on local interactions, which malicious nodes can abuse. The team's 2026 preprint names the threat the Pac-Man attack.

In this attack, a malicious node probabilistically swallows any random walk that visits it. The proposed defense uses self-creating random walks, which can replace the ones destroyed. The contest between attack and defense is studied directly. Such work matters as learning moves onto untrusted networks of devices. The paper speaks to distributed systems and security scholars.
arxiv-2601-07974:
Yuxi Xia, Kinga Stańczak, and Benjamin Roth explain why detectors of AI-written text fail on new material. Such detectors score highly on familiar benchmarks. They often struggle with unseen prompts, model families, or domains. Prior work reported these generalization gaps but offered few explanations. Their 2026 preprint presents a systematic study using linguistic analysis. The goal is to explain the behavior, not just measure it.

Detectors lean on linguistic cues that may be artifacts of one generator or genre. When conditions change, those cues vanish or mislead. Knowing which cues carry the signal helps build detectors that travel better. It also warns against trusting detector verdicts in schools and courts. The paper serves NLP scholars and anyone who deploys AI text detection. It shifts the question from accuracy to mechanism.
arxiv-2601-08074: Xavier Hernandez proposes a new way to tune twelve musical tones in his 2026 arXiv paper. Standard equal temperament cannot give exact perfect fifths in every key. The math is stark: twice two to the seven-twelfths power does not equal three. So the second harmonic of a fifth can never match the third harmonic of the root note. Hernandez uses elastic overtones to build a twelve-tone system that keeps fifths exact. The paper speaks to readers in music theory, acoustics, and tuning design.
arxiv-2601-08474: Marcelo Coniglio, Francesc Esteva, Joan Gispert, and Lluis Godo wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on fuzzy logics built by Godel. Godel fuzzy logic grades truth on a scale. The team studies the degree-preserving companion of that logic, in a form with an involution, a flip that twice applied gives back the start. They sort the logics that sit between that companion and classical propositional logic, and do the same for their finite-valued forms. The study covers paraconsistency, where a clash need not cause collapse.
arxiv-2601-08774:
Christian Bernert and three co-authors count whole number points on a rough shape from algebra. The shape is a quartic del Pezzo surface, a surface set by a fourth degree rule. They count points whose height stays below a set cap. The count must work over any number field, not just the plain whole numbers.

They prove a growth rule for that count. The proof is hard in a plain way. The shape that guides the count breaks into a huge set of small blocks. Like a jigsaw, those blocks fit back into one large block. A reader in number work gets both the rule and a new view of why the blocks must fit.
arxiv-2601-09174:
Kaue Cardoso studies a graph built from a hypergraph, where each link can join more than two points. Take each such wide link as a point in a new graph. Join two new points by as many lines as the wide links share in points. The new graph is called a line multigraph. It codes how wide links cross and share.

He proves traits of these graphs, both in shape and in their spectra. Spectra here are sets of counts that code how a graph waves and links. Such graphs can model group ties, where one tie binds a whole team. A reader in graph work gets a new class with firm first laws to build on.
arxiv-2601-09974:
Seoyeon Kim and Jaehyung Kim study how a language model can track a user over time. Most tailoring tools rest on fixed user facts. They fetch past text or tune the model once. But what a user likes can drift week to week.

A model that fails to drift with the user grows stale. A model that retunes too much can lose old likes. The pair give a plan that does both jobs in parts. It picks which weights to tune for new likes. It also blends in fetched past text at reply time. The aim is tailoring that moves with the user and keeps the past.
arxiv-2601-10374:
Tuomas Lappi, Risto Paatelainen, and Mikko Seppälä work out a two loop split rule for quarks and gluons. As a fast grain hits a proton, its parts share its push. Split rules say how that share shifts with scale. They are core to collider math.

The team use light cone methods, a frame where one push part is plus at all times. That trait makes some poles easy to tame. A plain cut off does the job, and it drops out of the end math. They get the next to lead split rule. The work shows the frame can bear two loop tasks.
arxiv-2601-10474:
Optimal error bounds are proved for a Galerkin method on curved edges with straight meshes. The method splits a field into parts on each cell. It is named discontinuous Galerkin. It is strong for laws with sharp fronts. But a curved edge cut by straight cells can lose grade.

The loss comes from the gap twixt the true edge and the mesh. Past runs oft drop one full grade from that gap. The paper gives best bounds for that case. It shows when the full grade can be kept. The work guides mesh picks for rigs with curved walls.
arxiv-2601-10674:
Lorenzo Ricci and Raman Sundrum use energy correlators to probe strongly coupled field theories. A correlator tracks how energy flows out in set patterns after a clash. For theories that are nearly conformal, direct math is hard. Holography offers a dual picture in terms of curved spacetime, where the math can be done.

The authors study warped geometries, spaces that bend away from pure anti-de Sitter form. They also study cut-off versions that mirror a mass gap in four dimensions. These features match what realistic theories beyond the standard model would need. The results show what energy flow can reveal about hidden strong dynamics.
arxiv-2601-10774:
Mathis Gerdes and Miranda C. N. Cheng design building blocks for normalizing flows. Flows turn simple random noise into rich data by a chain of smooth, invertible maps. Each scalar map in the chain must be expressive, smooth, and easy to invert with a known Jacobian. Existing choices force trade-offs among those needs.

Affine maps are smooth and easy to invert but weak. Splines give local control yet are only piecewise smooth and work on bounded ranges. Residual flows are smooth but need slow numeric inversion. The authors seek analytic bijections that keep all the good traits at once. Better blocks mean flows that train faster and sample more faithfully.
arxiv-2601-11274:
Sylvia Novo, Rafael Obaya, and Ana Sanz revisit families of rough ODEs. Their 2026 preprint deals with Caratheodory differential equations. Such equations allow rough, jumpy terms on the right side. Precompact families of them are the focus of the study.

The team builds a space of parametric b-measures for the work. Fit topologies on that space set the stage. From it they define a new class of generalized ODEs. The class is given by those parametric b-measures. Nonautonomous dynamical systems tools then do the heavy lifting. That route gives a fresh way to handle the families. The work sits in the core theory of differential equations.
arxiv-2601-11374:
Furkan Sahinuc, Subhabrata Dutta, and Iryna Gurevych grade scientific writing by machine. Their 2026 preprint builds reward models for that task. Scientific writing is expert work with strict demands. It needs deep domain knowledge and sharp reasoning at once.

Making scientific text by machine has been widely studied. Grading such text is still an open, hard problem. A reward model scores drafts so systems can learn from scores. Scores must track task specs, not just fluent style. The team tackles what a good reward for science prose is. Sound grading could lift AI help for authors and reviewers. It could also flag weak claims dressed in fine words.
arxiv-2601-11474:
Olivier Benoist proves a negativity claim about resultant divisors in this work. His 2026 preprint sits in birational geometry, a pure math field. Fix two degrees d and e, with d the smaller one. The space in play parametrizes pairs of polynomials.

Each pair holds homogeneous polynomials in two variables. One has degree d and the other has degree e. The higher one is set only up to a multiple of the lower. That gauge freedom shapes the parameter space's geometry. Resultants test when the pair shares a common root. The divisor they form is shown to be negative here. Negativity results guide how such spaces can be mapped and split.
arxiv-2601-11774:
Haoyu Xie, Jichao Fan, Zarif Ahmad Razin Bhuiyan, and their co-authors report a new kind of sensor for handed forms of molecules. Many drugs and scents come in left and right hand forms. Light based tests for which form is present are weak, and past boosts add hard steps.

Their sensor joins two effects in one stack built at wafer scale. One part uses twisted carbon tubes, and one part can change phase. Taking in molecules shifts the light read-out. The team frame this as a new route to sense work that is fine, large in scale, and open to control.
arxiv-2601-11874:
Suchana Datta, Dwaipayan Roy, Derek Greene, and their co-authors link search science with cultural analytics for fair access to old texts. They use the British Library BL19 set, with more than 35,000 works from 1700 to 1899. The set holds both fiction and non-fiction from the 19th century.

They build a test bed for shifts in words, terms, and search over that span. Old terms can hide works from modern search terms. The test bed can show where search fails past users. It aims to open old culture to all readers on fair terms.
arxiv-2601-11974:
Xinmeng Hou, Peiliang Gong, Bohao Qu, and their co-authors give language model agents a way to improve with less waste. Agents today rest on fixed prompts made by humans. That caps how well they can adapt to new tasks.

Past self-improve tools use loops that run many turns and cost much compute. The team take a cue from human meta-cognition, our skill at thinking about our own thought. Their method uses brief self-review to guide change. A leaner loop could make agents adapt at lower cost.  Brief self checks keep the cost of each task in bounds.
arxiv-2601-12174:
Haiman Guo, Cheng-Yi Li, Yuli Wang, and a large clinical team build a multitask agent to read right upper quadrant ultrasound. Ultrasound is a key tool in emergency and liver-bile care. Yet its reads rest much on the operator and are time pressed.

Their vision-language agent helps across the full read workflow. It does many linked tasks in one system, not just one label call. A broad aide could cut missed signs and speed reports. The work tests it on multi-frame scans from real care.  The agent is built for multi frame scans, not still shots.
arxiv-2601-12274:
Mahdi Eslamimehr joins concolic testing with large language models to guide path search in big programs. Concolic testing runs code with both real and symbolic inputs. It is strong, but path counts explode and constraint solving is costly.

His frame uses a language model to pick which paths to try and to ease solving. That pairing aims to make the method work on large, real software. Better test coverage finds flaws before release. The work sets out the algorithm and its claims.  LLM guides may cut the cost of search by a lot.
arxiv-2601-12374:
Akram Elbouanani, Aboubacar Tuo, and Adrian Popescu take on the task of bias checks in large language models. Past checks face a hard trade off. Fake prompts give tight control but do not match real use. Real tasks match real use but lack scale and rigor. The field needs a way to get both at once.

The team builds a framework that uses named entities as probes. Names of people, places, and groups can be swapped in a planned way. That swap lets them test how model behavior shifts across groups. The design aims to be large in scale and firm in method. It seeks gaps in how a model treats distinct sets of entities.
arxiv-2601-13074:
Shi-Cong Mo, Hongyi Yu, and Wei Wu study a rare route to superconductivity in flat layered matter. The route is the Kohn-Luttinger path, where pairs form from pure push away forces. In the plain form, pairs carry high spin like waves and form only at very low heat levels.

The team finds a new case in a stacked model of flat electron sheets. Such stacks stand in for layered van der Waals matter, sheets held by weak forces. In their model, pairs form in a plain s wave form with no spin like twist. The heat level for the change is also much higher than in the plain case. The result hints that layered matter may host this rare pairing at more apt heat levels.
arxiv-2601-13274:
Akinlade Akintunde and Stewart A. Mallory trace self spread in active matter back to hits between bits. Active matter is made of bits that move on their own, like cells or bots. Much is known about how crowds of them act as a whole. Far less is known about why one bit spreads as it does.

The pair build a frame that ties self spread to hit forces. They also track how those forces link over time, their memory. Both the plan of hits and their memory shape the spread. The frame gives a micro cause for a bulk trait. For staff who design smart stuff or study cell crowds, that cause is a design knob.
arxiv-2601-13374:
Bao-An Li reads the trace anomaly of dense matter from two harsh realms. The score is set by the gap of one third less the ratio of pressure to energy density. It marks how far dense stuff strays from a scale free form. That stray steers both fluid reply and star hold.

Li draws on two data pools. One is bulk flow in heavy ion crashes in the lab. The next is bulk traits of neutron stars, such as mass and size. By join of the two pools, he pins the score across a wide density span. Few scores can be tied from both a lab crash and a dead star at once.
arxiv-2601-13774:
Yan-Cheng Wang, Zheng Yan, and Xue-Feng Zhang probe a candidate quantum phase change point in 2026. Their setting is an extended hard-core Bose-Hubbard model on a kagome lattice. A kagome lattice has a woven pattern of triangles and hexagons. The point in question is a deconfined quantum critical point, or DQCP.

They use quantum Monte Carlo simulations to study the point. Two probes guide the work: entanglement entropy and the U(1) disorder operator. Both can reveal hidden order at a phase change. Firm proof at this point would test bold ideas in quantum matter theory.
arxiv-2601-13874:
Shijie Zhong, Yikun Yang, Da Gong, and Jiangfeng Fu refine a key statistic for two-sample testing in 2026. Maximum mean discrepancy, or MMD, compares two samples via kernels. Its inferential accuracy hinges on how well its variance is known. Past estimators differ under null and alternative hypotheses, and for balanced or imbalanced data.

The team gives a unified unbiased variance estimation for MMD. They target robust finite-sample performance with imbalanced data. They also give exact acceleration under both hypotheses. A single sound estimator could make two-sample tests simpler and more trusted.
arxiv-2601-13974:
Shih-Yao Lin builds a new way to judge which video frames a system picks in 2026. Frame sampling is a core step in video understanding and video-language pipelines. Judging the quality of sampled frames remains challenging. Old metrics focus on perceptual quality or reconstruction fidelity of single frames.

They do not test if a frame set captures informative, representative content. Lin's STEC is a reference-free spatio-temporal entropy coverage metric. It needs no ground-truth frame set to score a sample. Better frame picks could make video models faster and more accurate at once.
arxiv-2601-14174:
Myung-Sin Song and James Tian attach a notion of content to wavelet packet trees in 2026. Wavelet packets split a signal into a tree of finer frequency bands. The team gives a simple way to attach content to the tree's nodes, given a positive operator. At a fixed packet depth, packet projections split the operator.

The split yields positive pieces of the original operator. This decomposition induces a boundary measure on the packet path space. Vector-dependent densities show how energy distributes across the tree. Such maps help analysts see where an operator's strength concentrates.
arxiv-2601-14274:
Anh-Tuan Mai, Cam-Van Thi Nguyen, and Duc-Trong Le work on emotion reading in this 2026 paper. Their task is multimodal emotion recognition in conversation. A system must judge feelings from speech, text, and face cues at once. Each cue type can add its own facts.

Some facts are unique to one cue type. Some are shared across types. Some appear only when types are combined. The authors use those three kinds, named unique, redundant, and synergistic. A good system should use all three in balance, but that balance is hard to reach. Their divide-and-refine method aims to improve both the mix and how well the system can explain its calls.
arxiv-2601-14374:
Daniella van der Boom and Doron Kushnir revisit a key distance in this 2026 paper. The galaxy NGC 4258 holds a water maser system, gas clouds that beam microwaves. Tracking it gives a geometric distance to the galaxy. That distance is commonly reported as about 7.6 megaparsecs, with percent-level accuracy.

The value anchors the extragalactic distance ladder. It also feeds recent measures of the Hubble constant, the rate at which the universe expands. The authors reanalyze the maser system by tracking individual maser components. Their aim is a fresh check on a number that much of cosmology leans on.
arxiv-2601-15074:
Srinath Srinivasan, Tim Menzies, and Marcelo d'Amorim build a smarter judge for fuzz testing. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with differential fuzzers. These tools run the same input through rival versions of one spec, such as JavaScript interpreters, and flag where outputs differ.

Someone must decide which output is right. That judge, the oracle, is built by hand for JavaScript tests. Hand work is slow, costly, and prone to false alarms, and it must be redone when the spec changes. Their SmartOracle uses an agentic approach to cut that noise down.
arxiv-2601-15374:
Shravya Shenoy, Daniel J. B. Smith, and co-authors ask what sets the radio brightness of a star-forming galaxy. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the radio continuum to star formation rate relation. Radio light offers a view of star birth that dust cannot hide.

New evidence hints that stellar mass bends that relation. The authors ask which other galaxy properties shape it too. They build a new calibration from the LoTSS-DR2 survey data. A cleaner relation means radio surveys can read star formation rates with far more trust than ever before.
arxiv-2601-15474:
Md Nabi Newaz Khan, Abdullah Arafat Miah, and Yu Bi study attacks on graph neural networks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Such networks do well on hard tasks in many fields. Yet they can be fooled by backdoor attacks. In these attacks, a hidden trigger is planted in the model. The model then acts as the attacker wants when the trigger appears.

Past work on graph classification mostly covers single-target attacks. There, one trigger is implanted by swapping in a subgraph. The title signals the step this paper takes. It moves to multi-targeted attacks, with more than one target in play. For defenders, that shift matters. A guard built for one trigger may miss a broader attack.
arxiv-2601-15774:
Mathew Duong and four co-authors build a yardstick for firmware fuzzers in a 2026 arXiv paper. Monolithic firmware runs countless devices. Fuzz testing it is an active research field. New methods claim gains in this hard domain. Checking those claims is messy, though. Metrics like code coverage and unique crashes are unreliable guides. Two fuzzers can post similar coverage while finding very different bugs.

Their answer is FirmReBugger, a benchmark framework. It is bug-based rather than coverage-based. A benchmark keyed to real bugs measures what users care about: found flaws. Fair comparison speeds progress across the field. Firmware flaws are security risks in routers, cameras, and industrial gear. Better fuzzers, honestly ranked, mean safer devices.
arxiv-2601-16074:
Annemarie Jutte and Uraz Odyurt ask how to trust machine learning in plant systems. Their 2026 preprint deals with plants and grids that join code and real gear. Such plants are key for safety and cost. Deep models now help run them, but their steps are hard to see. A model that acts in odd ways on new data can pose real risk.

The pair stress strict tests before trust is earned. Clear accounts of why a model acts as it does form part of that test. Tests must catch odd acts on data the model has not seen. The work frames a path to safe use of deep models. It speaks to teams who run plants where faults cost much.
arxiv-2601-16474:
Kaur Kristjuhan and Dominic Berry cut the cost of phase sums with three guide bits. Their 2026 preprint deals with quantum phase sums. Those sums sit in many quantum plans, most of all for chem ground states. Past sums use a guide state built on a bank of bits. Powers of a step are then run as that guide tells.

Three guide bits turn out to give best trust marks. Best marks mean the true phase sits in a tight range. Tight range with few bits cuts gear needs much. Chem sums could then run on more small gear. The work finds the sweet count for guide bits.
arxiv-2601-16674:
Shamim Haque, Atharva Shinde, Asim Kumar Saha, Tuhin Malik, and Ritam Mallick study twin stars. These are star pairs of a rare sort, not two stars in space. One branch holds plain dense stars of crushed matter. A twin branch holds stars mixed with quark matter. A sharp shift in dense matter can split the branches. Their 2026 preprint weighs which mixes can form twins.

Fresh sky data now bound the size and mass of dense stars. The team checks which shift points fit those bounds. They also gauge how strong the shift must be. Such checks test our grasp of matter at crush depth. They link lab ideas to what scopes see in deep space.
arxiv-2601-16774:
Yiheng Jiang, Biao Tian, Haoxu Wang, Shengkui Zhao, Bin Ma, Daren Chen, and Xiangang Li tackle echo in calls. When a speaker's voice loops back through a mic, talks get hard. Old fixes first strip the straight part of the echo. They also gauge the lag of the echo path. Their 2026 preprint drops both old steps for one neural net.

Their net learns the whole clean-up task end to end. It runs as a stream, fit for live calls. A step-wise training plan lifts its skill bit by bit. The goal is clear speech with no harsh cuts. Such nets could serve phones, meets, and smart speakers.
arxiv-2601-16874:
Fangzheng Wu and Brian Summa build a check kit for the guts of neural nets. A net's train state hides in its weights and steps. Gauges can read that state from in-house signs. Signs span slope size, faith, doubt, and margin. Their 2026 preprint treats train state as one hidden root. Each sign is then a view of that root.

The views are set next to fixed anchor marks. That set lets signs from unlike nets share one scale. An early form of the kit picked good save points. The full kit may flag bad runs while they train. It could save power and time in big model labs.
arxiv-2601-17074:
Akila Sampath, Vandana Janeja, and Jianwu Wang gauge Arctic snow depth from scarce, noisy signs. Snow depth drives ice growth and melt in the far north. Gauges there are few, and their marks are rough. Past models lean hard on those few marks. Or they skip the physics that makes marks make sense. Their 2026 preprint codes physics in an inverse model named PhysE-Inv.

The model works back from signs to depth with rules built in. Rules keep the depth calls in the true range. Sparse north data then yields more trust-worthy maps. Such maps feed climate and ship route plans.
arxiv-2601-17274:
Samar Hadou and Alejandro Ribeiro build neural networks that solve constrained optimization fast. Classic dual ascent methods solve such problems step by step. They are sound but can be slow. The authors unroll those steps into a learned network. Their frame is called constrained dual unrolling. Two coupled networks learn the two sides of the problem.

Together the networks near the saddle point of the Lagrangian. That point holds the best primal and dual values at once. Learned solvers can then answer new cases in one pass. Speed like that helps control, planning, and design tools. The work keeps the shape of a trusted method while adding learned pace.
arxiv-2601-18174:
Kazutoshi Masuda and Miho Yanagisawa build a theory for the skins of synthetic cells. Their 2026 preprint deals with lipid membranes, the soft sheets that wrap living and artificial cells. Such interfaces are basic to cell science and to soft materials. Yet a quantitative link between molecular layout and nonlinear surface mechanics has been missing. The authors set up an analytic frame for how lipid-coated synthetic cells respond when a micropipette pulls on them.
