Lipid geometry and DNA nanostructures both enter the design. Together they let a builder program how stiff or springy a cell's skin is. Programmable skins serve drug carriers and cell models alike. The frame turns guesswork into design rules.
arxiv-2601-18274:
Sicheng Shen and co-authors add a temporal module to spiking transformers. Their 2026 preprint presents TEFormer. Spiking neural networks promise energy-efficient sequence modeling, and spiking transformers are a rising design in that space. Yet they lack a principled way to fuse information across time. That gap limits how well they use spatiotemporal patterns. TEFormer adds structured bidirectional temporal enhancement, letting each moment draw on both past and future context.

Bidirectional flow suits spikes, whose meaning often depends on what follows. Better temporal fusion could close the gap with standard transformers. It would do so at a fraction of the energy cost. Efficient sequence models matter for edge devices and sensors.
arxiv-2601-18374:
Rodrigo Silva and twelve colleagues built CitiLink to make city council records easier to search and read. Council minutes tend to be long and formal, with a stiff style set by office rules. The files are open to the public, yet their form makes facts hard to find.

Reporters and local people both need to find single facts fast, such as who voted for a road plan. Long files slow that search down and can hide choices from public view. A tool that lets users search the text and jump to the right part could save hours of work. It could also help more people take part in town life. The record would no longer feel locked to staff and lawyers alone.
arxiv-2601-18774:
Jonathan Pipping-Gamón and Abraham Wyner study a trap in sports talk: the team that had the best shot to win, yet lost, is said to have blown the game. Live win odds now run with each game on air. When a team that once stood at a high mark falls to a loss, the mark is read as proof of a choke. The pair ask what mark a sound set of odds would give by chance to a team that goes on to lose.

That mark has a spread set by the odds them-selves, if the odds are right. A big blown lead may be no more than what chance gives in a fair game. The pair work out that spread for a clean kind of odds path. Their sums give fans a yard stick: past it, a loss may be a choke.
arxiv-2601-18874:
Francis Burk and five colleagues show how a known beam trick could make new bits at labs that fire a beam at a still mark. The trick makes pairs of bits and anti-bits when a beam hits the mark's cores. Those pairs could, in a set world view, spawn a light go-between bit. That bit could then die in-to a pair of hid bits that barely act at all. Such hid bits are a prized hunt in the field.

The team take one such hid bit as their case: a heavy kin of the neutrino. They work out how oft the chain would fire at mark labs, for a range of go-between weights. Their sums show mark labs have a real shot at this hunt. That is a gain: mark labs are far more cheap and swift to run than smash labs.
arxiv-2601-19074:
Dariy Guzairov, Alex Potanin, Stephen Kell, and Alwen Tiu audit the safety of two systems built on guarded memory. Memory corruption attacks have plagued software for decades. The CHERI design fights back with capabilities: pointers that carry strict bounds on where they may reach and what they may do.

The team checks CheriBSD and Morello Linux, two systems built on that design. Guards are only as good as their setup in real code, so an audit hunts for gaps between the promise and the build. What they find guides both CHERI's growth and users who bet their safety on it.
arxiv-2601-19174:
Nirhoshan Sivaroopan and eight co-authors defend language model services against sponge attacks. Such attacks feed inputs crafted to make the model burn huge compute, a form of denial of service. Old defenses lean on statistical filters, which miss attacks that read as normal text, or on fixed detectors that cannot adapt.

Their framework, SHIELD, heals itself: it adapts as attack styles shift. Agentic defense means the guard can act, not just flag. As model services grow into public infrastructure, guards that keep pace with new drains on resources become a basic need.
arxiv-2601-19374:
Bahruz Suleymanli and Kutsal Bozkurt build an exact framework for protons bouncing off nuclei below the energy barrier. Stellar reaction rates depend on such scattering, and fresh experiments have refined them. Resonances caused by impurities inside the nucleus can spike the rate at set energies.

Their Green's function formalism rests on the exact solution of the Dyson equation, with no perturbative shortcut. A non perturbative tool can capture strong resonance effects that approximations smear out. Better rates feed straight into models of how stars burn, age, and forge the elements that later build planets and people like us.
arxiv-2601-20174:
Alexander Benanti, Xi Han, and Hong Qin present NeuraLSP, a neural preconditioner for solving large sparse linear systems. Such systems arise when partial differential equations are solved on a grid, and preconditioning is what makes them tractable. Graph neural networks have shown promise here by speeding up convergence.

NeuraLSP targets the left singular subspace of the system matrix, and it is built for use with conjugate gradient methods. The authors stress both efficiency and rigor in the design. Faster solvers for these systems would speed up simulation work across engineering, physics, and other fields that rely on such equations.
arxiv-2601-20274:
Fan Lin and Xinyang Wang propose a picture of the baryon, the family that includes the proton and neutron. In this picture, a gluon knot sits at the core. In this conjecture, the knot is a topologically knotted configuration of color-magnetic monopole condensates. Quarks interact with the knot through color-electric fields of an abelian kind.

Those fields are squeezed into flux tubes by the dual Meissner effect. That squeezing leads naturally to confinement, the fact that quarks are never seen alone. The picture offers a concrete shape for the inside of a proton, and a target for tests by theory and lattice work.
arxiv-2601-20474:
José F. B. Afonso, Stefan Kirchner, and Pedro Ribeiro study charge and current fluctuations at a phase transition driven by voltage. Their setup is a workhorse of quantum transport: an interacting quantum dot joined to non-interacting metal leads. Using the random phase approximation, which is exact when the dot has many levels, they map the zero-temperature phase diagram.

The map spans interaction strength and applied bias. Fluctuations of charge and current are sharpest near the transition, so they serve as sensitive probes of it. The work speaks to nanoscale electronics, where a biased dot is both a device and a lab for non-equilibrium physics.
arxiv-2601-20774:
Steve Hanneke and Mingyue Xu find cases where extra data from sister tasks stops helping. Their 2026 paper studies the limits of adaptation in multitask learning. Multitask learning pools datasets from related source tasks. The hope is to beat what each task could achieve alone. The framework has scored tremendous successes in modern applications. The authors ask when that hope fails. Their answer draws a boundary around the method's promise.

Adaptation means bending a shared model toward one target task. If the source tasks differ too much, pooled data can mislead. The paper characterizes when transfer gains vanish. Such limits guide practitioners who must choose between pooling and going solo. Knowing a method's failure zone is as useful as knowing its strengths. The work is learning theory with direct design advice.
arxiv-2601-20874:
Mustafa Cavus and four co-authors study how anxiety and depression relate to who we are and when symptoms strike. Their 2026 paper brings a new modeling view to public mental health. It centers on the Rashomon effect. That effect notes that many models can predict almost equally well. Yet each may rest on a different internal structure. Choosing just one can mislead interpretation.

The authors use that view to read the links between symptoms and factors. The factors include demographic traits and temporal patterns. With many good models in hand, only links that recur across them deserve trust. This robust reading suits health data, where stakes are human. The paper offers officials a steadier way to see what drives distress. It also warns against over-reading any single model's story.
arxiv-2601-21074:
Erik Lentz and four co-authors reinterpret a classic signal tool as a measure of information. Their 2026 paper concerns the Wigner-Ville transform in radio-frequency signal analysis. The transform maps a signal into a joint time-frequency picture. The authors present novel interpretations of it as an information measurement tool. Its utility lies in detecting and localizing signals of interest. Those signals sit amid noisy, cluttered backgrounds.

The transform can also measure the information volume of a signal. The authors use Tsallis entropy and related functionals for that job. Such measures could help analysts rank which signals deserve attention. Radio bands are crowded and growing more so. A tool that finds and weighs information at once is valuable. The paper joins classical signal processing with information theory.
arxiv-2601-21174:
Yuanning Cui and four co-authors break a reasoning limit in models that align entities across knowledge graphs. Their 2026 paper concerns entity alignment, a critical step for knowledge graph fusion. Alignment matches the same person, place, or thing in two graphs. Existing models lack transferability. They cannot align unseen graphs without retraining. Graph foundation models promise a fix. Yet the authors find that adapting them to alignment directly remains largely ineffective.

The title names the barrier: the reasoning horizon. Models reason too shallowly to match entities in new graphs. The paper works to break through that horizon. Transferable alignment would let fused graphs grow without constant retraining. Search engines and data platforms depend on such fusion. The study diagnoses why foundation models stumble here. It then pushes their reasoning further for this task.
arxiv-2601-21274:
Shinji Tsujikawa studies how the dark energy that speeds up the cosmos might cross a key boundary. In some theories, dark energy can act stronger than a pure vacuum push. One family of theories uses a vector field whose basic symmetry is broken.

The author shows how such fields, alone or with a scalar partner, can realize the crossing. Crossing this divide has long been hard to achieve without unstable models. A clean route matters because surveys keep hinting that dark energy may not be constant. The work gives model builders a tested path to match those hints.
arxiv-2601-21574:
A measurement study reports the photon-fusion production of W boson pairs in proton collisions, using the CMS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. Two protons can graze past each other and trade photons, which then fuse into the boson pair. The data come from several years of running at high energy.

The team measures the total rate of this rare process. The result tests the standard model in a clean channel, since grazing collisions leave little debris. It also probes how photons behave inside fast protons. Rare clean events like these are sharp tools for spotting any crack in the current theory.
arxiv-2601-21674:
Ivan Biočić and Vanja Wagner study boundary value problems for nonlocal operators of spectral type. The operator is built from a function of a standard operator restricted to a bounded domain. The boundary condition here is nonhomogeneous, meaning the outside values are prescribed and nonzero.

The equation is semilinear and elliptic, set in a domain with a fairly smooth edge. Such problems model processes where long jumps, not just local spread, drive the physics. Handling nonzero outside data is essential for real use, since the world outside a region is rarely silent. The theory extends tools that were mostly built for the silent case.
arxiv-2601-21774:
M. Timmermans and a large team report two new rocky planets found hiding in existing data. The Hidden Gems project searches observations from the TESS space telescope for extra planets around low-mass stars in systems already known to host planets. Many such worlds sit below the detection limits of the standard pipelines.

The team uses a specialized pipeline called sherlock, built to find and vet faint transit signals with care. Applying it, they report two new rocky planets around nearby M dwarfs, the small red stars that are the most common in our galaxy. Extra planets in known systems help scientists see how full those systems are. And nearby rocky worlds are prime targets for later study of their atmospheres.
arxiv-2601-21974:
Collin Dabbieri and co-authors build a catalog of how quasar light changes over time. Quasars are brilliant galactic centers powered by black holes. Their broad emission lines, including the hydrogen line known as H beta, vary as conditions near the black hole change.

The team studies every quasar spectrum in a major Sloan Digital Sky Survey data release with low redshift and at least two observations. For each spectrum they decompose the light to isolate the broad H beta emission and measure its variability. Their 2026 catalog gives the community a uniform record of that behavior. Such catalogs power reverberation mapping, the technique that weighs distant black holes by watching their light echo.
arxiv-2601-22074:
Kevin Zakka and co-authors release a lightweight framework for robot learning called mjlab. Robot learning needs fast simulation, since policies improve through millions of trial actions. Heavyweight simulators with painful setup slow that loop and shut out smaller labs.

mjlab pairs GPU-accelerated simulation with composable environments and minimal setup friction. It adopts a manager-based design where users assemble modular blocks for observations, rewards, and events, and it runs on MuJoCo Warp for GPU speed. Their 2026 preprint presents the framework as open source. Lowering the cost of entry to robot learning research could widen who gets to train the next generation of capable robots.
arxiv-2601-22374:
Samyak Jain and four co-authors test whether a deep-ice detector can spot new kinds of neutrino contact. Neutrinos shift form as they fly, and matter can warp that shift. Their 2026 preprint uses DeepCore, the dense heart of the IceCube detector at the South Pole.

Odd contact terms, beyond the standard model, would leave a mark on shifts through the Earth. DeepCore watches neutrinos that have crossed the planet. The team map how well it can bound those odd terms. A clear bound, or a real mark, would test physics past the known rules.
arxiv-2601-22474:
Jian Xiong and a large team find hints of latent learning — grasp gained with no reward — inside large language models. Tolman's rats learned a maze while just wandering, then used that grasp once food appeared. Their 2026 preprint contrasts this with reward-led learning, which leans hard on outside feedback.

The team probe whether models build inner maps during unrewarded play. If they do, those maps could let models adapt fast when goals arrive. The claim links model science to a classic idea from psychology. It may reshape how agents are trained to explore.
arxiv-2601-22874:
Alessandro Pignedoli, Atreya Majumdar, and Karin Everschor-Sitte borrow an idea from swarms to solve hard search tasks cheaply. They use tiny particles that jitter with heat inside a material. Short-range attraction lets the particles help each other, like ants or birds moving as a group.

On a test landscape with a warm and cold pattern, interacting swarms find the best spot reliably. They beat lone searchers by a wide margin in the right range of group size and pull strength. The result hints at computers that optimize using physics itself.
arxiv-2601-23274:
Guantao Chen and three co-authors study edge coloring in graphs with no short cycles. Vizing and Gupta bounded the chromatic index, the number of colors needed for edges, by the maximum degree plus the maximum multiplicity. Steffen proposed a sharper bound that some graphs achieve.

The authors focus on graphs whose girth, the length of the shortest cycle, is at least five. They examine which such graphs reach Steffen's bound exactly. Edge coloring results support scheduling and network design, where edges are tasks needing distinct slots. Maximum degree and maximum multiplicity set the classical ceiling that Steffen's sharper bound tries to lower.
arxiv-2603-01674:
Boriana Chtirkova explains why near-term warming lags behind the warming a fixed climate would reach. Her 2026 analysis treats the transient response, where forcing keeps rising, against the equilibrium response for the same forcing. The gap between them is not fixed; it shifts with time and with key climate traits.

She solves a heat equation with surface feedback under forcing that rises in a straight line. At first the surface warms more slowly than its steady-state twin, then speeds up toward a parallel path. On that path, both curves rise together with a constant offset set by forcing rate and heat capacity. Reaching that path takes thousands of years, shaped in part by ocean mixing. Over the next century, the gap grows, which matters for reading near-term change.
arxiv-2603-01874:
Tailai Song, Pedro Casas, and Michela Meo catch phishing webpages with a light model that needs no outside reference lists. Their 2026 work notes that top detectors lean on cloud services and knowledge bases, which hurts scale and reproducibility. Classic deep models, meanwhile, often fail as phishing campaigns evolve.

Their system, SpecularNet, reads only a page domain name and its HTML structure. The page tree becomes a graph, and a hierarchical autoencoder passes messages level by level along it. That design captures structural habits of phishing pages while running fast on plain CPUs. Against thirteen top detectors, scores stay competitive at a tiny fraction of the compute cost. Scores on benchmarks sit just below the best reference-based rival, with per-page checks in milliseconds, and field tests catch most live phishing sites.
arxiv-2603-02574:
Rhitankar Bandyopadhyay and Diganta Mukherjee build a fairer rating system for Test cricket in this 2026 paper. The current global ranking ignores home advantage, toss effects, and scheduling gaps. Those omissions produce inconsistent team evaluations. Their framework adapts Glicko's rating model, a probabilistic system from competitive games.

Context factors enter the ratings alongside margin of victory, a marker of dominance. The enhanced model estimates expected scores more accurately on past match data. Predictive accuracy improves over the standard approach as well. Bootstrap resampling confirms the ratings stay stable under scheduling changes. Resampled schedules barely move the rankings, which supports their robustness. The authors present the system as a fairer, more consistent basis for ranking Test teams.
arxiv-2603-02874:
Georgios Pantazopoulos compares three model families at finding and reusing information inside long inputs. Transformers excel at such in-context retrieval but grow costly as inputs lengthen. State space models process inputs in linear time yet retrieve less reliably, and hybrids mix the two designs.

Two synthetic tasks test the difference: copying a short pattern that follows a query, and a two-step lookup that ends by reporting a position. Hybrids matched or beat transformers on the dense copying task and used training data more efficiently. Transformers still won the position task outright. Probing the learned signals showed state space models place nearby positions close together in their internal space, a tidy structure that explains both their strengths and their limits.
arxiv-2603-03074:
Xiaohan Peng, Wendy Mackay, and Janin Koch redesign how creative professionals steer generative AI. Design work is nonlinear and reflective, yet most AI tools force designers to type prompts or accept whole-image changes. Their 2026 workshop paper presents three systems that spread control across different moments of the process.

DesignPrompt, FusAIn, and DesignTrace let practitioners guide intent, inputs, and process itself, rather than fixing outputs afterward. The authors argue alignment is an ongoing negotiation, not a one-shot command. The AI should sometimes lead, when the designer wants inspiration, and sometimes follow, when precise craft matters. Which role fits depends on the creative stage and the designer's current need.
arxiv-2603-03474:
Shiqi Cao counts permutations that dodge two forbidden patterns at once. The patterns are partially ordered patterns, flexible templates that each stand for whole families of classical permutation patterns. Gao and Kitaev had settled many counting problems for avoiding one such pattern. Cao's 2026 paper starts the harder joint problem, for pairs drawn from the flat pattern class.

Avoiders of these pairs connect unexpectedly to the k-Fibonacci numbers, a generalization of the famous counting sequence. A bijection to certain restricted permutations then lets Cao import an established method and derive the generating function for the avoiders. For separable permutations, the paper extends single-pattern results: joint counts by six different statistics for patterns up to length five. When both patterns have length five, the generating function is rational, with a numerator of hundreds of terms.
arxiv-2603-03874:
Xueke Chen, Xinyi Zhang, and others study thermal leptogenesis in the minimal left-right symmetric model, asking whether one measured value can explain the universe's matter excess. Leptogenesis links neutrino physics to the observed baryon asymmetry, but unknown high-energy parameters usually hide the link. In this model, with general parity as the left-right symmetry, the hermitian Dirac neutrino coupling lets the right-handed mixing matrix be fixed with minimal assumptions.

The authors show that a real right-handed mixing matrix favors CP-conserving Majorana phases, leaving the Dirac CP-violating phase as the sole source of asymmetry. Exploring all four leptogenesis scenarios numerically, they find this phase alone can make the observed asymmetry with the correct sign in set parameter regions. Results depend sensitively on neutrino mass ordering and the lightest neutrino mass, making the approach testable by future measurements.

brentano-psychologie-empirischen-standpu:
Franz Brentano published his Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint at Vienna in 1874, and modern thought on the mind starts there. The text here is the German first edition, complete as issued. No English version in the public domain exists. Brentano had been a priest and a professor, and he wrote to put psychology on firm ground.

His key claim is that every mental act points at an object: we believe something, love something, judge something. That pointing, which he named intentionality, became the seed of phenomenology through his pupil Husserl. The book also shaped the study of mind in the analytic line. It stands in German as a founding record.
cairnes-leading-principles-1874:
Cairnes published Some Leading Principles of Political Economy Newly Expounded in 1874, his restatement of the classical creed. He wrote as the old Ricardian system was coming under strain and a new economics of marginal utility was gathering force. The book defends the old faith by arguing it afresh, not by merely repeating it.

Its three parts treat value, wages and profits, and trade between nations. Cairnes refines the labor theory of value and gives a famous account of how wages are set when groups of workers cannot compete freely. The writing is exact and unadorned. Historians often call the book the last great statement of the classical school, the old economics at its best just before the subject changed direction.

Early status reports set the baseline for everything filed later about these men. If the 1966 picture was wrong, later files inherited the error. Analysts therefore wrote them with unusual care on thin evidence. This item preserves that baseline for the Sam Neua pilots, the forgotten front's first prisoners.

The paper weighs how much Europe depended on that oil and what interruption would do. Months later, Iran's oil nationalization turned the study into front-page crisis. Analysts had stated the stakes in advance, in writing. This file preserves that warning, a resource study that reads like a forecast of the decade.
cia-0000010774:
By 1960, oil from the Middle East powered much of the world's economy. That October the CIA surveyed the region's petroleum in a single paper written at the height of the Cold War. Western oil companies still ran most of the fields, but the producing states were pressing for a larger share of the wealth.

The survey covers the size of the reserves, the companies that pumped the oil, and the politics around both. It treats oil as a strategic prize that shaped alliances and rivalries across the region. For readers, it lays out why control of these fields mattered so much to Washington.

The translation preserves the words while the censor's marks hide the people. Such letters were the operation's lifeline and its greatest danger at once. For readers, the page carries the tension of a case moving toward its end.

cia-0000135874: Filed on 4 October 1953, this CIA summary concerns a summary of the directives and instructions on PBSUCCESS, the orders gathered in one place. PBSUCCESS was the code name for the CIA effort to bring down President Jacobo Arbenz of Guatemala, which ended with his fall in June 1954. Read on its own terms, the record shows the operation at work in its own words, with some names still blacked out.
cia-0000136174: The open CIA files hold a cable dated 1 April 1954 that deals with a compromise, bad news about blown cover. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. The heading alone tells a reader the topic, the channel, and the moment, even where names stay deleted.
cia-0000136374: P-51s are wanted, and F-47s should then be sold to CALLIGERIS, in this June 1954 LINCOLN cable on aircraft sales and delivery. The station strongly concurs and urges every possible effort to win a favorable decision on the request and expeditious delivery of the aircraft. Supporting points note that PBSUCCESS leaders had emphatically pointed up opposition to something the transcription garbles. The cable shows the rebel air force becoming the new government's inheritance.
cia-0000137474: Central American unity has failed for a century, this January 1961 study recounts. A federal constitution was decreed in 1824. Local factionalism dissolved the federation within fourteen years. A confederation of three states failed within two years. Guatemalan opposition helped kill it. A Guatemalan strongman tried to unite the area in 1870. He failed too. The United States and Mexico sponsored a 1907 meeting in Washington. It created a Central American Court of Justice. The court functioned until 1917. The present ODECA arose from a foreign ministers' conference.
cia-0000141174: An official superior's report of injury and death, filed with the U.S. Department of Labor in March 1969, covers Juan Gonzalez Romero. The form gives his age as 22, his sex as male, and his citizenship as Cuban. His home address is listed in Miami, Florida. Most other boxes on the scan are blank or hard to read, so the paper trail stays thin.
cia-06702774: ARMY VIEWS ON THE REORGANIZATION OF THE ARMED FORCES AND ON ARMED FORCES RELAT, a CIA document. The military views. This file preserves that declassified paper. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
cia-06887974: SOUTH KOREA: PRESIDENTIAL CAMPAIGN COMMENCES, a CIA document. The Korean campaign. This file preserves that declassified paper. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
crookes-researches-phenomena-spiritualis:
Sir William Crookes, one of Britain's leading chemists and physicists, published his Researches in the Phenomena of Spiritualism in 1874. The text here follows the 1926 reprint, which adds his 1898 address and an appendix by Arthur Conan Doyle. Crookes brought lab habits into the séance room.

He reports tests on famous mediums, above all D. D. Home and Kate Fox. Under his watches and scales, tables moved, sounds came, and forms seemed to appear. Crookes would not call the force spirits, but he said the facts were real. The book still fuels debate on science and belief.
cyril-commentary-john-pusey-1874:
Cyril of Alexandria, the fifth-century patriarch, read the Gospel of John as the great proof of his teaching on Christ. His commentary covers the whole gospel in twelve books. P. E. Pusey translated the first volume in 1874, and Thomas Randell finished the work in 1885 for the Library of the Fathers.

Verse by verse, Cyril draws out the claim that the Word is true God and truly became man. He fights the Arian reading of John at every turn, and he feeds the reader moral counsel as he goes. The commentary shows the Alexandrian school at its most intense. It shaped how the Greek church read John for a thousand years.
daneau-de-veneficis-latin-1574:
Lambert Daneau, a Reformed pastor and teacher, published his Latin dialogue on witches in 1574. Its subject is the venefici, the poisoners and sorcerers once called sortilegi. Scholars count the book as the first French Protestant demonology, the work that launched the Reformed tradition of witchcraft theory.

Daneau writes in dialogue, letting questions draw out his doctrine step by step. He grounds witchcraft in Scripture and urges magistrates to act. Geneva's learned answer to the demonologists of Rome found readers across Protestant Europe. The Latin dress gave it reach among scholars everywhere. Reformed writers on witchcraft followed the path Daneau opened here.
darwin-descent-of-man-2nd-ed-1874:
Charles Darwin published The Descent of Man in 1871, and the 1874 second edition is his revised, fuller text. In it he applies his theory of evolution to human beings. He also adds a long study of sexual selection in animals and man.

Darwin argues that humans share ancestors with other animals. He points to body structure, early growth, and shared traits as proof. Sexual selection, he says, shaped traits from bird song to human looks. The book caused fierce debate and still anchors talks on human origins. He revised with care as new facts and letters arrived.
dawkins-cave-hunting-1874:
W. Boyd Dawkins, a geologist and cave explorer, published Cave Hunting in 1874. The book synthesizes the cave archaeology of his generation: what caves hold about the early inhabitants of Europe. Dawkins dug many of the sites himself, above all in Britain.

He shows human tools and bones lying with the remains of mammoth, hyena, and reindeer in cave earth. From that company he argues the great antiquity of man in Britain. Caves in France, Germany, and Belgium extend the case. The synthesis was bold for 1874 and has been much revised since. It marks the moment cave evidence became central to the human story.
draper-conflict-religion-science-1874:
John William Draper published History of the Conflict between Religion and Science in 1874. Draper, an American scientist and historian, states the conflict thesis in classic form. Science and faith, he argues, have fought through the ages, and faith's rule has stalled progress. He surveys astronomy, geology, medicine, and the theory of evolution.

Draper aimed much of his fire at the Catholic Church of his day. His history is vivid, learned, and partisan in equal measure. The book defined the science and religion debate for a century. Later historians have shown the real story to be more tangled. Even so, Draper's volume remains the thesis's arsenal and a key text.
europmc-pmc10097874:
Liu and co-workers review patient-derived xenograft models in cancer therapy in a 2023 paper. In these models, pieces of a patient's tumor are grown inside mice with weak immune systems. The grafts keep much of the original tumor's structure and variety, which makes them strong test beds for drugs.

The review covers how the models are built and checked. It describes their use in drug screening and in matching treatments to patients. It also notes limits, such as cost and slow growth. The paper helps readers judge where these models fit in cancer research.
europmc-pmc10558674:
Feng and Wang reviewed hydrogels with tuned swelling in 2023 for medical uses. A hydrogel is a water-holding gel network. Some uses need a gel that swells a lot, soaking up wound fluid and passing food and drugs. Soaking helps heal deep skin wounds and regrow tissue.

Other uses need the reverse, Feng notes. Glues for inner tissue and worn electronics must hold their size in the body. Gels that shrink can pull a wound shut with no stitches. Shrinkage can also squeeze out a stored drug on cue. The review sorts build tricks for each behaviour. It ends with the gaps that block use in clinics.
europmc-pmc10584674:
Victorelli and co-authors found in 2023 a leak from cell power units that stokes the harmful output of aged cells. Aged, or senescent, cells stop dividing and pour out swelling signals, a mix called the SASP. That mix drives tissue decline with age. Power units, the mitochondria, help steer that output.

In aged cells, a few power units spring small leaks in their outer wall. Victorelli shows that DNA escapes through those leaks into the cell body. The loose DNA trips an alarm path, cGAS-STING, which feeds the SASP mix. Two pore proteins, BAX and BAK, open the leaks. Blocking the leaks in aged mice cut swelling marks and raised health in later life.
europmc-pmc10602574:
Andrabi and co-authors reviewed nitric oxide in 2023, a gas that acts as a signal in the body. The gas widens blood vessels, carries nerve signals, and steers swelling and cell death. It fades fast, so its acts stay near the spot where it forms. That brevity limits its use as a drug given from outside.

The review explains how body enzymes make the gas from raw stock. It then sorts donor compounds that release the gas on cue. Andrabi covers ways to load donors into gels, films, and other materials. Release can be tuned to last and to hit one tissue. Uses span wound care, heart disease, and tumour work.
europmc-pmc10767974:
Abarenkov and co-authors updated UNITE in 2024, a data bank that names fungi and other eukaryotes from DNA. It centres on one gene stretch, the ITS region, used as a barcode for species. The bank holds nearly 10 million such sequences for reference. Users world-wide add notes to its records.

Sequences group into about 2.4 million species hypotheses, Abarenkov reports. Each group holds a DOI, a stable code that papers can cite without mix-ups. Users have added over 600,000 third-party notes so far. Fresh tools spot links between kingdoms, such as a fungus on a plant host. The bank also folds in unnamed groups that field work keeps finding. It acts as a digital twin of eukaryote diversity.
europmc-pmc10989974:
Shen and colleagues describe a web platform that puts clinical gene data analysis in reach of non-programmers in this 2022 paper. High-speed DNA reading now floods medical research with data, and most clinical teams hold their own gene datasets. Many proven analysis methods, though, sit unused because they demand coding skill. Older web tools cover narrow tasks or have aged badly.

Their platform, Sangerbox, bundles a wide range of analyses in one place with a click-friendly design. The authors contrast it with tools that do only one job, such as gene annotation or drug resistance notes. They built it to handle large processing loads that single-purpose sites cannot. The paper presents the platform as a full workshop rather than a single tool. Updates from their earlier versions are part of the redesign.
europmc-pmc11303474:
Jomova and colleagues lay out the layered defences that guard cells against oxidative stress in this 2024 review. Oxidative stress is harm done when reactive oxygen species, unstable oxygen molecules, build up faster than the body can clear them. It is a shared factor in cancer, heart disease, diabetes, and brain diseases such as Alzheimer and Parkinson disease.

Living things run a three-line defence, the review says. The first line is enzymes, proteins that speed chemical work. They include superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione peroxidase, which break down superoxide radicals and hydrogen peroxide. The second line is small molecules that soak up radicals directly. A third line repairs or clears damaged cell parts. The review also covers nano-sized materials, tiny man-made specks, that mimic several enzymes at once.
europmc-pmc1160574:
Barberi, Willis, Socci, and Studer derive versatile precursor cells from human embryonic stem cells in this 2005 study. Embryonic stem cells can become any cell type and open a window on the first stages of human growth. For regenerative medicine, meaning care that rebuilds tissue, labs need ways to steer them into one chosen cell family.

The authors give culture conditions that yield pure mesenchymal precursors in unlimited numbers. Mesenchymal precursors are early cells that can form fat, cartilage, bone, and skeletal muscle. Their cells did form all four types in tests, which proves the cells are true precursors. The work clarifies how the mesoderm, the embryo layer behind these tissues, is set. It also gives a platform to make specialised human cell types in bulk for future clinical use.
europmc-pmc1278474:
Srám, Binková, Dejmek, and Bobak reviewed air pollution and pregnancy outcomes in 2005. A decade of studies had probed pollution effects on births. Nearly all were population studies using routine monitoring data. Outcomes ranged from birth weight to infant deaths.

Evidence was judged strong enough for one causal claim. Particle pollution causes respiratory deaths in newborns after the first month. For low birth weight, evidence suggests causality but needs confirming. Timing of the most sensitive pregnancy window stays unclear. Preterm birth and womb growth evidence fell short of causal claims. Srám grades the record outcome by outcome.
europmc-pmc1563474:
Tiny RNA samples from needle biopsies can now be profiled in bulk. Mattie and co-authors built that method in 2006 for microRNAs, small gene regulators tied to cancer. Older methods needed far more tissue than a biopsy gives.

Their trick boosts and labels microRNAs from mere picograms, trillionths of a gram. Readings matched a standard lab method closely. In prostate biopsies, the profiles split advanced cancers from healthy tissue. In breast biopsies, they split tumor types by two key markers. Mattie shows biopsy microRNA profiles could serve as cancer biomarkers.
europmc-pmc1564174:
Shigella, a germ that causes bloody diarrhea, hits poor countries hardest. von Seidlein and co-authors tracked it across six Asian countries from 2000 to 2004, watching over 600,000 people. They caught nearly 57,000 diarrhea cases and grew Shigella from five percent.

Treated illness ran at 2.1 cases per thousand people per year. In children under five, the rate hit 13.2 per thousand. One species, S. flexneri, caused 68 percent of cases, except in Thailand. Most strains resisted two common antibiotics. A few in China, Pakistan, and Vietnam resisted ciprofloxacin, a key drug. von Seidlein shows the burden is higher than thought.
europmc-pmc1570474:
Airborne particles may travel from lung to brain and do harm there. Peters and co-authors updated the evidence in 2006, from a workshop on particle movement. Fine and ultrafine particles land on the lung's air-liquid film, are pushed by surface forces, and meet cells.

From there they can cross lung tissue into blood capillaries. Blood then carries them to the liver, spleen, kidneys, heart, and brain. Immune cells can also ferry larger particles to lymph nodes. Brain tissue from dogs and people exposed to heavy pollution shows signs of nerve decay. Peters flags the entry routes as plausible but not yet fully proven.
europmc-pmc1851974:
Alao reviewed in 2007 how the cell cycle protein cyclin D1 is destroyed, and why failed destruction feeds cancer. Cyclin D1 pushes cells from the resting G1 phase into DNA copying, partnered with enzymes CDK4 and CDK6. It also helps regulate gene activity directly, and excess cyclin D1 is tied to many cancers.

In several cancers the excess comes not from making more protein but from breaking down too little of it. The review gathers newer findings on the signals and machinery that set cyclin D1's stability. Several existing therapeutic agents turn out to force its degradation. Destroying cyclin D1 on purpose, called ablative therapy, could prevent or treat some cancers. The review closes with open questions about how cell levels of this protein are truly governed.
europmc-pmc1892574:
Pridgeon, Li and co-authors found in 2007 the first known target of a protein whose faults cause inherited Parkinson disease. The protein is PINK1, a kinase, an enzyme that tags other proteins with phosphate. No target of PINK1 was known, and how its mutations kill brain cells was a mystery.

The target is TRAP1, a chaperone that helps proteins fold inside mitochondria, the cell's power plants. PINK1 binds TRAP1 there and tags it with phosphate in both test tube and living cells. That tagging helps PINK1 stop stressed cells from releasing cytochrome c, the trigger for self-destruction. Three Parkinson-linked PINK1 mutations blunted both the tagging and the protection. The pathway gives a concrete lead on how this form of Parkinson disease begins.
europmc-pmc1952074:
Tamm, Villems and co-authors used full mitochondrial DNA sequences in 2007 to retime the peopling of the Americas. Native Americans descend from a small group of Asian founders who crossed Beringia, the land bridge region near the Bering Strait. The details of that first phase stayed murky.

The team analyzed 623 complete mitochondrial genomes from the Americas and Asia, including 27 newly sequenced ones, plus focused typing across 46 populations. The founder pool carried more diversity than earlier reports suggested. Its family tree shape indicates the founders paused in Beringia, where New World lineages split from their Asian sister lineages. A swift migration then spread those founder types south to the tip of South America. Younger gene flow ran both ways between Siberia and the North American Arctic.
europmc-pmc1964774:
Bomblies, Weigel and co-authors showed in 2007 that crossing two healthy plant strains can produce sick offspring through an autoimmune-like clash. About two percent of crosses within the species Arabidopsis thaliana yield first-generation hybrids with necrosis, dying tissue, under normal growing conditions. Such hybrid necrosis is a classic case of genes that clash only in combination.

Several independent cases traced to interactions between two loci that switch on immune-like responses in the hybrid. In at least one case, one gene variant was both necessary and sufficient to trigger necrosis. That gene belongs to the NB-LRR class of disease resistance genes, and it acted only when paired with a specific partner allele. Resistance genes evolve under pathogen pressure, so the work suggests host-pathogen conflict can accidentally split populations. The syndrome models how simple gene clashes drive broader incompatibilities.
europmc-pmc1977874:
Barton and colleagues examined pancreatic cancer in 1991 for faults in p53, a gene that normally stops cells growing out of control. When p53 is mutated, that brake can fail. The team looked for excess mutant p53 protein in exocrine pancreatic cancers, the most common type. They used special antibodies that stain the protein in tissue.

Staining found p53 in 13 of 22 frozen cancers, which is 60 percent. It also appeared in seven of 13 pancreatic cancer cell lines. One antibody, CM1, worked in stored wax-embedded tissue. It found p53 in 28 of 124 cancers there. Direct gene reading confirmed point mutations in stained samples. The authors concluded that p53 activation helps drive this cancer.
europmc-pmc2125274: A medical paper comparing autoplastic and homoplastic thyroid transplantation. The gland grafts. This article preserves that surgery. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2125374: A medical paper studying cultivation of the tubercle bacillus directly from sputum. The TB from spit. This article preserves that bacteriology. Coming generations can find it. The historical record keeps it. The paper lived through the years.
europmc-pmc2125474: Infection reshuffles the blood's proteins, and this first study tracked the serum globulins during bacterial disease. The globulin fractions shifted with illness. The blood's changing makeup, measured. The article preserves that biochemistry. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2128374: Setting tissues ablaze with chemicals was the point of this second experimental study on inflammation. Lab workers induced the reaction deliberately and watched it unfold. The provoked swelling, documented. The article preserves that pathology research.
europmc-pmc2130974: A medical paper on variations in specificity and virulence of pneumococci during growth in vitro. The changing germ. This article preserves that bacteriology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2131074: A medical paper on nuclear inclusions in the testicles of monkeys injected with human tissue. The monkey testes. This article preserves that pathology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2140874: A biology paper on temperature characteristics for speed of movement of thiobacteria. The sulfur germs' speed. This article preserves that bacteriology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2180274: A medical paper on the etiology of verruga peruana. The Peruvian wart disease. This article preserves that tropical medicine. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes.
europmc-pmc2233674:
Keyburn and co-workers discovered a new toxin in 2008 behind necrotic enteritis in chickens. The disease is caused by Clostridium perfringens and costs poultry producers over two billion dollars yearly. For thirty years an enzyme called alpha-toxin was blamed, but the team's knockout mutant proved it is not essential. They found a different toxin, NetB, in a strain from a sick chicken. It resembles pore-forming toxins from related bacteria.

NetB appeared only in type A strains from chickens with the disease. Purified and lab-made NetB both killed chicken liver cells, causing rounding and bursting. A mutant lacking the netB gene could not cause disease in chickens. Restoring the gene restored virulence. NetB is thus the first proven virulence factor for this disease, and the weakened mutant has vaccine potential.
europmc-pmc2375874:
Leigh and Milgrom mapped risk factors for depression around childbirth in 2008. About 13% of mothers face depression before or after birth, with real harm to mother and baby. The team recruited 367 pregnant women from two major hospitals and gave them a large set of standard questionnaires at 26 to 32 weeks of pregnancy.

A subgroup of 161 women answered again at 10 to 12 weeks after birth. Depression before birth was predicted by low self-esteem, anxiety, weak social support, negative thinking style, major life events, low income, and a history of abuse. Depression after birth was predicted mainly by depression before birth and any past depression. That earlier depression also carried the effect of seven other risk factors forward. In turn, postnatal depression alone predicted parenting stress, leading the authors to urge early detection and treatment.
europmc-pmc2375974:
Conesa and Götz described a software suite for plant genomics in 2008. New sequencing projects produce thousands of DNA sequences with no labels saying what they do. Blast2GO assigns those jobs, called functional annotation, by comparing each new sequence with known ones.

The suite transfers function labels from similar known sequences using a scoring method that weighs similarity, match length, database choice, and label quality. Labels come in a standard vocabulary called Gene Ontology, which sorts gene jobs into a family tree of terms. The tool then lets users view, manage, and test their label sets, including enrichment tests that spot jobs appearing more often than chance. It also supports protein domain data, enzyme codes, and pathway maps. The authors stressed easy installation and a friendly interface for plant researchers.
europmc-pmc2453774:
Naranjo and colleagues, for the QUEST-RA Group, surveyed heart disease in rheumatoid arthritis patients across 15 countries in 2008. The study enrolled 4,363 consecutive clinic patients between 2005 and 2006, recording heart events, classic risk factors, arthritis features, and drug history.

Lifetime heart or stroke events affected 9.3% of patients: 3.2% had suffered a heart attack and 1.9% a stroke. Risk factors were common, with 32% having high blood pressure, 43% having ever smoked, and 73% physically inactive. Classic factors, except obesity and inactivity, tracked heart events clearly. Arthritis spreading beyond joints also tracked heart attacks. Longer use of standard arthritis drugs linked to fewer events: methotrexate gave a hazard ratio of 0.85, leflunomide 0.59, and biologic drugs 0.42 in the adjusted models.
europmc-pmc2467474:
Zotenko, Mestre, O'Leary, and Przytycka re-examined why hub proteins tend to be essential in yeast in 2008. In protein interaction networks, hubs are proteins linked to many partners. A famous rule says hubs are usually essential, meaning the cell dies without them, but why was unclear.

The team tested six versions of the yeast protein network built by different methods. Two popular explanations failed their checks: hubs are not essential merely because they hold the network together, nor because of specially essential single interactions. Instead, most hubs belong to essential complex modules: tight clusters of proteins sharing one job and rich in essential members. A hub inside such a module is essential because the module is. The authors said topology predicts importance only through this module membership.
europmc-pmc2564974:
Ridley, Ainsworth, and Olds built a reference compendium in 2008 for the energy cost of young people's activities. Researchers scoring activity questionnaires need standard values, expressed in METs, where one MET is the energy used at rest. An adult compendium existed, but children's bodies spend energy differently, leaving youth studies to guess.

The new compendium lists more than 200 activities common among children and adolescents, each with its MET level. About 35 percent of the values come from measurements actually taken in young people. The rest were estimated by adapting the adult values. The authors intend the list for researchers and practitioners who need to convert reported activities into energy expenditure estimates for children in schools, clinics, and community settings.
europmc-pmc2629474:
Expósito-Rodríguez, Borges, Borges-Pérez, and Pérez carried out in 2008 the first careful hunt for reliable internal control genes for gene expression studies in tomato. PCR results mean little unless they are normalised against a reference gene whose level stays steady, yet tomato researchers had never validated candidates across development. The team tested eleven housekeeping genes, seven traditional and four novel, in 27 samples spanning tomato tissues and organs at different stages.

Three statistical approaches converged on the same winners. Four genes, identified as CAC, TIP41, Expressed, and SAND, gave better normalisation than the traditional controls, and were more stable. Different pairs of these genes suited different developmental series. The authors recommend specific combinations. One set covers the complete tomato development process. The toolkit gives tomato researchers vetted controls for measuring transcripts.
europmc-pmc2644974:
Gao and Xing reviewed in 2009 how weak laser light can make cells divide faster, an effect used in clinics to aid healing. Red and near-infrared light at low power does not heat tissue, yet many cell types grow more after treatment. The review pulls together work on the signals inside the cell that drive this growth.

A key first step sits in the mitochondria, the cell's energy makers, whose activity the light boosts. From there, signal chains switch on, including paths named Ras/Raf/MEK/ERK and PI3K/Akt, which push cells through their division cycle. A growth receptor called c-Met is also switched on, while another receptor, for TNF-alpha, is not. Treated cells release more growth factors and signal molecules as well, spreading the effect to neighbors.
europmc-pmc2648874:
Bennett and a large team updated in 2009 the standard list of gene changes used to track drug-resistant HIV passed from person to person. Health programs count this transmitted resistance to check whether treatment and prevention work. To compare counts fairly across places and years, everyone must count the same gene changes.

The World Health Organization had backed such a shared list, first built in 2007 with 80 changes. Since then, new drugs had reached clinics and new resistance changes had come to light. Following the same rules as before, the team rebuilt the list. It now holds 93 changes in the two viral genes that HIV drugs target. The groups cover the three main drug families used against the virus. Programs worldwide can now measure spread on the same footing.
europmc-pmc2686174:
Brinkhof, Pujades-Rodriguez, and Egger pooled in 2009 what happens to HIV patients who vanish from treatment programs in poor countries. Clinics lose many patients to follow-up, and their fate was a blank spot in judging whether programs work. The team found seventeen studies, nearly all from sub-Saharan Africa, that had traced lost patients by phone, home visit, or word of mouth.

Of 6,420 lost patients, trackers learned the fate of about 63 percent. Among those, two in five had died. Death rates varied hugely, from 12 to 87 percent across programs in Africa. Curiously, programs that lost the most patients showed the lowest death rates among the lost, suggesting many silent transfers to other clinics hide in the numbers. Ignoring the lost, the authors warn, badly flatters a program's results.
europmc-pmc2688074:
Wagner and co-authors compared gene activity in 2009 between human stem cells from young and old donors. They asked whether body aging mirrors the wearing out of cells in a dish. They sampled bone marrow stem cells from donors aged 21 to 92, and blood-forming progenitors from donors up to 73.

Both cell types changed with age, but in largely different ways: a few hundred genes rose or fell in each. The surprise was the overlap with dish aging. Many genes that shifted with donor age also shifted when marrow stem cells aged by dividing repeatedly in culture. The fading genes clustered in guarding the genome and in controlling gene reading. Telomeres, the chromosome caps blamed for dish aging, did not shrink convincingly with age in the blood progenitors. Body aging, the authors say, shares real machinery with replicative senescence, the dish process, without being the same thing.
europmc-pmc2702274:
Mariat and colleagues measured in 2009 how the balance of gut bacteria shifts across a human lifetime, comparing infants, adults, and the elderly. The gut community feeds and protects its host. Most of its members refuse to grow in lab dishes. So the team counted major groups directly from stool DNA, using a quantitative gene method.

Infants carried fewer bacteria overall, with two Clostridium groups oddly dominant. Adults carried the richest, most balanced mix. The elderly tilted toward E. coli and the Bacteroidetes phylum. The headline measure was the ratio of the two great phyla, Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes. It swung from 0.4 in infants, up to 10.9 in adults, and back down to 0.6 in the elderly. The gut community, the authors conclude, is not set in childhood: it matures, peaks, and remodels again in old age.
europmc-pmc2733374:
Knoepfler examined in 2009 why stem cells so readily form tumors. He focused on embryonic stem cells and their risk for regenerative medicine. The earliest stem cell work used embryonic carcinoma cells from tumors. Those cells share with embryonic stem cells the power to become many cell types. Both also form teratomas, tumors with mixed tissues, with ease.

Decades later, what drives that tumor formation is still largely open. Induced pluripotent stem cells may carry equal or greater risk. These are adult cells reset to an embryonic state. Knoepfler explores links between pluripotency and tumor growth. He proposes sharper tests of tumor risk for cell batches. He also highlights new ways to purge or control risky cells before therapy.
europmc-pmc2775274:
Zhu, Smith, and Huang reviewed in 2010 mass spectrometry-based label-free quantitative proteomics, methods that compare protein amounts across samples without chemical tags. Studying how protein levels change in complex mixtures needs fast, reproducible, and accurate measurement. Labeling with isotopes or fluorescent dyes works, but many researchers now prefer label-free shotgun approaches for simpler, cleaner workflows.

The review sorts label-free methods into two families. One measures chromatographic ion intensity, such as peptide peak areas or heights. The other counts spectra matched to each protein, more matches meaning more protein. They discuss the technologies behind both, the statistics used to judge real changes, and the software available. Applications in complex proteomics studies round out the survey. Their aim is a practical map for researchers choosing how to quantify proteins without labels.
europmc-pmc2791174:
Pogosyan and co-authors asked whether beta waves in the motor cortex merely accompany movement or actually shape it. Beta activity runs at about twenty cycles per second, grows while a muscle hold stays steady, and fades when a new movement starts. Their 2009 study used weak electric stimulation through the scalp in fourteen healthy volunteers.

The stimulation, too faint to feel, boosted cortical activity at the beta frequency while people moved a joystick to chase a jumping target. Movements grew slower under the boost than without it. That direct effect marks the first causal proof linking a natural brain rhythm to behavior, and it may help explain the slowness seen in Parkinson disease.
europmc-pmc2809074:
Wetterslev, Thorlund, Brok, and Gluud tackled a sizing problem in 2009 for meta-analyses, the studies that pool many trials into one result. Just like a single trial, a pooled study needs enough total patients before its answer can be trusted, a target called the required information size.

When trials disagree with each other, that target grows, and the usual gauge of disagreement can set it too low. The authors derived a new measure, called diversity, that captures the share of total variation coming from differences between trials. They proved with math and test examples that diversity is always at least as large as the older gauge, so sizing by diversity guards better against chance findings.
europmc-pmc2811174:
Alirol, Sharma, Bawaskar, Kuch, and Chappuis reviewed snake bite across South Asia in 2010, calling it one of the most neglected health problems of poor rural tropics. The region carries the world's heaviest bite burden, thanks to dense farm populations, many venomous species, and weak control programs.

India alone loses an estimated thirty-five to fifty thousand people a year to snake bite, the review reports. Victims often lose vital hours to home remedies and long trips, and care at clinics suffers from untrained staff and antivenoms that miss some local species. No field test names the biting snake, so treatment leans on antivenom alone. The authors call for joint work by researchers, makers, and funders.
europmc-pmc2826374:
Shaman, Pitzer, Viboud, Grenfell, and Lipsitch showed in 2010 that dry air explains when winter flu epidemics start across the continental United States. Lab work had already shown flu virus survives longer and spreads better between guinea pigs as air dries. The team tested whether real epidemic timing follows the same rule.

They matched thirty years of epidemic onset dates against humidity records for the same places. Drops in absolute humidity, the actual water content of air, lined up with outbreak starts across states. A transmission model driven only by humidity reproduced the timing and geography of real epidemics. The result names a physical driver behind flu's winter season in temperate lands.
europmc-pmc2832674:
McGuffee and Elcock built an atom-level computer model in 2010 of the inside of an E. coli bacterium, to test whether molecules act the same in a crowded cell as in a clean test tube. Their model packs fifty of the most abundant molecule types at real measured levels, over a thousand molecules in all.

Simulations of jostling motion were tuned until a test protein wandered at the speed seen in living cells. The model then matched measured stabilities of proteins folding and pairing inside E. coli. Simple crowding, the sheer lack of free space, could not explain the match alone. Extra effects from the cell soup itself had to be included, the authors show.
europmc-pmc2872874:
Young, Wakefield, Smyth, and Oshlack fixed in 2010 a hidden flaw that skewed a standard analysis of RNA sequencing studies. After finding which genes change activity, researchers group them by function using gene ontology, a catalog of gene jobs. Longer genes collect more sequencing reads by chance, so standard grouping favors long-gene functions and distorts the answer.

Their method, called GOseq, models each gene's chance of being picked as a function of its length and corrects for it. Without the fix, harmless categories like nerve signaling can look falsely involved in almost any experiment. With it, the enriched functions reflect the biology under study rather than gene size. GOseq became a standard option in the main software pipelines for this kind of analysis.
europmc-pmc2887474:
Zaragoza and co-authors reported in 2010 that a pathogenic yeast grows into giant cells inside infected lungs. The yeast, Cryptococcus neoformans, normally stays round and small and was not thought to change form like other fungi. In mice, though, a share of the lung population ballooned to several times the usual size, wrapped in extra-thick capsules.

Giants made up anywhere from a tenth to four fifths of the lung burden depending on timing and on each mouse's immune response. Their capsules resisted stripping even by radiation and solvents. Returned to growth medium, a giant budded off normal small daughters that pushed out through the mother's capsule. Starved lab cultures eventually produced similar giants, linking the form to harsh conditions rather than host signals alone.
europmc-pmc2898074:
Faghihi and co-authors found in 2010 that a natural mirror-image RNA can shield a key Alzheimer's gene from being silenced. The gene, BACE1, makes an enzyme that starts production of the amyloid protein that clumps in Alzheimer's brains. Its antisense partner, an RNA copied from the opposite DNA strand, rises in patient brains and steadies the gene's message.

The team showed the antisense RNA works partly by covering a landing site used by a microRNA, miR-485-5p, which would otherwise repress the gene. The two RNAs compete for the same stretch of the message, and extra antisense lifted BACE1 protein levels in cells. Both RNAs are off-balance in Alzheimer's brain samples. A three-way RNA contest at one binding site emerges as a new control layer in the disease.
europmc-pmc2975074:
Aldana-Masangkay and Sakamoto reviewed HDAC6, an enzyme that removes chemical tags from proteins, as a cancer target in a 2011 article. Unlike relatives, its main target is a structural protein of the cell skeleton rather than DNA packaging proteins.

Extra HDAC6 appears in many tumours and tracks with spread and survival patterns, making it both a marker and a suspect. Blocking it killed blood cancer cells in earlier work. The enzyme also switches on heat shock defences, steadies a major chaperone, and helps cancer cells move. The review gathers these threads into a case for selective drugs.
europmc-pmc3013074:
Zhou led a large team that profiled both ordinary gene messages and tiny regulatory RNAs in clear cell kidney cancer using deep sequencing in a 2010 study. The most common kidney cancer type needed a fuller molecular census.

Comparing tumours with matched healthy tissue from ten patients, they found hundreds of small RNAs. Nearly ten thousand genes showed different activity levels. Dozens of brand-new small RNA candidates also turned up. Checks in a larger patient group spotlighted a small RNA cluster on the X chromosome whose level tracked with the cancer. Pathways governing cell fate and cell contact were broadly disturbed.
europmc-pmc3087974:
Broadhead, Clark, Myers, Dass, and Choong reviewed in 2011 the molecular roots of osteosarcoma, the most common primary bone cancer. It strikes mainly teenagers and young adults during spurts of rapid bone growth. Survival has sat at roughly two thirds of patients for decades, stuck since combination chemotherapy arrived, because care still rests on anatomy rather than on the cancer's inner workings.

The review maps the gene faults and signaling breakdowns that drive these tumors to form and spread. As those mechanisms come into focus, each offers a possible drug target tailored to the tumor instead of blanket chemotherapy. The authors survey the most advanced attempts to turn that knowledge into safer, targeted treatments. Their message is that real gains in survival now depend on molecular understanding catching up with surgical skill.
europmc-pmc3131274:
Alejandro Sarrion-Perdigones and colleagues presented a modular DNA assembly system for plant engineering in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Building new genetic circuits needs standard parts joined in order, again and again, without starting over each time. Their system uses cutting enzymes that leave parts ready to combine in pairs, like links in a braid.

Four carrier plasmids accept standard parts and then pair up into larger assemblies, which can pair again without limit, so complexity grows step by step. Parts stay reusable at every level. The team adapted the carriers for delivering genes into plants and built several multi-part constructs, including two modules of five devices each from nineteen basic parts. They propose the system as a shared standard for plant synthetic biology.
europmc-pmc3146474:
Aaron Gassmann and colleagues reported the first field case of a corn pest beating an engineered crop toxin in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Maize bred to make a bacterial toxin kills rootworm beetle larvae and covers millions of hectares, cutting spray use. Farmers in some fields, though, reported severe root damage on the protected maize.

Rootworms from damaged fields survived the toxin maize far better in lab tests than worms from undamaged fields. Every damaged field had grown the same toxin maize for at least three straight years, and longer use matched stronger survival. The worms still fell to a second toxin, so no cross-resistance had formed. Too few refuge plantings and partly dominant resistance likely sped the change, the authors warn.
europmc-pmc3153174:
Ronald Miller and colleagues reviewed how a leading cancer drug damages kidneys in a 2010 paper in Toxins. The platinum drug cures or controls many cancers of the head, lung, ovary, and testis, but kidney injury limits how much can be given. A decade of work had uncovered much of the cell-level story, which the review gathers.

The drug enters kidney tubule cells and triggers several death routes at once, while injured cells spark inflammation that deepens the damage. Acute kidney injury strikes a sizable share of patients. Understanding the chain, from drug uptake to cell death signals to immune amplification, points to targeted shields that might protect kidneys without weakening the drug's attack on tumours.
europmc-pmc3198674:
Chantal Loirat and Véronique Frémeaux-Bacchi wrote this 2011 review of atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome for the Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases. The condition is defined by mechanical destruction of red blood cells, low platelets, and kidney failure. Unlike the typical form, it is not caused by Shiga toxin, but by faulty control of the complement system, part of the immune system.

The review covers the genes involved, including factor H, factor I, and membrane cofactor protein, plus antibodies against factor H found in some patients. It explains how doctors rule out look-alike conditions, why relapse and kidney failure are common, and how outlook differs by gene. Plasma treatment was the standard, and the complement-blocking drug eculizumab looked highly promising.
europmc-pmc3231874:
Adele D'Amico and colleagues summarized spinal muscular atrophy in this 2011 review in the Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases. The inherited disease kills the motor neurons of the spinal cord, causing progressive weakness and paralysis that is worst in the muscles closest to the trunk. It appears in roughly one in six thousand to one in ten thousand births.

Severity falls into four types based on age of onset and the motor milestones a child reaches. The cause is loss of both copies of the SMN1 gene, and a genetic test detecting the missing piece confirms most cases with high accuracy. The review covers how the disease is distinguished from look-alikes, carrier and prenatal testing for families, and the coordinated care, spanning breathing, nutrition, and bone health, that patients need. Outlook depends heavily on type.
europmc-pmc3326674:
Pinato, North, and Sharma built a simple survival score for liver cancer from two routine blood values, reporting in 2012. Growing evidence shows that whole body inflammation predicts poor outcomes across cancers, whatever the stage. Their score combines albumin, a nutrition linked protein, with the count of lymphocytes, a type of immune cell, both measured when patients first arrive.

Patients whose combined value fell below the cutoff had a poor score and died sooner, in a group of more than one hundred patients treated in London over two decades. The score predicted survival even after accounting for tumor spread, clots in the liver's vein, and standard staging. It held up again in a separate matched group of patients from another setting. The authors offer the score as a cheap, validated way to flag high risk liver cancer patients.
europmc-pmc3346774:
Crouse and a large Canadian team measured death risk from long term exposure to fine air pollution particles, in a 2012 study. Such particles, small enough to lodge deep in the lungs, have been tied to heart deaths in other countries, often at higher pollution levels than Canada's. This was the first national level study of its kind in Canada, following two point one million adults who filled detailed census forms in 1991.

Exposure estimates came from satellite readings matched to home addresses, and deaths were tracked through 2001. Each standard step up in particle levels came with a clearly higher risk of death overall and a still higher risk of death from ischemic heart disease. The pattern held when checked against ground monitors in eleven cities. The authors stress that harm appeared even at the low concentrations typical of Canada.
europmc-pmc3386974:
Mirelman and colleagues followed older adults for five years in 2012 to see whether thinking skills predict falls. Executive function, the mental skill for planning and focus, helps control walking when conditions get tricky. The study enrolled over two hundred fifty healthy, mobile, community-living seniors and tested their cognition and gait at the start.

Monthly fall calendars then recorded who fell. Weaker executive function and attention scores at baseline meant more falls ahead, even after accounting for age, sex, and past falls. Walking while doing a second task also flagged risk through uneven stride timing. Seniors with the lowest scores fell sooner and more often, arguing for thinking tests in fall screening.
europmc-pmc3410874:
Köser and colleagues argued in 2012 that whole genome sequencing of microbes is ready to enter routine diagnostic and public health labs. Sequencing a bacterial genome had fallen to a modest cost and was speeding from weeks toward hours. The article takes a practical view: where would sequencing pay for itself against today's methods first?

Two uses lead their list. Tracking outbreaks and watching germ spread through genome-based epidemiology is one; the other is reading drug resistance from DNA for germs that grow poorly in culture. Both need new technical setups and trained staff, which the authors detail using England's system as the example. They call the shift the biggest advance in the field since growing germs in dishes.
europmc-pmc3463874:
Leshner and co-workers studied an enzyme called PAD4 in a 2012 paper in Frontiers in Immunology. PAD4 changes histones, the proteins that pack DNA, and earlier work had tied it to the web-like traps that white blood cells cast out to catch bacteria. The team asked what heavy use of this enzyme does to packed chromatin in cultured cells.

Raising PAD4 levels in bone tumor cells made their chromatin loosen and spread widely, without the cells dying. The loose chromatin was even released outside the cells, much like the traps white blood cells form. Leshner's group also showed the change can push a key packing protein off the DNA. The findings help explain how these traps form in the body.

frus-1861-d174:
On 8 August 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Carl Schurz with orders stressing calm and law. The letter is document 174 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's August orders to Madrid stress calm and law over bluster. Spain must see a Union that could lose a battle and keep its course. The letter guided Schurz through the court's new doubts in the weeks after Bull Run. Calm and law, after Bull Run, became the twin themes of Seward's whole foreign line. Twin themes of calm and law run from his Madrid letters through the whole file.
frus-1861-d274:
A dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Mr. Morris on 28 August 1861. It was printed as Document 274 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The letter comes from the first summer of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d74:
On 30 August 1861, Charles Francis Adams sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a calm end of summer report. The dispatch is document 74 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

As summer ended, the question in London was whether the war would spread or stall. Adams's reports avoided drama and stuck to fact. That plain style won him trust at home and respect abroad. His end of August letter is one more brick in that wall of trust. Trust, once won in this service, was a form of power no fleet could match. Trust of that kind cannot be bought, and Seward spent it with great care.
frus-1862-d174:
A report dated 23 October 1862 from Charles Francis Adams in London reached Secretary of State William H. Seward as part of the file printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume, where it is Document 174.

By the last week of October, Adams could watch France pressing London to act jointly on the American war. His job was to make joint action look needless and risky to British ministers. Reports like this one carried his account of that effort home, where Seward weighed it against news from Paris and the battlefronts alike. Union consuls in British ports fed the legation word of ships fitting out for the South.
frus-1862-d274:
Document 274, dated 2 May 1862, is a general instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to all the diplomatic and consular agents of the United States abroad. It was printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume within the French papers.

A general instruction went to every post at once, setting one line for the whole foreign service. Consuls in small ports and ministers in great capitals alike worked from it. Placed among the Paris papers, this one shows the Department speaking past Dayton to its entire network. It came in a week when Union arms were winning on several fronts.
frus-1862-d374:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, wrote to Viscount Treilhard on 20 August 1862. In a letter printed as Document 374 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The catalog title carries a stray comma after Treilhard's name.

By 20 August the armies were converging on Manassas for the second Bull Run battle, fought nine days later. Treilhard's business with the Department ran on through the crisis weeks without pause. A letter from this date belongs to the file's steady middle stretch, before the September battles changed the setting for every foreign channel in Washington. Mercier had served in Washington since 1860 and knew the capital's politics at close range.
frus-1862-d474:
A second instruction of the same date, 9 July 1862, went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to James E. Harvey in Lisbon. It is Document 474 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed beside its companion.

Two orders on one day usually meant two separate subjects, each kept in its own letter as the Department's practice required. For Lisbon in 1862 the standing subjects were neutral-port rules, Confederate attempts to use Portuguese waters, and the safety of American trade. Harvey needed clear lines on all of them. Paired with the previous document, this instruction shows how the paperwork of neutrality was built: one question, one letter, one clear answer from Washington.
frus-1862-d574:
A second instruction of 12 December 1861 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to James Watson Webb in Rio de Janeiro. It stands as Document 574 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, beside its same-day companion.

Paired orders meant paired subjects, kept separate by the Department's one-question practice. For Brazil in that December the questions were wide. They ran from the treatment of belligerent ships in Brazilian ports to the presentation of the Union's cause. That cause had to be put across South America. Webb, a forceful personality, was not a man to leave instructions unexecuted.
