The two letters together give the reader the whole of Washington's December brief for its most distant major post in the Americas.
frus-1862-d674:
Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this letter to Anson Burlingame on 2 April 1862. Burlingame was the American minister to China, half a world from Washington. The letter stands as document 674 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Orders sent to China had to be broad, since months passed before an answer could come back. Seward's letters therefore set aims and limits, then trusted the envoy on the spot. This one falls in the spring run of the China file, between Burlingame's reports of March and May. It shows the trust, and the strain, built into running foreign ties by sail and steamer.
frus-1862-d74:
A dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 31 May 1862. It was printed as Document 74 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. By then, in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1863p1-d174:
April closed at the London legation with this dispatch from Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 30 April 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 174 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It is the last of the run in this part of the file.

Adams closed April with a report from the post he had made the Union's shield in Europe. His spring mail had charted Britain's turn on the ships and the slow fade of the South's hopes there. This dispatch is a fitting tail to the run: one more cool, exact sheet from London. The file goes on past it, but the spring's story is whole in these pages.
frus-1863p1-d274:
A dispatch dated 27 August 1863 carried news from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It is document 274 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

The CSS Alabama, built in a British yard, had escaped to sea in 1862 and was burning Union merchant ships. London's handling of such ships hung over every report Adams sent home. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d374:
One entry in the running Washington exchange, this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, is dated 28 January 1863. It stands as document 374 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

After the Emancipation Proclamation in January 1863, Seward could frame the war as a fight against slavery. That put Britain, which had banned slavery at home, in an awkward spot when it aided the South. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d474:
Under the date 23 April 1863, the record holds a letter from Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d574:
Document 574, dated 19 June 1863, records a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d674:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 23 November 1863 letter from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d74:
From the London legation on 6 February 1863, Charles Francis Adams sent dispatch number 316 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 74 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

In it, Adams sent Washington a copy of the Queen's speech at the opening of Parliament the day before. The speech said Britain's ties with foreign powers stayed warm. It said the Queen had held back from any step to stop the fight in North America. For Seward, that was the news that counted: Britain would not step in. The letter is a small hinge in the file, proof on paper of British calm.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d174: Roosevelt wrote to Secretary Hull on October 30, 1943, in a letter placed in the Moscow section as Document 174 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Three presidential letters or drafts to Hull share that closing date in this volume, counting the main sequence and this section together. The record for this one gives the parties and the date only. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d274:
A memorandum of conversation dated 26 November 1943, kept secret, records John Winant and an unnamed American colleague talking with British foreign secretary Anthony Eden about the European Advisory Commission. The body, set up at the Moscow conference, was meant to handle questions arising as the war in Europe ended.

The Americans worry that too much post-hostility planning has been handed to a London body at the start, which could stall real work and sour American opinion. Eden pushes back, calling the commission an achievement backed by Secretary Hull, and warns against seeming to slight it before the Soviets. The meeting settles on a working path: commission proposals would pass through the Combined Chiefs of Staff for comment before going to the governments.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d374:
Minutes kept for the Combined Chiefs of Staff record the same plenary session at Tehran on 30 November 1943 at four in the afternoon, in the staff version paralleling the Bohlen minutes. The decisions and pledges are the same, set down for the military record.

Brooke reads the staff conclusions: Overlord in May 1944, plus a supporting operation against the south of France at the largest scale the landing craft of the time permit. Churchill promises to keep Stalin and the Soviet staff informed as the circle closes on Germany, and hopes Yugoslav resistance and a Turkish entry will add pressure. Stalin repeats his undertaking to mount a large-scale offensive in May to contain the most German divisions possible in the east. Roosevelt closes the military business by promising the supreme commander's appointment within days of reaching Cairo.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d474:
Two days after the Tehran Conference ended, on December 3, 1943, President Roosevelt wrote to Marshal Stalin. The two leaders had met face to face for the first time at Tehran, where they agreed on the broad course of the war. The State Department printed this follow-up message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Roosevelt treated his direct line to Stalin as a key tool of the alliance, and the days right after Tehran were full of loose ends to tie off. A message from this moment shows the President working to keep the new personal relationship warm. It forms part of the famous Roosevelt-Stalin correspondence that ran through the war.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d574:
The Secretary of State wrote to the President on September 3, 1945. That was the day after Japan's formal surrender. The surrender took place aboard the Missouri. James F. Byrnes then led the department under President Truman. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

A secretary's letter on the first day of peace belongs to a great transition. Armies had to be brought home. Settlements had to be negotiated. Pledges made at Tehran and Cairo had to be honored or revised. For readers, the message closes the volume's war story. It also opens the aftermath. The department was turning from coalition warfare to a divided peace.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d74: Hull wrote to Roosevelt again on October 30, 1943, the day after the Moscow Conference ended. The letter is Document 74 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Four letters from the president to Hull, or drafts of them, share the same date in this volume, which shows the day's weight. The record for this item gives the parties and the date. Its contents rest in the printed Foreign Relations text.
frus-1944-quebec-d174:
Another luncheon at Quebec left no official record, and the editors again rely on Mackenzie King's notes. The conversation ranged widely: the Soviet position toward Japan after the European war, conditions in India, the instability of French governments, and the United States Constitution all came up. So did the race problem in South Africa and the entry of troops into Berlin and Vienna.

De Gaulle, a possible civil war in France, and China also figured in the talk. After luncheon, the party moved to the conference room at the Citadel. There Churchill demonstrated models of the ships and equipment used to form the artificial harbors for the invasion of France. The note preserves the texture of a working lunch at the summit.
frus-1944-quebec-d274:
The Japan section of the draft final report, C.C.S. 680 of September 14, 1944, states the agreed objective and the operations accepted for planning. Japan's unconditional surrender would be forced by blockade, bombardment, and destruction of her air and naval strength, then by invading her industrial heart. Plans were to stay flexible and exploit naval and air superiority, avoiding costly land campaigns where possible.

The schedule runs from Talaud in October 1944 to the Tokyo Plain in December 1945, by way of Leyte and either Formosa or Luzon. Very-long-range bombers would strike Japan from China and the Marianas. The report also records agreement that the British Fleet should join the main operations, balanced and self-supporting.
frus-1944-quebec-d74:
Assistant Secretary of War John J. McCloy wrote on August 28, 1944. His recipient was H. Freeman Matthews, a senior European affairs official. The State Department printed the letter in its Quebec 1944 volume. McCloy often linked the War Department with the diplomats.

War and State officials had to align their views on Europe. The Quebec Conference opened two weeks later in Canada. Leaders there faced the treatment of a defeated Germany. For readers, the letter shows that alignment being built at staff level. Senior aides exchanged views before any summit could decide policy.
frus-1945-50-intel-d174:
Minutes record the Ninth Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board on 31 October 1946. It survives in print as document 174 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. The National Intelligence Authority, set up in January 1946, oversaw the Director of Central Intelligence and his Central Intelligence Group.

As minutes, the text sticks to the business of the meeting: items raised, views stated in brief, and the choices the group reached. The brevity is the point: what the group did not settle, the minutes do not claim it did. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d274: The title "Draft Report by the National Security Council" heads a text dated 12 May 1948. It stands as document 274 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. With the Soviet threat in mind, the Council was deciding what secret work the United States should do abroad. A report differs from a memo: it surveys a subject, weighs the facts, and offers findings that others must answer.
frus-1945-50-intel-d374:
A memorandum dated 17 March 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was the Acting Director of the Policy Planning Staff (Butler). The reader was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Armstrong). The State Department prints it as document 374 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The CIA was settling into its shape, while the Dulles Report's advice worked its way through office after office.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d74:
Acting Secretary Acheson wrote to McCormack, the special assistant for research and intelligence, on 1 October 1945. McCormack's office had just received the research branch of the dissolved OSS. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

The acting secretary wrote directly to the new intelligence chief. That shows the office's standing in its first days. It was high enough to draw the top's attention, yet new enough to need shaping. Acheson's hand in these papers is worth watching, since he would later, as secretary, oversee the office's fate. Readers meet here the start of the State Department's brief season as the home of American intelligence analysis.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d174:
Ambassador Richard Patterson sent Washington the Tito–Subasic agreements on 16 December 1944. Writing from London, where the Yugoslav exile government sat, he reports that Premier Subasic handed him translations of the texts that day. His despatch is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Four papers are enclosed. First comes the main agreement of 1 November 1944 between Subasic and Marshal Tito. Two supplemental agreements of 7 December follow. One covers elections for a constituent assembly and the ordering of public powers. The other treats the King's property and a regency council. A communiqué of the same date completes the set. Patterson warns that the wording is far from precise in places, and leaves wide room for differing readings.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d274:
Moscow named its negotiators on prisoners on 29 December 1944. Harriman's short confidential cable to the Secretary of State, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, reports a letter from Deputy Commissar Vyshinsky. It follows Molotov's note on two-way repatriation of the month before.

Lieutenant General K. D. Golubev and Major General N. V. Slavin, Vyshinsky writes, have been appointed by the Soviet government. They will conduct negotiations with General Deane. The subject is the plan to repatriate, each to his own country, American and Soviet prisoners of war and civilians. The principles are those set out in Molotov's letter to Kennan of 25 November. The appointments move the prisoner question from letters to a working table in Moscow.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d374:
Matthews's record of the February 7, 1945 plenary opens with Roosevelt on Poland. The President said he had nothing special to add to the day before. Finding a solution to the governmental question mattered most to him. Frontiers concerned him less. Continuity concerned him less still.

There had not really been any Polish government since 1939, he said. It fell to the three powers to help set up something new, to last until the Polish people could choose. He called for something drastic, like a breath of fresh air. Then he asked Molotov to report the foreign ministers' meeting. Matthews gives the same session as Bohlen, in a blunter voice.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d474:
A Polish prime minister's plea reached Yalta by hand and by wire in this cable from Ambassador Winant, sent February 3, 1945. The Polish Foreign Office in London had delivered a letter from Prime Minister Arciszewski to the President, asking that it be telegraphed urgently. Schoenfeld forwarded it from London. At this time, Arciszewski wrote, the fate of many nations rests in your hands.

The whole world, he said, expected the talks to lay foundations for a future peace. That peace should bring freedom of conscience and speech, and freedom from fear and want. He trusted those freedoms would also be granted to Poland, fighting since the first day of the war. The letter arrived as the leaders settled Poland without the Poles.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d74:
Voting procedure in the Security Council is the whole subject of this 15 November 1944 memorandum to the President. Acting Secretary Stettinius lays out where each great power stood after Dumbarton Oaks. The paper belongs to the set prepared for a White House meeting and printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Three issues are in dispute: the size of the majority, whether permanent members must agree, and whether a member involved in a dispute may vote. The Russians wanted a simple majority but a veto that applied even to parties in a dispute. The British and Chinese wanted a two-thirds majority and no vote for disputing parties. The American delegation, by the President's instructions, stood close to the British.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d174:
General Deane predicted the Soviet staff's shopping list in a telegram to General Marshall on June 29, 1945. The message is document 174 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Deane had asked General Antonov what the Russians would want to discuss with the American chiefs at the conference.

Pending Antonov's reply, Deane expects the Soviets to raise Pacific convoys once they enter the war. He also expects heavy bombers. He expects Atlantic lend-lease shipments if the Pacific route closes. And he expects goods thus far refused, from A-26 aircraft to canned meats and uniform cloth. They will also want the American strategic plans. The Americans, he says, should raise joint estimates on Japan, liaison once fighting starts, repairs for U.S. ships in Soviet ports, and emergency use of Soviet airfields. He urges decisions in advance on how much to disclose.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d274:
A briefing paper listed the Austrian economic questions Washington should raise, in an undated paper printed as document 274 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. The paper assumes Austria will be treated as one economy, since no occupying power wants her partitioned and any recognized Austrian government will insist on it.

Two questions lead. The first is financing Austria's imports, to be solved on the same lines as Germany's. The second is payment for Austrian exports: goods should not in general be taken from Austria without payment, the proceeds going against her imports. Two exceptions apply: return of identifiable looted property, and plant built in Austria after the Anschluss for Germany's war effort, which might count toward German reparations. The paper warns against the Soviet claim that all German property in Austria is reparations loot.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d374:
Pauley's letter to Maisky of July 11, 1945, presses for settlement before both men leave for Berlin. Pauley means to depart with a few of his staff for the Big Three meeting. The matters in his July 3 letter, he writes, urgently need resolving, so the heads of government can give final decisions.

He lists the state of each question. The percentage formula for dividing reparations among the three governments is thoroughly discussed and near agreement. The rules for fixing other claimants' shares are also near agreement. A definition of restitution has been agreed, and he encloses his proposed definition of war booty. The letter is a negotiator clearing his desk for the summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d474:
Troop distribution in Italy is recommended in a memorandum Kirk relays from Rome on June 20, 1945. Rear Admiral Stone, chief commissioner of the Allied Commission, had sent his recommendations on redeployment to Field Marshal Alexander. First, Stone argues, the question must be examined with external and internal security in mind.

The allied governments, he adds, have an undoubted duty to ensure, so far as possible, that free elections are held. Italians must be able to express their opinion, without fear, on the institutional question and on the constitutional government of the country. He turns next to the size and location of Italian land forces, and to a proposed interim Italian army of 140,000 men.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d574:
A top secret briefing paper extract dated June 29, 1945, deals with Japan's surrender and the Far East. It is document 574 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The part printed here sets out U.S. policy toward liberated areas of China.

The paper backs full respect for China's sovereignty in freed areas. Those areas should return to Chinese control as soon as military rule can end. No outside power should meddle in China's inner politics. It cites the Nine Power Treaty and its pledge of equal trade rights for all. It also warns that freeing Manchuria will sharpen the clash between China's government and its communist rivals. The three great powers, it urges, should avoid feeding that split and should back unity instead.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d674:
Henry Villard reported a French counter-move on the Tangier talks from Paris on July 12, 1945. His secret wire is document 674 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The U.S. team had met again with Britain's Peake and France's Meyrier.

Meyrier handed Peake a note answering the British note of July 9. Putting the conference off to an unnamed date, it said, would gravely harm French and Sherifian interests. No bar of principle, it argued, stood against Soviet or U.S. participation. The 1923 convention looked to adherence by all the Algeciras powers. France proposed to sound out Washington and Moscow without delay. It suggested July 16 as the formal opening date for a four-power conference. If Britain still held out for delay, France would seek the two governments' views through normal channels.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d74:
Churchill repeated for Truman, on June 17, 1945, the full text of a telegram he had just sent Stalin about the conference site. The message, his number 94, is document 74 in the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. With the meeting a month away, the exact venue near Berlin was still unsettled, and much preparatory work waited on it.

Churchill tells Stalin that each delegation should have a separate enclave and run its own housing, food, transport, guards, and communications. A fourth place should be set up for joint sessions, arranged by the Soviet hosts. He notes Truman's full agreement. He asks Stalin to name the area and the precise spots for each delegation, and for an airfield near the British area, so advance parties can start work at once.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1074:
Ambassador Alexander Kirk cabled Washington from Caserta on July 20, 1945. He relays a talk between two British and Soviet generals in Bulgaria. General Oxley had asked General Biryusov directly whether Russian occupation forces there had grown. Oxley had himself seen troops moving through Sofia and the countryside.

Biryusov answered that Soviet armies in southeast Europe were regrouping, and the moves ran through Bulgaria. Asked if the troops were heading home to Russia, he paused, then said other countries lay beyond Bulgaria and he did not know the General Staff's plans. He countered with fears over British troops in Greece and wild talk in the Greek press. Oxley assured him the British garrison had not grown.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1174:
Kennan wrote to the Acting Secretary of State on 1 August 1945, the day before Potsdam closed. From Moscow, America's Soviet-watcher sent his view straight to the department's home team. His cables were valued for their plain, unsparing read of the Kremlin's conduct.

A dispatch sent at the summit's end could sum up how Moscow would meet the deal being signed. Kennan's post gave him the long view: he watched what the Soviets did, not just what they said at the table. This cable is that view, sent home at the finish. Later fame should not hide its plain use at the time.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1274:
Secretary of War Stimson wrote to the President on 16 July 1945. It was the second Stimson letter of that eve-of-summit day in the volume. His counsel reached Truman from two angles as the team prepared for Germany.

Stimson had more in his brief that week than any other cabinet man. Beside the armies stood the secret atomic project, tested that very day in the New Mexico desert. His letters of 16 July belong to that charged moment. This one is the war secretary's word to his president on the threshold of Potsdam. The writer knew more of the government's secrets than any other man.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1374:
George Allen wrote to Assistant Secretary James Dunn yet again on 25 July 1945, the same day as his earlier note in this run. Two papers in one day from the Near East desk point to a pressing file. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

When a desk sends twice in a day, readers should picture the phone calls and drafts that sit between the printed papers. Allen's office was pushing its case to a man at the heart of the American delegation's support staff. This note keeps the run of Near East papers moving through the volume's final section. It shows the steady pressure a regional bureau could bring to bear at a summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-74:
Molotov's rapporteur report on the foreign ministers' meeting of July 23, 1945, is printed in translation here. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Molotov reported the morning's work to the heads of the three governments.

On reparations, Molotov handed Byrnes and Eden two Soviet drafts that morning. One covered reparations from Germany, the other advance deliveries from Germany on account of reparations. Both drafts went to the economic subcommittee for preliminary examination. The ministers would discuss them at their next meeting. On economic principles, paragraphs 13 and 18 were debated, with a new Soviet paragraph 19. Molotov said he withdrew his own amendment to paragraph 13. For paragraph 18 he proposed exclusion, leaving its questions to the Allied organs in Germany and the Control Council. No agreement was reached on that point.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d774:
John Erhardt, political adviser for Austrian affairs, reported to the Acting Secretary of State on July 19, 1945. Document 774 opens Erhardt's thread in this part of the volume. Austria had been freed from Nazi rule and divided among the occupiers. Erhardt worked on its political future. His report joined the second Potsdam volume.

Advisers in the field wrote the raw material of policy. Erhardt could report what occupation looked like on the ground. Readers meet Austria as a live problem, not a map color. The document shows the conference's penumbra: lands whose fate was argued at Potsdam being managed, day by day, by men like him.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d874:
James Riddleberger, chief of the Division of Central European Affairs, wrote this secret memorandum for Assistant Secretary of State James Dunn on July 23, 1945. It weighs a proposal by Soviet Foreign Minister Molotov. Molotov had suggested that paying for a minimum import program be a first charge on German exports.

Riddleberger points to the rules of the Control Council. Its decisions had to be unanimous, so any import program needed all four commanders to agree. Without agreement, each zone commander kept supreme power in his own zone. Riddleberger concludes the American commander would not owe reparation deliveries from his zone. He advises making that point very clear to Molotov.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d974:
William Clayton drafted this memorandum for General Clay on August 1, 1945. It asks Clay to press the Control Council to adopt an attached principle on restitution. The principle would sit beside the economic principles and the reparations deal approved by the heads of government.

Restitution would cover identifiable loot taken from occupied land. The classes are heavy farm and factory equipment, unique machinery, rolling stock, and transport gear. They also include art, religious and cultural objects, libraries, and lab equipment. Owners' claims would be handled by their own governments. A later note by Pauley says the draft was never formally delivered, since both men judged it incomplete.
gao-gaoreports-b-295574: Supreme Edgelight Devices lit up a March 2005 protest at GAO, and the ruling is the decision. The device maker's claims went under the lamp. The spotlight fell on the merits alone. The merits were illuminated. The decision was bright. The lamp was bright.
gao-gaoreports-b-297374: Remington Arms doubled its January 2006 protest — two case numbers, one arms fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-299674: International Garment Processors tripled down in July 2007 — three case numbers, one apparel-contract fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles all three. The firm challenged the awards; the call works each claim. Stitched-together protests get a single, sewn-up answer.
gao-gaoreports-b-304474: Insurance's antitrust shield got a legal reading in March 2005, and GAO's ruling defines the federal scope. The decision maps the exemption's borders. The lawyers got their map. The map was drawn. The scope was set. The line was drawn. The shield was defined.
gao-gaoreports-b-308774: The Capitol's architect owed the compliance office money in this March 2007 GAO ruling, which settles who reimburses the investigation and monitoring costs. The call reads the fiscal law against the bill. The ruling decides which Capitol purse pays for the watchdog's work.
gao-gaoreports-b-311074: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by ManTech International Corporation. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-174: Elderly housing aid got a GAO catalog in 2005, and the report covers the federal programs for seniors. The review lists the roofs state by state. The aging deserved the shelter. The shelter was listed. The catalog was complete. The roofs were listed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-274: Watching Pentagon service contracts needed sharpening in 2005, and GAO's report says the watch could be keener. The review calls for the binoculars. The service dollars deserved the eyes. The eyes had to be sharper. The watch was needed. The binoculars were out.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-374: Replanting America's burned forests needed a plan in 2005, and GAO's report says the Forest Service lacked the data to set priorities. The review calls for the maps. The charred hillsides deserved the seedlings. The data had to come first. The charred hillsides deserved the seedlings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-474: China tariff fights hit snags in 2005, and GAO's report says the trade cops faced legal and practical walls. The findings map the obstacles fully. The report warns that the trade remedies deserved honest application. The trade remedies deserved honest application.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-674: Transit funding changes needed better communication in 2005, and GAO's report says opportunities existed to improve transparency. The findings demand the openness. The report warns that the riders deserved honest changes. The communication had to be improved. The riders deserved honest changes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-774: IRS business modernization spending got a GAO review in 2005, and the report examines the fiscal year 2005 expenditure plan. The findings take the measure. The report shows the tax agency's tech budget was studied. The plan had to be understood. The tax agency's tech budget was studied.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-874: Federal student loan subsidy costs were hard to estimate in 2005, and GAO's report says challenges existed in projecting the costs. The findings map the difficulty. The report warns that the borrowers' subsidies deserved honest math. The challenges had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-274: Marine and Army logistics were out of sync in 2006, and GAO's report says the lack of a synchronized approach affected timely production. The findings target the disconnect. The report warns that the two services' supply lines needed joining. The approach had to be synchronized.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-674: Data brokers were not required to protect everything in 2006, and GAO's report says key privacy laws did not require resellers to safeguard all sensitive data. The findings expose the hole. The report warns that the personal dossiers deserved locks. The laws had to catch up.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1174: The green-card lottery was leaking in 2007 — scammers and fake applicants gaming the Diversity Visa draw. GAO's report shows how fraud hobbled the State Department's grip on the popular program. The findings press for tougher screens on a beloved lottery whose cheaters threatened to kill it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-74: The anti-piracy strategy needed an overhaul in 2007, and GAO's report says the STOP program required changes for long-term success. The findings prescribe the fixes. The report warns that the fake-goods fight needed more than slogans. The strategy had to stop the fakes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-774: Troops voting from afar faced tech troubles in 2007 — GAO's report says electronic absentee voting needed real action plans to work. The findings map the obstacles between the soldier and the ballot box. The report's cause: the ballot should follow the soldier, with the glitches fixed first.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-874: The Coast Guard's dream fleet was taking on water in 2007 — GAO's report says the Deepwater program's ships and planes faced deployment and management storms. The findings track the troubled modernization. The report warns that the guardians of the coast needed rescuing themselves.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-374: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance: DOD Can Better Assess and Integrate ISR Capabilities and Oversee Development of Future ISR Requirements. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-74: Who watches the toxic waste that leaves Army, Navy, and Air Force bases? This 2007 GAO report maps the tangle: the Pentagon, federal rule-keepers, and state offices all share the job of tracking where the waste goes and how it is handled. The report spells out each player's part — and where the hand-offs could let poison slip through the cracks.
hardy-far-from-madding-1874:
Thomas Hardy published Far from the Madding Crowd in 1874, a novel set in his Wessex countryside. Bathsheba Everdene inherits a farm and runs it herself, to local surprise. Three men seek her hand: the steady shepherd Gabriel Oak, the bold farmer Boldwood, and the dashing Sergeant Troy. Her choices bring joy and harm in turn.

Oak works for Bathsheba in silence after his own losses. Troy's charm hides a faithless past that returns to haunt the parish. Harvests, storms, and fairs mark the seasons of the tale. Hardy writes with love for rural work and custom. The book was his first great success.
hegel-logic-wallace-1874:
William Wallace translated Hegel's Encyclopaedia Logic into English in 1874, giving British readers their classic Hegel. The German work first appeared in 1817 as part one of Hegel's Encyclopaedia system. Scholars call it the lesser Logic, to mark it from his larger logic book. Its subject is pure thought itself.

Hegel moves through three great stages: being, essence, and notion. Each stage shows a basic form of thought giving way to a richer one. The path is hard, yet Wallace's version guided generations of students. Readers meet here the engine of Hegel's whole system. Everything else he wrote builds on it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lucca-hebr-1017:
Lucca, a city of Tuscany, Italy, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Richard Gottheil, Ismar Elbogen, and Vittore Castiglione. Its small Jewish community appears in literature through the Kalonymus family and through Abraham ibn Ezra, who lived there for a time. Benjamin of Tudela found only forty Jews there in 1165.

The article follows Jewish bankers licensed from 1431, a papal ruling that confirmed Jewish privileges, and a heavy fine imposed in 1489 after anti-Jewish preaching. Jews later left, returned after 1500 only under a fifteen-day stay limit, and numbered about thirty in 1904. Records of residence permits run as late as 1728. The entry shows how a tiny community survived for centuries on licenses and loans, never growing large yet leaving a long paper trail in city archives.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-magnus-laurie-1:
Laurie Magnus, an English author and publisher, receives an entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born in London in 1872, he was the son of Sir Philip Magnus. He studied at Magdalen College, Oxford. By 1904 he was joint managing director of the publishing house George Routledge and Sons.

The article sketches a career split between journalism and books. Magnus served as Berlin correspondent of the Morning Post in 1897 and 1898. He then became a leader-writer for the same paper. For John Murray he edited a series of textbooks on secondary education. His own books include a primer on Wordsworth and a translation of Gomperz's Greek Thinkers. He also edited anthologies of prayers and poems from English verse. In 1902 he published Aspects of the Jewish Question, grown from a journal article. The entry catches a young publisher at the start of his influence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-matalon-jacob-b:
Jacob ben Solomon Matalon was a Turkish rabbinical scholar of the sixteenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at Salonica. Even his surname is unsettled. De Rossi took “Matalon” as the Hebrew form of “one of Toulon,” while Zunz derived it from Mataloni, an Italian town.

The main point of the entry is how much he wrote before an early death cut his work short. Two of his books were published at Salonica in 1597. “She'erit Ya'akob” is a volume of sermons. “Toledot Ya'akob” comments on the legendary and homiletic passages, the haggadot, scattered through the Talmud and the Midrashim. Brief as it is, the notice preserves the outline of a scholar known mainly through these two posthumous-looking volumes and older bibliographies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-b-isaac-of:
Meir ben Isaac of Trinquetaille, a French scholar of the twelfth century, is entered in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and S. Kahn. Born at Carcassonne and taken by his father to Provence, he became one of the most distinguished pupils of Abraham ben David of Posquières. He belonged to the same family as Menahem Me'iri of Perpignan, and he settled at Trinquetaille, a suburb of Arles across the Rhone.

Two books make his record. "Sefer ha-Ezer" defends the great code of Alfasi against the attacks of Zerahiah ben Isaac ha-Levi of Gerona, a classic Provençal quarrel over how Jewish law should be studied. "Hibbur ha-Mukzeh" is a practical list of everything that may not be touched on Sabbaths and feast-days. The entry's authorities are the standard works on medieval French Jewry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendesia-gracia:
Gracia Mendesia, born Beatrice de Luna, is remembered as Doña Gracia, the great Marrano philanthropist. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling give her a long narrative entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born about 1510 in Portugal, she was widowed young by Francisco Mendes-Nasi. In 1536 she fled the coming Inquisition for Antwerp, where the family bank's branch stood. Esteemed there, she still chafed at living as a seeming Catholic and planned escape to a land where she could avow Judaism openly.

Her brother-in-law's will chained her to Antwerp. She was trustee of an empire of loans. Indebted rulers tried to seize those loans under cloak of religion. She reached Venice in 1549. Her own sister betrayed her there. She was denounced as a secret Jewess and imprisoned. France and Venice confiscated the family wealth meanwhile. The entry's headings promise the sequel. Her cause would set Venice and Turkey at odds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mezuzah-lit-doo:
Mezuzah, literally door-post, is the small parchment scroll fixed to the doorposts of Jewish homes, explained in a Jewish Encyclopedia article by Cyrus Adler and I. M. Casanowicz, published in 1906. The parchment holds two passages from Deuteronomy, written in twenty-two lines under the same strict rules as a Torah scroll. Rolled into a case, it is set slanting on the upper right door-post.

One missing letter makes a mezuzah unfit, and the pious touch and kiss it when passing, the article notes. Josephus already knew the custom as ancient, and Maimonides taught that it reminds a person of God's unity on leaving and entering. Later ages gave it protective, even magical, powers and added angel names, additions Maimonides fought and defeated.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-miriam-10874:
Miriam, prophetess and sister of Moses and Aaron, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia article by Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach, published in 1906. The biblical account gives her three great scenes. She watches over the baby Moses at the river and fetches their own mother as his nurse, then leads the women's song of triumph after the Red Sea crossing.

Her third scene is a fall: with Aaron she speaks against Moses over his Cushite wife, and God strikes her with leprosy. Moses prays, she is healed, and the whole camp waits seven days until she returns — a mark of her standing. She died and was buried at Kadesh, and Micah names her beside her brothers as a leader of the people. Rabbinic tradition then expands her story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-monzon-abraham-:
Abraham Monzon the Younger was a Talmudic scholar of the middle sixteenth century. He began as a merchant of Tetuan in Morocco, as the Jewish Encyclopedia notes in 1906. He left trade and the town behind. He settled in turn at Algiers, Oran, and Cairo. At Cairo a generous patron freed him to give his whole time to study.

Jonah Nabon of Jerusalem was among his correspondents. Four works came out of the Cairo years. The entry stresses that all four remained in manuscript. Toẓe'ot Ḥayyim answered Abulafia's 'Eẓ ha-Ḥayyim. Eshel Abraham was a book of responsa. He also wrote a commentary on the treatise Shabbat and 'Eẓ ha-Da'at on the Yoreh De'ah. A scholarly life is preserved by Azulai's notices rather than by print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mosse-markus-11:
Markus Mosse was a German physician of Grätz in Posen, born there on August 3, 1808. Isidore Singer and J. Friedmann wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Able and popular, he became a town councilor while still young and president of the Jewish community. He was the father of Rudolf Mosse, the Berlin publisher.

In 1848, when Polish rebels rose in Posen, Mosse broke with most of his coreligionists and joined the rebels. He was wounded, captured, and condemned to prison, and he later regretted the choice more than once. The rest of his life he spent quietly in practice at Grätz. The Dr. M. Mosse Hospital there, open to all faiths, keeps his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nagy-kanizsa-ca:
Nagy-Kanizsa, a Hungarian town, had Jews by the end of the seventeenth century, to judge by its old cemetery. Gotthard Deutsch wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on the community. A synagogue was dedicated in 1821 and a school established in 1831. The congregation stayed small until about 1840 and then grew fast.

Under Rabbi Leopold Löw the community became one of Hungary's most progressive, with a modern school of six hundred pupils. Jews, once shut out of the town's Casino club, by 1904 supplied its president. The article also records the darker side: in the riot of 1887 a Jewish railroad conductor was mortally wounded. About three thousand six hundred fifty Jews lived in the town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathanael-of-ch:
Nathanael of Chinon was a French writer of Talmud notes. Wilhelm Bacher and A. Peiginsky wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He flourished about the year 1220. He studied under Isaac ben Samuel of Dampierre. After 1224 he headed the yeshivah in Chinon.

Nathanael wrote letters to the great scholars of his day. They included Jehiel of Paris and Isaac of Evreux. One colleague called men like him pillars of the world. He wrote tosafot, or notes, on four Talmud treatises. They are Bezah, Hullin, Berakot, and Erubin. Some of his ritual decisions also survive. The entry shows a teacher honored well beyond his town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-noah-b-pesah-ca: Noah b. Pesaḥ was an acting rabbi in Pinsk. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote his brief entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He is also called Noah Dayyan ben Pesaḥ. He died at Pinsk in the year 1638. His work comments on Bereshit Rabbah, the great midrash. He titled that commentary Toledot Noaḥ. It was printed at Cracow in 1634. Four standard catalogues record the book and its author.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ohio-11674:
Ohio is a north central state of the United States. Cyrus Adler and H. G. Friedmann wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It joined the Union in the year 1803. Jews did not settle there till the year 1817. In that year Joseph Jonas came from England. He made his home in Cincinnati, in the south.

Jonas drew other English Jews to the state after him. They held the first divine service there in 1819. In 1824 they formed the first Jewish flock of the Ohio Valley. It was called B'ne Israel, or Sons of Israel. German Jews came in the next twenty years. One Bavarian man settled in Cleveland in 1837. By 1850 the state held six such flocks in all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ornstein-jacob-:
Jacob Meshullam Ornstein was a rabbi of high sway in Galicia. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died at Lemberg in the year 1839. His father was Mordecai Zeeb Ornstein, rabbi of Lemberg. That post had stayed in the family 150 years.

Jacob was too young to take the post at his father's death. So the post went to a man outside the kin line. He passed his youth at Jaroslaw, in Galicia. From there he was called as rabbi to Zolkiev. In 1806 the Lemberg post fell free once more. Jacob was called to it and held it thirty-three years. He was rich and owed no man his bread. He ran his office with force and with stern ways. He used that force against the men of new learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palma-11874:
Palma is the chief town of Majorca, a Spanish isle. Richard Gottheil and Meyer Kayserling wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews lived there in the days of Moorish rule. They lived in Almudayna, the most full part of town. That quarter held the Jews' castle with its walls.

About 1290 a king gave the Jews a set ghetto there. Its walls and gates were meant to guard the folk inside. In 1318 King Sancho gave them that ghetto for all time. The king had let them build a fine synagogue at first. In 1314 he took that house from them as a fine. He turned it into the church of Santa Fé. In 1331 a new king let them build a plain house. That house was for prayer and for school in one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-petra-12074:
Petra was the capital of Edom in northern Arabia. Emil G. Hirsch and Louis H. Gray wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The city lay in a rocky valley among mountains. Its Hebrew name, Sela, simply means rock.

King Amaziah of Judah captured Petra in war. He renamed it Joktheel, but the old name stuck. The Nabataeans later made it their rich chief city. Under Rome it headed the province of Arabia Petraea. The city faded after the fourth century. Burckhardt revealed its temples and tombs to Europe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinsker-dob-bar: Dob Bär Pinsker was a Polish Talmudist of the 1700s. The Executive Committee and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He descended from Nathan Spira of Cracow. His one known work is Neta Sha'ashuim, printed at Zolkiev in 1748. The book holds novellae on the order Nashim. It also treats the tractates Makkot and Shebuot. A few gathered notes close the volume.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-poppa-sabina-12:
Poppaea Sabina was the second wife of the Roman emperor Nero. Kaufmann Kohler and Eduard Neumann wrote her entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She wed Nero in the year 62 and died in 65. Josephus calls her a God-fearing woman. She had a clear liking for Judaism, the entry says.

Jews found a warm welcome at her court. The actor Alityros was one of them. In 64 Josephus came to Rome to free some priests. Her help won their freedom, and he went home with rich gifts. She also helped in a dispute over a wall at Jerusalem. Priests had blocked a king's view of the Temple with that wall. Her word settled the case for the priests.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-b-abuha-:
Rabbah bar Abuha was a Babylonian teacher of the second set of amoraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He taught Nahman ben Jacob and wed his own kin to him. He was kin to the house of the exilarchs. Some say he was an exilarch in his own right.

Rabbah lived at Nehardea for the first part of his life. That city was wiped out in the year 259. He then left with his son-in-law for a new home. A letter of Sherira Gaon tells of his house and kin. Later books weigh his rank among the teachers. The entry gathers those scant records of his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raphael-mark-12:
Mark Raphael was an Italian convert who lived at Venice. Isidore Singer and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He worked in the early sixteenth century. Before converting, he had a name as a Jewish law scholar.

The article says King Henry VIII sought his legal opinion. The king asked about his marriage to his brother's widow. Raphael first called the marriage legal under Jewish law. He then changed his view when that answer failed. His new opinion said the marriage was invalid. That opinion went before Parliament in a large collection. The king rewarded him with trade licenses. The entry shows scholarship pulled into a royal crisis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-remak-robert-12:
Robert Remak was a German physician born on July 26, 1815. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Posen. He died at Kissingen on August 29, 1865.

The article says he studied medicine at Berlin and graduated in 1838. From 1843 he assisted in the university's pathology work. In 1847 he won the right to lecture there. He was the first Jewish lecturer of that rank in Prussia. In 1859 he became an assistant professor. His research centers on nerve tissue and its diseases. He wrote on nerve fibers under the microscope. Later books treat electric cures for palsied muscles. The entry marks a pioneer in nerve science.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ritter-immanuel:
Immanuel Heinrich Ritter was a German rabbi born on March 13, 1825. Isidore Singer and E. Schreiber wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Ratibor, Prussian Silesia. He died on July 9, 1890.

The article says he studied classics and history at Breslau. He took his doctorate there in 1849. A minister hinted that only baptism could win him a professorship. Ritter instead taught religion at Berlin's Reform congregation. He became assistant to senior preacher Samuel Holdheim. His first ten sermons appeared in print in 1856. They ranked him among Germany's top Jewish preachers. His main work is a history of Jewish Reform. It appeared in four parts across many years. The entry honors a preacher who chronicled his own movement.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-max-1:
Max Rosenthal was an American painter and engraver born at Turek, in Russian Poland, on November 23, 1833. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied at Berlin and Paris before reaching America in 1849.

Settling in Philadelphia, Rosenthal helped introduce chromolithography, printing pictures in color. During the Civil War he followed the Army of the Potomac as official illustrator. In 1872 he invented the sand-blast process for engraving patterns on glass. He etched more than five hundred portraits during his career. A set of those portraits is kept at the Smithsonian Institution.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sacerdote-donat:
Donato Sacerdote was an Italian poet born at Fossano in 1820, and he died there in 1883. Isidore Singer and Flaminio Servi wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. From youth he compared the Greek tragedians with Italy's Alfieri and Del Monti.

Sacerdote's Bianca Cappello won great success at Turin's Alfieri Theater in 1874. His other dramas include Cola di Rienzo and a five-act tragedy, Catilina. Eglon, a dramatic poem in five acts, draws its fire from the Bible. He was also an accomplished writer of sonnets, odes, and songs. The entry thus shows a poet working both classical and biblical veins.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samson-ben-elie:
Samson ben Eliezer was a German scribe, or sofer, of the fourteenth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Michael Friedländer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He is called Baruk she-Amar, from a blessing he loved to repeat.

Orphaned at eight in Prague, Samson was adopted by a learned scribe. Issachar taught him to write tefillin, mezuzot, and scrolls of the Law correctly. He traveled widely, then studied the scribes' craft in Palestine itself. There he found most scribes ignorant of the true letter forms. His book Baruk she-Amar was written to correct that evil.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schindler-solom:
Cyrus Adler and Joseph Lebovich wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Solomon Schindler. He was a German-American rabbi and author. Schindler was born at Neisse, in Germany, on April 24, 1842. In 1868 he took charge of a small congregation in Westphalia. His Reform views forced him to resign. In 1871 he emigrated to the United States.

In America, Schindler led congregations at Hoboken and then Boston. Boston's Adath Israel called him in 1874. In 1888 he was elected to the Boston school board. All parties voted for him without a contest. In 1894 he left the pulpit for charity work. He ran the Federation of Jewish Charities of Boston. From 1899 he headed a home for infirm Hebrews and orphans at Mattapan. His books include Messianic Expectations and Modern Judaism. He also wrote Young West, a sequel to Looking Backward.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sedbon-joseph-1: Kaufmann Kohler and M. Franco wrote this short Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Joseph Sedbon. He was a rabbinical and cabalistic author of Tunis. He worked in the second half of the eighteenth century. His one known work is Ahabat Adonai, a treatise on the Cabala. It comments on the Idra Ẓuṭa, a core Zohar text. Sedbon wrote the book in 1778. It stayed unpublished for nearly a century. Natives of Tunis at last brought it out at Leghorn in 1871. The entry rests on Cazès's bibliographic notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shabbethai-b-me:
Shabbethai ben Meir ha-Kohen, known as the ShaK, was a Russian Talmudist born at Wilna in 1621. Crawford Howell Toy and Bernhard Friedberg wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He studied at Tykocin, Cracow, and Lublin as a youth. Back in Wilna, he married into a rabbinic family.

In 1647 he published Sifte Kohen, notes on a major Jewish law code. Eighteen top scholars of his day approved the work. A year later, Cossack attacks wrecked Polish Jewish communities, and he suffered too. He fled to Prague, then served as rabbi at Dresin and Holleschau. He died in 1662, honored by his peers as a leading mind.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shield-13574:
Shield covers the two kinds of shields carried by Israelite soldiers in Bible times. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on them. The large shield, called zinnah, covered the whole body. Heavy infantry and spearmen carried that broad defense.

Tribes like Judah and Naphtali fought behind the zinnah. Great warriors had bearers carry their shields before them. Psalms use that shield as a picture of God's favor. The small shield, magen, suited bowmen and light troops. Kings carried the magen as well, the entry notes. Its size differed hugely from the body shield. Solomon's gold shields, counted in Kings and Chronicles, prove the gap in scale and worth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sima-sama-13674: Sima, also called Sama, was a Babylonian amora of the late fourth and early fifth centuries. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was a son of the great Rab Ashi. Sima is known through legal questions he put to his father. Those questions appear across Ketubbot, Zebahim, Menahot, and Bava Kamma. Rashi's reading suggests Sima died before his father, hence before 427.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-singer-josef-13:
Josef Singer was an Austrian cantor born in Galicia on October 15, 1842. Isidore Singer and Alois Kaiser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. His father, a traveling cantor, wanted him for the stage. The boy chose study instead. He took a four-year course at the Conservatorium at Prague.

Singer first served as cantor in Beuthen, in Prussian Silesia. In 1873 he became chief cantor at Nuremberg. In 1881 he succeeded Salomon Sulzer in Vienna. He still held that post in 1905. He wrote a learned study of the modes of synagogue chant. He also wrote many articles on cantors and synagogue song.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-and-mar:
Solomon and Marcolf is a medieval tale or romance of two figures. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It tells the adventures and talks of Solomon and Marcolf. Their talks consist chiefly of riddles and sharp answers. They recall the riddles put to Solomon by the Queen of Sheba.

The tale likely derives from an Eastern original tale. Early versions in Anglo-Saxon appeared as Solomon and Saturnus. In Germany, Marcolf became a type of the wise fool. Hans Sachs and Hans Folz both used the legend. Versions spread into French, Italian, Dutch, and Welsh. An English version was printed by Pynson in 1530.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sop-s-fables-am:
Aesop's fables among the Jews is the subject of this study. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Recent research links Aesop's fables to the Buddhist jatakas. Those birth-stories tell of Buddha's past lives as beasts and trees. Such tales may be the natural source of Aesop's beast fables.

Pali versions of the jatakas survive from Ceylon today. A Ceylonese embassy may have brought them to Rome about 50. Later Greek fables match the Indian ones far more closely. Talmudic sages, the article argues, knew these fables well. Johanan ben Zakkai is said to have studied fox fables. He also studied the fables linked with the name Kybises.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spitz-zebi-hirs: Zebi Hirsch Spitz was a German author and Talmudist of the eighteenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He wrote Dibre Hakamim we-Hidotam, printed at Offenbach in 1802. That work comments on Talmud passages with a set theme. It deals with places where the Torah is said to speak in human language. It also covers passages explained by their literal sense alone.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-strauss-adolf-1:
Adolf Strauss was a Hungarian geographer and ethnologist born in 1853. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Cece, Hungary, on May 15. He studied at Fehervar and Budapest. He attended the military academy in Budapest as well.

Strauss knew the Balkan Peninsula and its peoples closely. The Hungarian government sent him east on repeated missions. His books describe Bosnia, its land and its people. Others cover Bulgarian industry and Bulgarian folk songs. He wrote a Bulgarian grammar and a study of superstitions. A later work treats Rumania's economy and peoples. He founded and edited journals on the Orient. By 1905 he taught at Budapest's Oriental Academy of Commerce.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-szanto-simon-14:
Simon Szanto was a Hungarian journalist born at Nagy-Kanizsa in 1819. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born on August 23, son of Rabbi Meïr Szanto. Orphaned at ten, he studied across Bohemia and Prague. He died at Vienna on January 17, 1882.

In 1849 Szanto founded a Jewish school in Vienna with his brother. He directed that school himself for years. He also taught at Vienna's theological institute. In 1861 he founded the weekly journal Die Neuzeit. He soon became its sole editor. Vienna's courts named him Hebrew interpreter in 1864. He supervised Jewish religious teaching from 1869. The entry follows a teacher who built a press voice for Austrian Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-taxation-14274:
Taxation in ancient Israel left only faint traces in the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch, Eduard König, Joseph Jacobs, and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Scripture says little about secular or political taxes. Abraham gave a tenth of war spoil voluntarily. Kings' subjects likewise brought gifts to their rulers.

Only the churlish withheld such presents, Samuel notes. Crown lands formed a chief source of royal income. Chronicles lists the king's fields, herds, and stores. No money or poll tax appears among royal rights. Samuel's warning speech omits any such levy too. David's census may have aimed at fair tax distribution. That census is the closest hint of a system. The entry admits how thin the biblical evidence runs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trajan-14474:
Trajan, Rome's emperor from 98 to 117, shaped Jewish history across the empire. Isidore Singer and Samuel Krauss wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. His eastern wars against Parthia strained the whole region. Meanwhile Jews rose in Egypt and Cyrene in wild revolt. Eusebius describes that rising in his church history.

Trajan sent Marcius Turbo to crush the Egyptian revolt. Cyprus saw a violent Jewish uprising as well. In 116 the Jews of Mesopotamia rebelled against Rome. They remembered Rome's harshness in Palestine and their own suffering. Lusius Quietus was ordered to purge the provinces of Jews. He obeyed so strictly that he won Palestine's governorship. Revolt also flared again in Judea itself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ulmann-benjamin:
Benjamin Ulmann was a French historical painter born in Alsace in 1829. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Paris. Drolling and Picot were his teachers there. In 1859 he won the coveted Prix de Rome.

His Sylla at the House of Marius dates to 1866. That canvas now hangs in the Luxembourg Museum. Other works show Patroclus, Junius Brutus, and the Lorelei. The Gitanos of Granada numbers among his subjects too. Paris Salons awarded him medals in 1859 and 1872. The Legion of Honor cross came in 1872 as well. He died at Paris in 1884.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vercelli-14674:
Vercelli is a city in Piedmont, in northern Italy. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The oldest record of its Jews dates to February 1446. That year the city let Abramo della Vigneria open a loan bank. Such permits ran for set terms and could be renewed.

The permits set the Jews' rights and duties in detail. Harsh laws of 1430 forced them to wear a red badge. Twice the duke ordered all Piedmontese Jews expelled. In 1560 the duchess won them a short delay. A court doctor then helped get the order withdrawn. The entry shows a community living on revocable terms.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wandsbeck-14774:
Wandsbeck is a town near Hamburg, in Schleswig Holstein. Gotthard Deutsch and Alfred Feilchenfeld wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. About 1600 Count Breido Rantzau let Jews settle there. They paid a small yearly fee for protection. Hamburg then barred Jews, so many came.

In 1637 the Jews gained a burial plot and worship rights. In 1674 Wandsbeck joined Altona and Hamburg in one union. The three towns shared a chief rabbi. Wandsbeck paid one eighth of his salary. A branch community grew inside Hamburg itself. After 1710 Hamburg opened to German Jews. Wandsbeck's community then shrank fast.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolf-emma-14974:
Emma Wolf (born 1865) was an American novelist whose Jewish tales drew wide note. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote her entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She was born in San Francisco to parents who came from France. She was schooled in that city and stayed there to write.

Her short tales ran in many American magazines. She then turned to full length books. Her first novel came out in 1892. Three more books came in the next eight years. Their names are Other Things Being Equal, A Prodigal in Love, The Joy of Life, and Heirs of Yesterday. The entry says her Jewish novels won the most praise. They show Jewish life in America through story and scene.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yekaterinoslaf-:
Yekaterinoslaf is a Russian city founded in the year 1787. Herman Rosenthal and S. Janovsky wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It rose in the reign of Catherine the Second. It is the chief town of its state of the same name.

By 1897 the town held more than one hundred twenty thousand souls. Jews made up near one third of that count. They worked in trade and in crafts in large shares. A third of them lived by trade of some sort. A third more worked as masters and hands in shops. The town held more than thirty mills and works then. Most of those shops were owned by Jews of the town. Few Jews worked as hands in those shops, all the same.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zarifa-15174:
Zarifa is the name of a goddess named once in the Talmud. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Her cult place was the port town of Ashkelon. Word men have sought her true self for long years.

Some link her with the god Serapis of Egypt. The Hebrew form points more to a form of Isis, men say. That form is Isis Pharia, whose feast fell in April. Since Ashkelon is her town, she may be Derceto. Derceto had the head of a woman and the trunk of a fish. The word zarifa means made of parts, which fits that shape. One mind links her to Zarpanit, the wife of Marduk. The short entry leaves the case wide open to thought.
justinian-institutes-sandars-1874:
Thomas Collett Sandars published his translation of The Institutes of Justinian in this 1874 form, first issued in 1853. Justinian I, the Byzantine emperor, had the Institutes made in 533 CE as the student part of his great codification of Roman law. Generations of law students began with it.

The Institutes teach the elements of law: persons, property, contracts, wrongs, and actions, in short and ordered rules. Behind them stood the full mass of Roman legal writing that Justinian's teams had sorted. The work became the foundation of civil-law systems across Europe and beyond. Sandars's English, the standard student version, keeps the clarity that made the original a textbook for over a thousand years.
livingstone-last-journals-vol1-1874:
David Livingstone, the Scottish missionary and explorer, kept journals on his final African expedition from 1866 until his death. Volume One of The Last Journals, edited by Horace Waller in 1874, prints that closing record. Livingstone's porters carried the books out after he died at Ilala.

Weakened by fever and bleeding, Livingstone pressed on around Lakes Tanganyika and Bangweulu, still hunting the Nile's source. He records slave caravans and his horror at the trade's cruelties. Waller adds letters and a narrative of the last days. The volume is both a travel record and a testament of endurance.
livingstone-last-journals-vol2-1874:
Volume Two of Livingstone's Last Journals completes the record of his final expedition, 1866 to 1873. Horace Waller edited the notebooks that Livingstone's faithful servants saved. The explorer's body itself was carried to the coast for return to Britain.

The entries grow sparser as illness and hardship mount, yet the observations on land, people, and the slave trade stay sharp. Waller's narrative fills gaps with accounts from those who were there. The story ends with Livingstone found dead, kneeling by his bed in prayer. Few exploration books carry such emotional weight alongside their geography. Waller's preface explains how the notebooks were saved and sorted.
martin-hyde-the-duke-s-messenger-pg1274: John Masefield's 1906 adventure novel for boys: young Martin Hyde serves the Duke of Monmouth and gets swept into the 1685 rebellion. Battles, escapes, and a boy's-eye view of history unfold in Masefield's stirring prose. A classic of British children's adventure.
memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-and-o:
Volume fifteen of Saint-Simon's memoirs opens at chapter one hundred thirteen. Saint-Simon has just come back from a stay in Spain. Cardinal Dubois now stands firm in the Regent's favor in Paris.

Dubois longs to be named prime minister in public form. The Marechal de Villeroy stands in his path as a foe. Dubois tries a peace made through Cardinal Bissy as go between. Foreign envoys wait in the next room as the two men meet. Foreign envoys had their day with the Cardinal that morning. Access and rank rule each step of the meeting's dance.
northampton-assizes-relation-1674:
Mary Forster stood trial at the Northampton assizes in 1674, and a relation of the proceedings keeps her case. Relation of the Proceedings at the Northampton Assizes prints the charge, her confession as reported, and her death. The trial falls in the Restoration years, well past the Civil War.

By 1674 many in England doubted witch charges, yet the courts still heard them and still hanged. Forster's case shows the old charge at work in a new and more wary age. The report is short, plain, and sad in the usual way of these prints. It proves the gallows for witches had not yet closed.
openalex-w1830509674:
R. Aaij and the LHCb Collaboration reported this rare decay study. It appeared in the Journal of High Energy Physics in 2015. The team studied a B meson decay into a phi and two muons. Data came from proton collisions at the LHC. Such rare decays can reveal physics beyond the standard model.

The team measured how often the decay occurs by energy range. They also mapped the angles of the decay products. Angular results matched the standard model well, they report. In one key range, the rate fell below model predictions. That gap passed three standard deviations in size. The finding drew wide interest among particle physicists.
openalex-w1977349774:
Talisa de Carlo, Jay Duker, and co-authors wrote this review. It appeared in the year 2015 in the catalog record. OCTA is a new, non-invasive eye imaging method. It builds full angiography images in mere seconds. Those images show blood vessels inside the retina.

The method could serve many retinal vascular diseases, they write. Evidence levels were still low when they reviewed it. The review explains how the imaging works in practice. It weighs strengths, limits, and likely clinical uses. Fast, dye-free vessel imaging is the core promise. Eye doctors gain a quick window on retinal flow.
openalex-w1994387974:
Nicholas Graham, Tim McClanahan, and co-authors studied coral reefs. The catalog record gives no author or year; the sample names them. The full title adds the ocean-scale integrity of coral reefs. Coral reefs rank among the systems most at risk from climate shifts. Marine protected areas are a leading tool to guard them.

The team asked if protected areas hold up under warming. Reef integrity was assessed at ocean scale, not just locally. Warming stresses reefs through bleaching and disease outbreaks. Reserves may protect fish while failing against heat itself. Knowing those limits guides smarter reserve design worldwide. The study spans teams from many reef nations.
openalex-w2000708574:
Jizeng Jia, Shancen Zhao, Xiuying Kong and colleagues sequenced the genome of a wild grass. Their paper appeared in Nature in 2013. The grass, Aegilops tauschii, is a parent species of bread wheat. Its genes helped wheat adapt to many climates. The team asked what its full gene set holds.

The team read the genome and the set of active genes. They produced a draft sequence with deep coverage. The gene set helps explain how wheat gained toughness and grain quality. Bread wheat formed when this grass crossed with an early wheat. Studying this simpler genome aids work on the huge wheat genome. The sequence is a tool for wheat breeding research.
openalex-w2034970874:
Jose Alexandre Diniz-Filho, Thannya Soares, Jacqueline Lima and colleagues reviewed the Mantel test in population genetics. Their paper appeared in Genetics and Molecular Biology in 2013. The test compares genetic distance with geographic distance. It is a popular way to study spatial patterns. Recent critics had questioned how well it performs.

The authors reviewed the test and its variants. These include correlograms and partial correlation methods. They applied the methods to a Brazilian savanna tree. The tree data covered twenty-five populations. Different approaches gave similar estimates of spatial structure. The results matched what ecology predicted for the species. The authors conclude that careful Mantel analysis remains useful. Clear reporting of method choices is essential.
openalex-w2090940374:
Georges Aad and colleagues in the ATLAS team described the simulation system for the ATLAS experiment. Their paper appeared in 2010. ATLAS is a giant particle detector at CERN. Fake collisions let physicists test their analysis methods. Huge numbers of events must be made on shared computers.

The system links many software parts together. Event generators first create the particle collisions. Other programs track particles through the detector. Grid computing spreads the work across many sites. Each step must match the real detector closely. The paper explains how the parts fit together. It also covers production workflows at large scale. Sound simulation underpins nearly all ATLAS physics results.
openalex-w2109543774:
Robin Carhart-Harris, Robert Leech, Peter Hellyer and colleagues proposed a theory of conscious states based on brain disorder. Their paper appeared in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience in 2014. Entropy measures uncertainty or disorder in a system. Brain imaging with psychedelic drugs informed the theory. Such drugs produce unusual conscious experiences.

Normal waking consciousness keeps brain activity fairly ordered. Psychedelic states raise entropy in brain networks. That rise loosens rigid patterns of thought. The authors link high entropy to a primary state of mind. It resembles dreaming and early psychosis in their account. Low entropy marks rigid states like deep anaesthesia. The theory aims to unify many findings on consciousness.
openalex-w2152628774:
Judit Barniol, Roger Gaczkowski, Eliana Barbato, and colleagues published this study in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2011. They tested the World Health Organization's revised dengue classification in real clinical practice. The old scheme split dengue into fever, hemorrhagic fever, and shock syndrome, and doctors had long debated its fit.

Expert reviewers, staff interviews, and focus groups covered eighteen countries. The old system left about fourteen in a hundred cases unclassifiable, and some severe cases fit nowhere. The revised system left under two in a hundred unclassified. Staff acceptance and ease of use were high, especially for triage and case care, though warning signs need more study and training.
openalex-w2396846174:
Matthew Page, Larissa Shamseer, Douglas Altman, and colleagues published this cross-sectional study in PLoS Medicine in 2016. Systematic reviews guide medical decisions by pooling whole literatures, but a flawed or poorly reported review misleads. The team took a census of reviews indexed in one month of 2014 to see how the species is doing.

That month alone yielded nearly seven hundred reviews, implying over eight thousand a year, a threefold rise in a decade. A random sample of three hundred was dissected in detail. Most tackled therapy questions; authors clustered in China, Britain, and the United States. The median review pooled fifteen studies and about two thousand participants. Roughly two-thirds included a meta-analysis, mostly standard pairwise pooling, with Cochrane and other reviews compared.
openalex-w2516525774:
William Manzanares, Margot Lemieux, Pascal L. Langlois, and Paul Edmund Wischmeyer published this review in Critical Care in 2016. It weighs probiotics and synbiotics for critically ill patients.
