Serious illness wipes out helpful gut bacteria and lets harmful ones multiply. That leaves patients open to infections caught in the hospital.

The authors pooled thirty randomized trials covering nearly three thousand patients. Probiotic treatment was linked to fewer new infections overall. It was also linked to fewer cases of pneumonia tied to breathing machines. No clear effect appeared on deaths, hospital stay length, or diarrhea. The findings support careful study of these live microbes in intensive care, while leaving open which patients and products help most.
openalex-w2888404374:
Maria Adriana Neag, Andrei Mocan, and Javier Echeverría lead this 2018 review of berberine in Frontiers in Pharmacology. Berberine is a plant alkaloid used in folk medicine for centuries, above all in China and India. Plants containing it treat infections, diarrhea, and diabetes in folk practice. Chemists prize it as raw material for designing new drugs.

The review covers where berberine occurs in nature and how it is extracted. It then surveys its roles across four disease areas: heart and blood vessels, metabolism, liver, and kidney disorders. Germ-killing and anti-parasite actions also receive attention, backed by many studies. Dietary supplements based on such plants are already widely sold. The authors assemble the science behind those uses, separating tradition from tested effect. For drug designers, berberine's structure offers a proven scaffold to modify.
openalex-w2920135474:
Moritz Kraemer, Robert Reiner, Oliver Brady, and colleagues published this study in Nature Microbiology in 2019. It tracks two mosquito species, Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, that spread dengue, yellow fever, chikungunya, and Zika. As these mosquitoes expand into new regions, the population at risk from those diseases grows.

The team shows that human movement patterns explain how both species spread through Europe and the United States after arriving. Aedes aegypti tends to appear through long-distance introductions, while Aedes albopictus expands along the edges of its current range. The authors then predict future distributions for both species as cities grow, travel links increase, and the climate changes.
openalex-w2961363174:
Alexander Voorhies, Charlie Ott, Satish Mehta, and colleagues published this study in Scientific Reports in 2019. It tracks how long stays on the International Space Station change the microbes living in and on astronauts. Crew members face many stressors in orbit that could shift their microbiomes and harm health.

The team followed nine astronauts who spent six to twelve months on the station. Microbe communities in the gut, skin, nose, and tongue all changed during the missions. Gut communities grew more alike across astronauts, mainly because a few bacterial types became rarer. Some of those shifts matched changes in immune signals. Skin changes may help explain the rashes astronauts often report in space.
openalex-w3029489574:
Sebastião de Freitas Netto, Marcos Sobral, Ana Ribeiro, and Gleibson Soares wrote this systematic review in Environmental Sciences Europe in 2020. It explores greenwashing, the practice of making a company or product look greener than it is. Worsening pollution has pushed firms to sell green products, and some mislead their audiences instead.

Following standard review practice, the authors searched ten years of literature for how greenwashing is defined and sorted. They found one major classification with four forms. Greenwashing can sit at firm or product level, and it can work through claims or through execution, such as imagery. Cataloging the forms in one scheme helps regulators, buyers, and researchers spot the practice and compare studies of it.
openalex-w7204469274: Forcing vulnerable people into psychiatric lockup raises hard questions. This article studies compulsory hospitalization in Brazil through the lens of the right to the city, human rights, and psychiatric reform, starting from the case of a homeless woman. The authors ask whether confinement protects or excludes. A challenging review of care that looks like control.
openalex-w7204533874: Wounds that will not heal need better options. This integrative review looks at platelet-rich plasma, or PRP, a treatment made from the patient's own blood, as a drug-free aid for healing injuries. The authors sum up what studies say about how well it works. A medical review of a therapy that turns the body's own repair tools into treatment.
openalex-w7205000174: Feelings run every classroom, and teachers ignore them at their peril. This article brings together social-skills theory and brain science to explain how emotions shape daily school life: friendships, self-control, and learning itself. The authors review research and draw lessons for teaching practice. A useful bridge between neuroscience and the very human work of managing thirty restless students.
openalex-w7206181474: Teenagers live on their phones, and this paper asks what that does to their reading and focus. The authors study how phones and apps have changed the way teens find facts, talk to each other, and learn. They note the good that digital life brings, but also the harm to steady attention in class. A timely study of how the battle for young people's attention is reshaping school.
openalex-w7211898174:
Frankleudo Luan de Lima-Silva leads a team on grief for a dead pet. When a dog or cat dies, the loss can cut deep. Yet those round the one who grieves oft treat it as small. The team spoke with dog and cat own folk, one score and one in count, from the first to the third month of 2025. Their read asks how this grief shows, and what sets it past grief for kin.

The study takes up the grief's shapes, the rites own folk make or miss, and the ways folk cope. Those ways span kept things and pics, and help sought that oft is not there. This grief is oft shut out: folk hide it, since the world round them grants pets a low place. By setting down the owners' own words, the team pleads to take such loss with weight, in wards and in daily life.
openalex-w7214241274:
Breno Henrique Monteiro Guedes wrote a 2026 article about motivation, based on the reflections of three English teachers working in different settings in Brazil. Motivation is hard to pin down, yet it shapes whether language students keep trying. Each teacher answered a questionnaire about the motivational side of their own classroom.

Analyzed qualitatively, their answers point back at the teacher. Teachers said their own behavior and attitude matter: showing enthusiasm and real commitment to students' success helps motivate a class. Lessons also need adjusting so they feel attractive and connect with students' real lives. The study is small, but it gives a grounded picture of motivation as something teachers build daily, not something students either have or lack.
openalex-w7221187574:
Wasiu Abiodun Makinde and Audrey H. Legodi, of the University of South Africa, studied what provincial governments reveal about their own governance in annual reports, publishing in 2026. They scored the health and basic education departments of all nine provinces against a twenty-item disclosure index built from finance law, audit guidance, and the King IV governance code.

Fifty-four audited reports from 2023 to 2025 showed many departments disclosing at a high level, using reports as a genuine signal of performance. Results varied sharply by province, though: the Western Cape stayed on top, while Limpopo's accountability signals fell steeply in 2025. Annual reports, they conclude, remain the main channel through which these governments answer to citizens.
phrenologische-bilder-zur-naturlehre-des: Phrenologische Bilder, 1874. The phrenological pictures. This book preserves that work. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
plos-pbio-0000074:
Alexei A. Sharov, Yulan Piao, Ryo Matoba, and co-workers charted gene activity in mouse stem cells for PLOS Biology in 2003. They measured which genes are switched on in stem cells and in very early embryos. Such a full survey is called a transcriptome analysis.

Stem cells can turn into many cell types, and genes switched on or off drive that choice. A clear list of active genes gives a baseline for spotting what keeps a cell flexible and what pushes it to mature. The data set became a shared tool for other labs. It helps compare cell lines, test culture methods, and hunt for the core genes of early development.
plos-pbio-0020174:
David R. Halpin and Pehr B. Harbury continued their DNA display series with part two in PLOS Biology in 2004. The first part showed how to route DNA pools by sequence. This part shows how to apply genetic tricks, like mutation and selection, to libraries of chemical compounds tagged with DNA.

Treating a chemical library like a population of genes lets researchers breed better compounds over rounds of selection. Weak binders are washed away, winners are copied, and the cycle repeats. That evolution in a test tube can find strong drug leads from huge starting pools. The paper sets out the rules for copying and varying the library without losing track of which DNA tag means which compound.
plos-pbio-0020274:
Eugene Hur, Samuel J. Pfaff, E. Sturgis Payne, and their team studied the androgen receptor in PLOS Biology in 2004. This receptor responds to male hormones and switches genes on with the help of partner proteins called coactivators. The partners dock onto a specific surface of the receptor.

The study shows how the receptor reshapes that docking surface to fit its partners, a process the title calls recognition and accommodation. A clear view of the fit matters for prostate disease, where this receptor is a main drug target. Drugs that block the docking site could work where current hormone blockers fail. The paper gives that search a firm structural base.
plos-pone-0000074:
Ines Van Bocxlaer, Kim Roelants, S. D. Biju, and a large team traced frog history in PLOS ONE in 2006. Gondwana was the ancient southern supercontinent that split into Africa, South America, India, and other lands. Frog groups found across those lands may have been carried apart as the continent broke, a process called vicariance.

Their genetic timelines fit a Late Cretaceous split, matching the continent's breakup. That match means the frogs' spread was set by geology, not by later ocean crossings. Old frogs are poor swimmers over salt water, so the vicariance story makes sense. The paper is a clean case of using DNA clocks to test a geological story.
plos-pone-0000174:
Jennifer L. Baxter-Roshek, Alexey N. Petrov, and Jonathan D. Dinman published this molecular biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Ribosomes, the machines that build proteins, are themselves built from RNA and protein. The authors study how chemical modifications to ribosomal RNA bases fine-tune the ribosome's structure and function.

Those small chemical marks can change how accurately and how fast proteins are made. The authors review and test the optimization these modifications provide. Because antibiotics often target ribosomes, and because faulty ribosomes cause disease, understanding this tuning has use well beyond basic biology.
plos-pone-0000274:
Kirsten E. Nicholson, Luke J. Harmon, and Jonathan B. Losos published this lizard evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Anolis lizards carry a dewlap, a flap of skin under the throat that males flash in display. Its color and pattern vary richly between species. The authors study the evolution of that dewlap diversity across the Anolis group.

Dewlaps are signals, used to claim territory and attract mates, so their variety may track how species recognize their own kind. The authors test patterns in that diversity against the lizards' history. The work is part of a famous research program using Anolis as a model of adaptive radiation.
plos-pone-0000374:
Marion Coolen and colleagues used a shark relative to study how body plans evolved, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. All jawed vertebrates, from fish to humans, build their bodies along a head-to-tail axis using inherited genetic programs. The team asked how those axis-setting programs changed as jawed vertebrates evolved.

Chondrichthyans, the group that includes sharks and skates, split early from other jawed vertebrates, so their development preserves clues about the ancestral state. Comparing their axis-forming mechanisms with those of other animals shows which parts of the program are ancient and which are new. The work helps explain how a shared body plan diversified across half a billion years.
plos-pone-0000474:
Sofie Ignoul and colleagues characterized a little-known human chloride channel protein, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The protein, ClC-6, is a glycoprotein found in late endosomes, sorting compartments inside cells. The team also reported that it associates with detergent-resistant lipid domains, the membrane patches known as lipid rafts.

Members of the ClC family move chloride ions and help set the chemistry inside cell compartments; faults in relatives cause kidney and bone disease. Placing ClC-6 in late endosomes and in raft domains narrows down what it likely does. Basic placement work like this precedes any understanding of a protein's role in health and disease.
plos-pone-0000574:
Christopher C. Hemond, Nancy G. Kanwisher, and Hans P. Op de Beeck reported a spatial bias in the brain's object areas, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Human cortex contains regions that respond strongly to objects and faces. The team found a preference for contralateral stimuli in that cortex. In plain terms, each side of the brain favors sights from the opposite side of view.

A contralateral bias is expected in early vision but was less charted in high-level areas that supposedly see the whole scene. Showing the bias persists there reshapes how researchers read brain scans of recognition. It also bears on patients with one-sided brain damage, whose neglect of one side of space may start in these regions.
plos-pone-0000674:
Athanasios G. Michos, Vassiliki P. Syriopoulou, Christos Hadjichristodoulou and colleagues reviewed 506 cases of aseptic meningitis in children for PLOS ONE in 2007. Aseptic meningitis is inflammation of the membranes around the brain without a bacterial cause. Non-polio human enteroviruses are its leading cause in children. A PCR test can spot enterovirus directly.

The role of that PCR test in diagnosis and management had not been fully explored. In a look-back study of past cases, the team gathered epidemiological, clinical, and laboratory details. Patterns across 506 cases can show which children need the test, and how results change care and hospital stays.
plos-pone-0000774:
Elisabetta Mattei, Nicoletta Corbi, Maria Grazia Di Certo and colleagues tried a gene-therapy route for Duchenne muscular dystrophy in mice. DMD is a severe muscle degenerative disease caused by absence of the protein dystrophin. No treatment yet works, as the authors state. Their aim was to raise levels of utrophin, a related gene, to complement the missing dystrophin.

They used an artificial transcription factor, a built protein meant to switch the utrophin gene up. In transgenic mice, the factor up-regulated utrophin as intended. Substituting a stand-in protein is a clever strategy when the original gene is too large or too broken to replace directly.
plos-pone-0000874:
Jonathan Aldridge, Tomohisa Horibe and Nicholas Hoogenraad hunted for genes switched on by the mitochondrial unfolded protein response, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Mitochondria are the cell's power plants. When their proteins fold badly, the cell answers with a stress program that turns certain genes on.

A companion study had shown the response starts through a gene called chop and a partner called C/EBP beta. Here the team looked for the wider set of genes that follow, and for the promoter elements, the DNA switches that control them. Mapping that set helps explain how cells cope when their power plants are under strain.
plos-pone-0000974:
Kelly Rogers, Sandrine Picaud, Emilie Roncali and colleagues built a genetic way to watch calcium signals inside living mice, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Calcium surges inside cells help run many signaling pathways. Those surges are fast, local and hard to catch without cutting tissue.

Their approach makes cells produce a detectable signal when calcium rises, readable from outside the body. Non-invasive imaging means the same animal can be followed over time. It also lets signals be watched in deep tissues where microscopes cannot reach. Tools like this turn fleeting chemistry into a picture doctors and biologists can use.
plos-pone-0001074:
Guohua Yang, Peng Gao, Hua Zhang and colleagues found a kinesin mutation that worsens a root hair growth fault, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Root hairs grow only at their tips, making them a clean model for plant cell polarity. Plants with an always on form of the ROP2 switch lose that polarity and grow stunted, misshapen hairs.

A mutation in MRH2, a kinesin motor protein, enhanced that defect. Motors haul cargo along the cell's tracks, so a faulty motor deepening a polarity fault makes mechanical sense. The interaction maps two parts of the tip growth machine. Plant roots feed the world, and their smallest parts still hold basic lessons.
plos-pone-0001174:
The striatum is a set of deep brain structures involved in planning movements and in thinking. Javier Bernácer, Lucía Prensa, and José Manuel Giménez-Amaya mapped one of its cell types in the human brain. Their 2007 PLOS ONE article covers the cholinergic interneurons. These interneurons use the chemical acetylcholine and help coordinate the striatum's main output cells.

The authors describe how cholinergic interneurons are distributed differently across the caudate nucleus and putamen in humans. Detailed maps of the healthy human striatum are basic reference material. They matter for understanding diseases such as Parkinson's and Huntington's, where this region is central.
plos-pone-0001274:
Genome-wide association studies often include relatives, which complicates the statistics: related people share genes for reasons other than disease. Najaf Amin, Cornelia van Duijn, and Yurii Aulchenko present a method for that setting in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Genotyping hundreds of thousands of markers in thousands of subjects had created demand for fast, powerful, and reliable analysis methods.

Their genomic background based method performs association analysis in related individuals by accounting for the shared background. Family-based studies are common in isolated populations, where this problem is unavoidable. A sounder method protects such studies from false alarms.
plos-pone-0001374:
David Klinke wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on type 1 diabetes, a disease where the body can no longer make its own insulin. Doctors had long said that signs of the disease start when most insulin making cells are lost. The usual figure given was a loss of 80 to 95 percent. Klinke asked whether that loss alone can predict when illness starts.

He argues that the scale of cell loss matters, but it is not enough on its own to forecast onset. Other steps must shape the timing as well. The paper urges a broader view of how the disease builds. That view could shape how risk is judged in people near the start of illness.
plos-pone-0001474:
Paul Feldblum and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE trial report on a gel meant to block HIV in Nigeria. The gel, called SAVVY, was used in the vagina before sex. The trial enrolled women at high risk of HIV. It was a large phase 3 trial, with women split at random to gel or a dummy gel.

Women were followed for up to twelve months with regular HIV tests. The team weighed whether the gel cut new infections in real use. Gel based guards would give women a method they control themselves. Each such trial, win or lose, shapes the search for a workable guard.
plos-pone-0001574:
Tamar Geiger and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on odd traits when skin cells turn cancer like. As skin cancers grow, cells often shed their skin traits and gain a roving form. That shift is called EMT. The team tracked early stages of the shift in skin cells changed by a virus oncoprotein.

They found the shift here broke the usual pattern in key ways. Some marks moved in the wrong direction for classic EMT. Odd cases test the rules that cancer labs rely on. They show one road to cancer can bend the standard script, which matters for how early cancers are read.
plos-pone-0001674:
Shai Markman and co-authors reported that pollution changed both song and brain growth in a songbird, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Some pollutants disrupt hormones, and such disruption is known to cut breeding success in water animals. Far less was known about land animals living where land and water meet.

Exposed birds sang more complex songs, and the brain area called HVC, which controls song learning and production, was larger. The full text gives the exposure details, the song analysis, and the brain measurements. The result is a warning in an odd direction. A pollutant can make a mating signal stronger while still harming the animal. That could mislead both birds and the scientists who score their health by song.
plos-pone-0001774:
Peter Garvin, Lennart Nilsson, John Carstensen, and their co-authors measured a vessel-wall enzyme in healthy middle-aged people in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The enzyme is matrix metalloproteinase-9, or MMP-9, which cuts structural proteins in tissues. High circulating levels had been shown in patients with established coronary artery disease.

The team instead studied a population free of symptomatic heart disease and asked how MMP-9 levels associate with cardiovascular risk factors. The full text gives the blood values and the links to factors such as smoking and blood pressure. If MMP-9 tracks risk before symptoms start, it could join screening panels that aim to catch heart disease early.
plos-pone-0001874:
Ligia Antunes Goncalves and colleagues mapped a gene site that guards mice against malaria in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Genes were already known to help hosts resist the blood stage of the malaria parasite and to curb how sick they get. Far less was known about the liver stage, the first stop after the parasite enters the body.

The team used congenic mapping, breeding mouse lines that differ in one small stretch of DNA, to pin the effect to chromosome 17. They first showed that some mice carry fewer parasites in the liver. Finding the site is a step toward the gene itself, and toward why some hosts stop malaria early.
plos-pone-0001974:
Stephen Gammie and co-authors studied mouse mothers that neglect their pups, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Child neglect is the most common form of child maltreatment in humans, yet its biology is poorly known and no rodent model existed. The team had a mouse line, called MaD1, whose mothers by nature give pups little or no care.

They charted this line and asked what sets its mothers apart. As the title states, signaling by dopamine, a brain messenger tied to reward, was altered in these mice. If poor care has a brain basis that can be modeled, the model can be used to test what restores care.
plos-pone-0002074:
Scott Garforth, Michael Parniak, and Vinayaka Prasad tested whether HIV's copying enzyme can use a cheaper fuel, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. DNA polymerases, the enzymes that build DNA, normally use deoxynucleoside triphosphates, energy-rich building blocks. HIV reverse transcriptase is one such enzyme, and it is the target of many HIV drugs.

Cells also hold large amounts of diphosphate forms of the same blocks, with one less phosphate. The team asked whether HIV's enzyme can build DNA from those instead. If it can, drug tests that assume only the standard fuel may miss part of how the virus copies itself inside cells.
plos-pone-0002174:
Déborah Tribouillard-Tanvier, Suzana Dos Reis, Fabienne Gug, and co-authors tested how two anti-prion drugs work, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Prions are faulty proteins that cause fatal brain diseases. Two drugs with no structural likeness, 6AP and guanabenz, were found through a yeast test to block prions. Both also work against mammal prions in cells.

The team reports that the folding help given by ribosomal RNA is the shared target of both drugs. Ribosomal RNA helps assemble the cell's protein factories and can aid protein folding. A single shared target for two unlike drugs is a strong lead for designing better anti-prion treatments.
plos-pone-0002274:
James Hodge and Ralf Stanewsky studied a potassium channel inside the fruit fly's body clock, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The daily clock in the brain runs on molecular feedback loops, but the electrical activity of clock neurons matters too for rhythmic behavior. Most earlier work had distorted that activity with foreign channels or drugs, which makes results hard to read.

The authors focused on the fly's own Shaw potassium channel and its function within the clock network. Using the native channel gives a cleaner view of how electrical signaling keeps time. Work like this connects the clock's gene gears to the firing of real neurons.
plos-pone-0002374:
A research team led by Laaksonen reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Toni Laaksonen, Juan J. Negro, Sami Lyytinen, and others. Its subject is effects of Experimental Brood Size Manipulation and Gender on Carotenoid Levels of Eurasian Kestrels Falco tinnunculus. Animals use carotenoid-pigments for colouring, as antioxidants and as enhancers of the immune system.

Carotenoid-dependent colours can thus signal individual quality and carotenoids have also been suggested to mediate life-history trade-offs. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002474:
Work from Buchholz and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Kathrin Buchholz, Stefan Rahlfs, R. Heiner Schirmer, and others. Its subject is depletion of Plasmodium berghei Plasmoredoxin Reveals a Non-Essential Role for Life Cycle Progression of the Malaria Parasite. Proliferation of the pathogenic Plasmodium asexual blood stages in host erythrocytes requires an exquisite capacity to protect the malaria parasite against oxidative stress.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002574:
In 2008, He and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Xiao-Song He, Tyson H. Holmes, Sanae Sasaki, and others. Its subject is baseline Levels of Influenza-Specific CD4 Memory T-Cells Affect T-Cell Responses to Influenza Vaccines. Factors affecting immune responses to influenza vaccines have not been studied systematically.

We hypothesized that T-cell and antibody responses to the vaccines are functions of pre-existing host immunity against influenza antigens. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002674:
Naoya Yuhki led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was sequences, annotation and single nucleotide polymorphism of the major histocompatibility complex in the domestic cat. The catalog record names Naoya Yuhki first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Two sequences of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) regions in the domestic cat, 2.976 and 0.362 Mbps. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002774:
Gašper Tkačik led a team whose 2008 PLOS ONE article deals with the role of input noise in transcriptional regulation. Authorship is credited in the record to Gašper Tkačik and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Gene expression levels fluctuate even under constant external conditions. The summary also notes a further point. Much emphasis has usually been placed on the components of this noise that are due to randomness in transcription and translation. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002874:
Manoj Gambhir and Edwin Michael modeled lymphatic filariasis in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The disease is spread by vectors such as mosquitoes and is caused by a large parasitic worm. Global health programs were then weighing whether such diseases could be wiped out for good, not just held down.

Their model works through the complex ecology behind spread, including hosts, vectors, and worm life stages. It asks what those links mean for eradication, meaning full removal of transmission. Public health readers get a careful test of when control can become elimination and when the biology makes that goal much harder.
plos-pone-0002974:
Yi-Hong Wang and Michael Campbell reported odd flower changes after Agrobacterium transformation of tomato in 2008. Agrobacterium tumefaciens is the standard tool for adding genes to plants, and it is known to cause unexpected traits. Mutations in homeotic genes can also alter floral structure in known ways.

The transformed tomatoes showed unexpected flower phenotypes, yet their gene expression profiles stayed similar, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, that mismatch is the puzzle. Plant breeders using transformation need to know when a visible change reflects deep expression shifts and when it does not. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003074: Thomas Brody, Amarendra Yavatkar, Yong Lin and colleagues reported horizontal gene transfer links between a human MRSA pathogen and contagious bovine mastitis bacteria in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. MRSA is Staphylococcus aureus resistant to methicillin, and mastitis is an udder infection of cattle. The catalog record gives title, authors, and year, with no abstract detail beyond the title. The article presents evidence that gene exchange connects the human pathogen with bacteria behind a costly cattle disease.
plos-pone-0003174:
Hiroaki Kimura, Kin Ming Kwan, Zhaoping Zhang and colleagues identify a promoter of bone formation in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Bone mass is kept up by continuous remodeling, with repeated cycles of bone removal by osteoclasts and bone formation by osteoblasts. Many body-wide and local factors regulate that process. The team identified collagen triple helix repeat containing-1, called Cthrc1, in this context.

The title states that Cthrc1 is a positive regulator of osteoblastic bone formation. Readers learn of a factor that pushes the building side of bone turnover. Such factors interest researchers who seek new treatments for bone loss.
plos-pone-0003274: A. Roxana Lescano and colleagues published a case study in PLOS ONE in 2008 on research ethics training in Peru. The title states the full subject, and the work describes a training effort rather than a lab test. No abstract beyond the title was supplied, so this record adds no claims about outcomes or reach.
plos-pone-0003474:
Feng Cao and co-authors profiled lab-grown heart cells in this 2008 paper. Human embryonic stem cells can become cardiomyocytes, the beating cells of heart muscle. Such cells might one day repair hearts hurt by ischemia, or low blood flow. The team studied the cells' gene activity and function together.

Their portrait shows what these stem cell products can and cannot do. Gene profiles and behavior tests mark how mature the cells are. That detail matters before any use in patients. The study helps set checks for future heart cell therapies. Heart failure is common and deadly, so even partial repair would help many.
plos-pone-0003574:
Guisheng Song and Li Wang untangled two small RNA genes in this 2008 paper. MicroRNAs help control development, metabolism, and cancer growth. Little was known about their primary transcripts and gene control. The pair miR-433 and miR-127 share one genomic locus.

The team cloned two primary transcripts, one for each microRNA. The transcripts overlap, yet arise independently of each other. Two regulators can thus be read from the same crowded address separately. Sorting that out clarifies how this neighborhood is controlled. Tiny RNAs like these are now tracked as markers in blood tests for cancer.
plos-pone-0003674:
Thomas F. Wierzba, Ibrahim Adib Abdel-Messih, Bayoumi Gharib, and colleagues published this neurology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Guillain-Barré syndrome is a sudden immune attack on the nerves that can leave people weak or paralyzed. Campylobacter, a common foodborne gut germ, is a known trigger elsewhere.

Working in Egypt, the team tested whether Campylobacter infection also sets the syndrome off there. Linking a routine gut infection to a rare nerve disease matters for both diagnosis and food safety. The study adds Egyptian evidence to the case that this bacterium can start the body's attack on its own nerves.
plos-pone-0003774:
Jingui Ma, Xianliang Xin, Linghua Meng, and colleagues published this cancer drug study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Drugs that block several tyrosine kinases at once have shown promise against tumors. Side effects and resistance remain concerns. The team tested a marine-derived compound, an oligosaccharide sulfate called MdOS.

MdOS blocked multiple tyrosine kinases and fought tumor angiogenesis, the growth of new blood vessels that feed tumors. It worked both in cell tests and in living animals. The compound joins the hunt for multi-target cancer drugs with fewer side effects and less resistance.
plos-pone-0003874:
Dominik Seelow, Jana Marie Schwarz, and Markus Schuelke presented a software tool called GeneDistiller in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article addresses a common problem in gene hunting. Studies that track traits through families often narrow the search to a stretch of DNA. That stretch can still hold several hundred genes.

GeneDistiller helps users rank those genes by how likely each is to cause a disease. It draws together data that researchers once gathered by hand. Manual searches stay flexible, but they take much time over large lists. The tool gives gene hunters a short list of strong leads to test first in the lab.
plos-pone-0003974:
Cedrick D. Dotson, Lan Zhang, Hong Xu, and co-authors studied bitter taste receptors beyond the tongue in 2008. Taste receptors of the TAS2R type detect bitter compounds. They also appear in cells lining the mammalian gut. There they help the body handle nutrients it takes in.

Their PLOS ONE article reports bitter receptors influence glucose balance. Gut sensing of bitter compounds may adjust sugar handling after meals. That role links taste machinery to metabolism and diabetes risk. Drugs aimed at these receptors might one day help control blood sugar. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004074:
Fiona M. Brandie, Veronica Aran, Avani Verma, and co-authors studied membrane fusion control in fat and muscle cells in 2008. Insulin moves the glucose transporter GLUT4 to the cell surface. That move raises glucose uptake into fat and muscle. It is a specialized form of controlled membrane fusion.

Their PLOS ONE article reports Munc18c restrains that fusion process in vitro. The fusion uses syntaxin4, SNAP-23, and VAMP2 proteins. A brake on fusion keeps glucose uptake off until insulin calls. Understanding the brake helps explain insulin resistance at cell level. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004174:
Jürgen Löhler and colleagues published this protein mapping study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Casein kinase 1 delta, or CK1δ, adds phosphate tags to many key proteins. Through them it touches cell growth, specialisation, cell death, the daily body clock, and transport inside cells. Faults in this kinase have also been linked to diseases of the degenerating brain.

Using antibody staining, the team charted which cell types in young adult BALB/c mice actually make CK1δ, tissue by tissue. A map of where a busy kinase works is basic knowledge for judging what goes wrong when it fails.
plos-pone-0004274:
Michael Allemand and colleagues published this study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Polycystic ovary syndrome, or PCOS, combines excess male hormones with frequent insulin resistance in skeletal muscle. The team asked whether testosterone itself worsens insulin action in muscle cells.

Working with primary rat muscle tubes grown in the lab, they tested whether testosterone increases serine phosphorylation of IRS1, a change that blunts insulin signalling. Their setup offers a potential model for PCOS-related insulin resistance. If a hormone drives the resistance directly, treatments could target that link. PCOS is one of the most common hormone disorders in women.
plos-pone-0004374:
Doctors often must decide for patients who cannot speak for themselves. One rule for those choices is substituted judgment, deciding as the patient would have decided. Farr Curlin, Ryan Lawrence, and Julie Fredrickson studied how well new medical students grasp that rule. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper followed a course on clinical ethics.

Students wrote essays on one of three hard cases given in class. The authors read those essays for signs of true understanding. Their title asks whether the students' grasp was an ethical facade. The paper shows future doctors can sound right while missing the point. That gap matters for how ethics courses should be taught.
plos-pone-0004474:
A three-generation family carrying affective disorder gave Shuzhang Yang, Kai Wang, Brittany Gregory, and co-authors a window on the genome, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Affective disorders include bipolar disorder, a common mental illness with a complex pattern of inheritance. Big studies of unrelated people need huge samples to find weak gene effects.

Studying one large family can be more powerful, because the same risk genes run through it. The team mapped the family's genomic landscape, including copy number variants, stretches of DNA gained or lost. Rare changes that travel with illness in a family can point at causes that mass studies miss. The family map gives later work a focused place to search for bipolar risk genes.
plos-pone-0004574:
Lowering dopamine makes male fruit flies more attractive to other males, report Tong Liu, Laurence Dartevelle, Chunyan Yuan, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dopamine is an important neuromodulator, a chemical that tunes nerve circuits, in animals. Its roles in mammal sexual behavior are extensively studied. The fruit fly Drosophila offers a simpler system for the same questions.

Earlier work had shown that reducing dopamine affects female receptivity in flies. This study turns to males: when dopamine levels were reduced, other males courted them more. The finding suggests dopamine helps set the chemical signals, or their reading, that guide male choice. Simple fly experiments like this expose basic rules of how brain chemicals shape social and sexual behavior.
plos-pone-0004674:
Glenn White and Harold Erickson compared a key chromosome protein across species for PLOS ONE in 2009. The proteins they studied help hold sister copies of DNA together and aid repair and packing. A long, bent coil shape is a hallmark of these proteins in most living things.

The coils act like spacer rods that give the protein its long shape. White and Erickson asked if that coil form is kept in both animals and yeast. They found the coil kept in animals but not in yeast. The contrast hints that the spacer role changed as complex cells evolved over time.
plos-pone-0004774:
Philipp Weyermann and colleagues tested oral blockers of a feeding receptor that boost intake and ease cancer wasting in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cancer cachexia is a wasting syndrome with loss of appetite, fat, and muscle. It is among the most debilitating parts of cancer and can threaten life on its own.

A brain peptide that suppresses appetite acts through the receptor targeted here. Blocking that receptor by mouth raised food intake in the mice. It also reduced wasting tied to tumors. The approach could help patients keep strength during treatment. The work also raises clear questions that targeted studies can now address.
plos-pone-0004874:
Marie-Martine Lefevre-Colau and colleagues studied frequency and interrelations of risk factors for chronic low back pain in primary care, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many risk factors have been identified for chronic low back pain, but only one study evaluated their interrelations. The team investigated frequency and relationships in patients consulting general practitioners for chronic pain in a cross sectional primary care survey across practices.

Risk factors cluster rather than act alone. Psychological and occupational factors intertwine strongly. Holistic management outperforms single factor fixes. Primary care sees the full picture first. The results give future studies a clearer base for comparison and follow up.
plos-pone-0004974:
Fat tissue needs new blood vessels to keep expanding. Joshua Tam and colleagues asked which vessel signals matter in PLOS ONE in 2009. They blocked two receptors for the growth factor VEGF. The receptors are VEGFR1 and VEGFR2. The tests ran in mice on a fattening diet. They also asked where the new vessel cells come from.

Only blocking VEGFR2 limited fat tissue expansion. Blocking VEGFR1 did not. The new vessels came from local tissue cells, not from bone marrow cells. The finding singles out one receptor as a lever against obesity. It also settles the source of fat's new plumbing.
plos-pone-0005074:
Cholera causes deadly diarrhea. The gut floods with salt and water. Cholera toxin gets most of the blame. Lucantonio Debellis and colleagues studied a second toxin in PLOS ONE in 2009. It is the Vibrio cholerae cytolysin. Many cholera strains lack the classic toxin yet still cause disease.

The cytolysin promotes chloride secretion from human intestinal mucosa. The tissue used was intact, not a cell line. Chloride leaving the gut drags water with it. That is the flood behind the diarrhea. The toxin doubles the fluid loss by its own route. The finding reveals a backup path for cholera's deadliest effect. Treatments may need to reckon with both toxins.
plos-pone-0005174:
Spain's Habsburg kings ruled from 1516 to 1700 and often married close kin. Uncle and niece unions and cousin marriages were common in the line. Alvarez and colleagues asked in PLOS ONE in 2009 whether that inbreeding helped end the dynasty.

Writers of history had long blamed inbreeding for the line's fall, but the claim needed numbers. The authors measured inbreeding across the family tree and weighed its role in the dynasty's end. Their work turns a famous royal story into a test of how close-kin mating can raise health risks in a whole ruling house.
plos-pone-0005274:
Insulin-degrading enzyme, or IDE, breaks down both insulin and the amyloid protein tied to Alzheimer disease. Too little amyloid clearance may help drive Alzheimer disease, so switching IDE on is an attractive idea. Cabrol and colleagues screened for such switch-on compounds in PLOS ONE in 2009.

High-throughput screening tested many compounds for the power to raise IDE activity. The screen found small-molecule activators of the enzyme. First activators give chemists starting points for drugs that might help in both diabetes and Alzheimer disease, where IDE sits at a crossroads.
plos-pone-0005374:
The forebrain changed more than any other brain region through vertebrate evolution. Lampreys, jawless fish from an early branch, preserve hints of the ancestral forebrain. Guérin and colleagues studied neurodevelopment genes in lampreys in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Comparing lamprey gene patterns with those of other craniates reveals trends in forebrain evolution. Traits shared with lampreys are likely ancient, while differences mark later inventions. The lamprey thus serves as a baseline for reading how the complex forebrain was assembled. Jawless fish split from our line more than five hundred million years ago, so each gene they share with us marks a part of the brain plan that is older than jaws. Limbs, or land life as we know it.
plos-pone-0005474:
Samantha Westrop and colleagues studied people who control HIV without drugs, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. A few people with HIV keep the virus in check for years without treatment. Their blood holds strong T cell responses and steady counts of key immune cells.

The team followed such controllers over time and tested their immune responses in detail. They found that this control can fade, and that the thymus gland keeps making fresh T cells in many of them. Knowing how control works, and why it can end, helps the search for vaccines and cures.
plos-pone-0005574:
Karin Ahrné, Jan Bengtsson, and Thomas Elmqvist counted bumble bees along a city gradient in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Bumble bees pollinate wild flowers and farm crops. Their numbers and variety have fallen in recent decades, mostly as their habitats are destroyed or split up.

The team compared bees from the countryside into the city to see how building up an area affects them. Knowing which bees cope with city life, and which vanish, helps planners keep pollinators in and around towns. That matters for gardens, parks, and nearby farms. City bees face extra stress from heat and sparse flowers, so the gradient captures several pressures at once.
plos-pone-0005674:
Hiroyasu Konno and co-authors traced how cells first sense a virus, in a 2009 study of innate immunity. When viral RNA or DNA shows up inside a cell, the cell sounds an alarm. That alarm brings on fever-causing signals and type I interferons, proteins that slow viral spread.

The team studied a protein called TRAF6 and the switches it turns on. They found TRAF6 helps fire up two master switches, NF-kB and IRF7, when viral material is sensed in the cell body. Knowing which parts carry the alarm helps explain how the body reacts fast, before tailored defenses are ready.
plos-pone-0005774:
Bolin Liu, David Morse, and Mario Cappadocia followed a self-defense system in a wild potato relative in 2009. Many plants refuse their own pollen when its type matches the style's, blocking self-fertilization. The block depends on a stylar enzyme called S-RNase.

After a compatible mating, the team saw both the enzyme and its gene message drop in the style. That drop may be part of how the style accepts the right pollen tubes. Understanding this switch helps breeders move traits between potato relatives. It also shows how precisely plants manage who fathers their seeds.
plos-pone-0005874:
Namni Goel and co-authors split the effects of sleep loss by gene variant in 2009. The circadian gene PER3 comes in long and short forms. The long form had been tied to sharper cognitive decline after a full night without sleep, at certain times of day.

Under chronic partial sleep loss, the long-form carriers showed stronger sleep-homeostatic responses, the mounting pressure to sleep. Yet their thinking performance did not decline more than others'. That split shows sleep pressure and performance are separable traits. Studies that lump them together may misjudge who suffers most from short sleep.
plos-pone-0005974:
A cough can blot out a word, yet listeners still hear the word as whole. Folkert Seeba and Georg Klump asked in 2009 whether birds share that knack. Their PLOS ONE study tests European starlings, which can restore a sound masked by noise much as people restore masked speech.

Familiar sounds were restored more readily than strange ones, the team found. Knowing a sound well thus helps the ear fill its gaps. The starling results show the trick is not a human gift alone, and they give hearing science a bird model for how the brain patches breaks in sound.
plos-pone-0006074:
Counting the genes of the human body now means counting our microbes too. Xing Yang, Lu Xie, Yixue Li and colleagues took that count in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper treats the person as a super-organism and estimates the number of distinct genes in the human gut bacterial community, a figure long debated in computational biology.

Their estimate tops nine million unique genes, dwarfing the human genome's own count. A number that large reframes what a person is, genetically: mostly microbe, by gene tally. The estimate also sets the scale for gut studies that hope to catalog the community fully, a task far larger than the human genome project itself.
plos-pone-0006174:
Keeping older people healthy matters more than simply keeping them alive longer. Ruth Hubbard and colleagues examined what exercise does for older adults who live at home, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Some doctors had worried that health measures might extend life without improving health, leaving more years of frailty.

The team tracked the chances of health getting better, getting worse, or ending in death. Exercise shifted those chances, and the paper weighs the gains against the feared trade-off. The findings matter for families, doctors, and planners who design activity programs for seniors. They help show where modest effort can protect strength and daily independence.
plos-pone-0006274:
Predicting how long a cancer patient will live remains one of clinical research's open problems. Jing Zhang and colleagues built a gene expression classifier for glioblastoma, a fast-growing brain tumor, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Earlier gene sets that claimed to predict outcome shared almost no genes with each other.

Their systems biology approach treats genes as a connected network rather than lone markers. The resulting classifier also predicted survival in other solid tumors, the authors report. Network-based signatures may prove steadier than single gene lists. The work offers a method others can test on further cancers.
plos-pone-0006374:
Glowing probes can reveal protease activity inside living tissue without surgery. Galia Blum and colleagues compared two probe families for imaging cysteine proteases in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Proteases are ideal imaging targets because their activity marks disease processes such as cancer and inflammation.

Substrate probes and activity-based probes were assessed side by side. The two designs differ in how they light up and how long they stay. A head-to-head comparison guides imaging scientists choosing tools. Better protease imaging supports earlier disease detection. The work gives labs a fair way to pick the right probe for each task.
plos-pone-0006474:
Ioannis Karakikes and co-authors studied gene changes in the diabetic heart for PLOS ONE in 2009. Diabetes alters the heart muscle, a condition called diabetic cardiomyopathy. That dysfunction comes with changed gene expression in heart tissue. The team investigated which gene expression changes accompany the disease.

They also tested a phenotypic rescue using SERCA2a, a protein that handles calcium in heart cells. Restoring calcium handling is a candidate route to repair the diabetic heart. Profiling the gene changes shows what goes wrong at the molecular level. Combined with rescue tests, the work points toward treatments aimed at the heart itself, not just blood sugar.
plos-pone-0006574:
Fatma Daoud, Aurora Candelario-Martínez, Jean-Marie Billard, and colleagues studied a brain form of dystrophin in PLOS ONE in 2009. Duchenne muscular dystrophy is caused by deficient expression of the cytoskeletal protein dystrophin. One third of patients also have mental retardation. A shorter dystrophin product called Dp71 is the main form in the brain.

The team examined Dp71's role in excitatory synapse organization and synaptic plasticity. Synapses are where neurons communicate, and their organization shapes learning. If Dp71 loss disrupts synapses, it could explain the cognitive side of the disease. The study links a muscle disease gene to brain function.
plos-pone-0006674:
Yui Harada and co-authors reported a new way to grow dendritic cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dendritic cells can train the immune system to attack disease. Doctors already use them in cell-based immunotherapy for some patients. Treatment is limited because each patient yields only small numbers of their own cells. Making the therapy at larger scale has also proved difficult.

The group built a simple method based on cytokines, the signaling proteins cells use. Their method expanded mouse dendritic cells on a log scale. The grown cells remained functional, not just numerous. A reliable supply of working dendritic cells could widen access to immunotherapy. It could also make production cheaper and easier to standardize.
plos-pone-0006774:
Megan E. Rokop and Alan D. Grossman studied backup mutations that rescue DNA copying in a bacterium in PLOS ONE in 2009. The bacterium is Bacillus subtilis. Its genes dnaD and dnaB are essential for starting DNA replication. They load the copying helicase at the chromosome's origin. Faulty versions of these genes fail at high temperatures.

The team searched for suppressor mutations that restore growth. Suppressors arose both inside the faulty genes and elsewhere in the genome. Each suppressor reveals a functional contact or workaround. Mapping them clarifies how the replication start machinery fits together. Such maps help explain a process every dividing cell must get right.
plos-pone-0006874:
François Cesselin and colleagues studied the body's own painkillers under multiple injury sites in PLOS ONE in 2009. Enkephalins are natural opioid-like molecules that process pain. Their functional significance remains puzzling. A painful mechanical stimulus, for example, does not change enkephalin release in matching spinal segments. Such null responses complicate simple pain models.

The team examined what happens with several noxious foci at once. Multiple pain sources seemed to freeze enkephalinergic functions. A frozen internal painkiller system could let pain sensitize instead. Sensitization means later stimuli hurt more than they should. The mechanism may contribute to chronic pain states.
plos-pone-0006974:
Kentaro Yamamoto, Saori Tanaka, Hiromi Kobayashi, and colleagues tested toddlers' reactions to a robot in PLOS ONE in 2009. Young infants are sensitive to whether a partner responds to them in time. Past studies used video setups or a still, unresponsive face. This team used a non-humanoid robot to probe the same sense.

Children aged two to three met a robot whose responses were either well timed or not. The setup relates to the uncanny valley, the unease oddly lifelike machines can cause. Their reactions show how early the sense of social timing appears, and what breaks it.
plos-pone-0007074:
Cristina Fragoso, Gabriela Burkard, Michael Oberle, and colleagues studied a parasite coat protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. Trypanosoma brucei causes sleeping sickness. Its surface is wrapped in anchored coat proteins, present in millions of copies. Each life stage wears a characteristic set. Bloodstream and insect-stage coats have been studied most.

The team characterized a membrane-spanning protein called PSSA-2. They found it required for the infection to mature efficiently. A protein the parasite cannot do without is a possible drug target. It also marks a step in how the parasite readies itself for its hosts.
plos-pone-0007174:
Vanesa Alonso-Camino, David Sánchez-Martín, Marta Compte, and colleagues introduced a new antibody selection method in PLOS ONE in 2009. They call the platform Lymphocyte Display. It is based on activating T cells, a type of white blood cell used by the immune system.

Older display tools often select antibodies that still need heavy changes before human use. They also reach only a limited set of targets. The authors present their lymphocyte-based system as another route to finding useful antibodies. Drug and lab researchers can compare its reach with existing platforms.
plos-pone-0007274:
Jitka Eryilmaz, Patricia Pan, Maria F. Amaya, and colleagues studied the structure of a developmental regulator protein in 2009. Polycomb group proteins control development by repressing key genes. They work in large complexes that establish and maintain that repression across cell divisions in embryos.

The protein here is MBTD1, named for malignant brain tumor domain repeats. It carries four MBT repeats, modules that read chemical marks on other proteins. The authors present structural studies of those repeats. Their work shows how this reader protein may help Polycomb complexes silence developmental genes.
plos-pone-0007374:
Ariane Biebl, Axel Muendlein, Zhyrgal Kazakbaeva, and colleagues studied immune gene variants in meningitis survivors in 2009. About a tenth of people carry Neisseria meningitidis without illness. Who develops invasive meningococcal disease cannot be predicted, and host factors behind bloodstream invasion remain unclear despite decades of study.

Innate immunity genes are prime suspects. The authors examine variants in CD14 and Toll-like receptor 4 in patients who survived meningococcal disease. These receptors sense bacterial components. Their PLOS ONE study tests whether inherited sensing differences help explain why carriage turns deadly in some people.
plos-pone-0007474:
Damian Williams, Henry Puhl, and Stephen Ikeda published a methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2009 on a tool for modifying proteins quickly inside cells. The system borrows a cutting enzyme from tobacco etch virus. That protease slices target proteins at chosen points. The trick is control: the cutter stays inactive until researchers say go. The signal they used is the drug rapamycin.

Adding rapamycin switches the protease on, and protein modification follows fast. Speed matters because many protein effects unfold in minutes, not days. A switchable cutter lets researchers change a protein in real time and watch the cell respond. That is far sharper than deleting a gene and waiting. The system offers cell biologists a new way to test what proteins do.
plos-pone-0007574:
Kistie Patch and colleagues published a genetic study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how animal tissues take shape. Rho1 is a small switch protein at the center of a conserved pathway that sculpts developing tissues. Many upstream signals can activate it, and many outputs follow. The team ran a second-site noncomplementation screen in fruit flies. Their arena was the imaginal disc, the tissue that becomes the adult wing.

A screen of this kind hunts genes whose mutations worsen or ease Rho1's effects. Each modifier found is a new suspect in the shape-making machinery. Because the pathway is conserved across animals, fly results inform development broadly. Tissue morphogenesis underlies everything from wing shape to organ form. The paper adds entries to the parts list of that machinery. Later work can test each part's exact job.
plos-pone-0007674:
Zhongming Ma and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns the channels that let nerve cells fire. These channels sit in the cell wall and open or close in response to voltage. Each one is built from segments named S1 through S6.

The authors focused on one piece, called S2D4, and asked how it twists and how it touches its neighboring pieces. Their results refine the working model of the voltage-sensing part of the channel. That model guides work on drugs and on diseases where these channels fail.
plos-pone-0007774:
Nicole Pohl and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines a protein called selenium-binding protein 1, or SBP1, in colorectal cancer. Levels of SBP1 drop sharply in several human cancers. How the gene is turned down, and what the protein does, were not yet established.

The team found the gene's on-switch is heavily methylated in colon tumors. Methylation is a chemical mark that silences genes. They studied SBP1's function in lab cells and in tumors grown in mice. The work links silencing of this gene to colon cancer growth.
plos-pone-0007874:
Rehan Baqri and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It uses fruit flies to watch what happens when mitochondrial DNA stops copying itself. A faulty version of the copying enzyme, pol gamma, causes several human diseases. They include Parkinson's disease, Alper's syndrome and a progressive eye muscle disorder.

When the enzyme fails, mitochondrial DNA is depleted inside cells. That disrupts the cell's energy supply. Surprisingly, the team found that fast transport along nerve fibers sped up in living flies. The response may be the cell's way of compensating. It offers a fresh clue about mitochondrial disease.
plos-pone-0007974:
Arie Meir and Boris Rubinsky sketched a new route to cheap medical imaging in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fine ultrasound gear costs far more than most clinics on earth can pay. Their plan splits the work: a simple scanner on site, with the hard computing done far away.

Data would travel by wireless links to shared cloud machines, then return as three-dimensional images. Spreading the cost this way could bring scans once found only in rich hospitals to small clinics. The paper lays out the design and the hurdles, as a call to build and test it.
plos-pone-0008074:
Xiaoming Zhou and colleagues built a test for modified crops that skips the usual DNA copying in PLOS ONE in 2009. The standard test multiplies target DNA over and over. That copying can also multiply stray contamination and give false alarms. Food inspectors need a cleaner way to check for gene-modified material.

Their method fishes target DNA out with magnetic beads, then reads it with a light-based technique that watches molecules meet. Skipping the copying step cuts the false-alarm risk at its root. Trials showed the direct test works, offering inspectors a second, independent check.
plos-pone-0008174:
Galina Demina and colleagues found small molecules that block the wake-up call of sleeping tuberculosis germs in PLOS ONE in 2009. TB germs can lie dormant for decades, walled off in the lungs. Proteins called resuscitation promoting factors rouse them, a step drug makers hope to bar.

The team screened for low-weight blockers of those factors and found some that halt both their enzyme work and their waking effect. Keeping latent TB asleep for life would end its threat without a long drug course. The blockers are early leads, but the strategy is sound.
plos-pone-0008274:
Andrew E. Teschendorff and colleagues searched blood for ovarian cancer signals in PLOS ONE in 2009. DNA methylation marks in blood may flag epithelial cancers early. Such marks could serve for diagnosis or risk prediction. No large study had yet tested their potential for ovarian cancer. The team evaluated that potential in a large case-control study.

They found an epigenetic signature in peripheral blood linked to active ovarian cancer. A blood-based signature could catch a cancer that often hides until late. Early detection would greatly improve treatment chances. The study is a step toward a blood test for this disease.
plos-pone-0008374:
Harald Niederstätter and Walther Parson presented a mitochondrial DNA test in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Large studies of mitochondrial DNA need reliable, low-cost, high-throughput genotyping. Haplogroup H is the most common maternal lineage in Europe. Sensitive mixture detection also matters, for example in forensics. Their method uses fluorescent duplex allele-specific PCR with amplicon melting.

One reaction can screen for haplogroup H and reveal mixed samples. Rapid homogeneous assays cut cost and handling steps. That makes population studies and forensic screening more practical. The paper is a methods advance for DNA laboratories.
plos-pone-0008474:
Kristin Fenton and co-authors trace lupus kidney disease in mice in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Lupus nephritis harms the kidneys in the autoimmune disease lupus. Deposits of DNA bits and antibodies build up in kidney filters. Those deposits define the most severe stage. The team study a mouse strain bred to develop lupus. They track antibodies to double-stranded DNA and a kidney enzyme called Dnase1.

They find the antibodies help start the kidney disease. Loss of Dnase1 in the kidney then helps it progress. Two steps thus drive the disease in sequence. Each step is a possible point for treatment to intervene.
plos-pone-0008574:
Gregory Simon and co-authors test a vaccine delivery method in mice in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. They first find HIV Gag peptides that fit a human immune type called HLA-DR4. Peptides are the small bits that immune cells learn to spot. They use computer analysis to pick the best bits. Then they deliver DNA plasmids by way of dendritic cells. The plasmids code for a fusion protein built to route the antigen well.

They vaccinate normal mice and mice carrying the human HLA type. Delivery by dendritic cells boosts T cell responses in those mice. How a vaccine is delivered may matter as much as what it holds. The method targets a common human immune type.
plos-pone-0008674:
Bonnie Taylor-Blake and Mark Zylka study a pain neuron marker in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Thiamine monophosphatase, also known as FRAP, is a classic marker of small dorsal root ganglia neurons. Those neurons carry pain signals from the body. The marker had primarily been studied in the rat. The team previously found that enzyme was molecularly identical to prostatic acid phosphatase. They now examine its expression in mice and rats. They sort nociceptive neurons into peptidergic and nonpeptidergic types.

They find prostatic acid phosphatase is expressed in both neuron types. That broad expression revises its use as a selective marker. It also suggests the enzyme modulates pain signaling widely. The enzyme is a known target of interest for pain treatment.
plos-pone-0008774:
Aya Takesono, Sarah Heasman, Beata Wojciak-Stothard, and colleagues asked how moving T cells keep a clear front and back. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Crawling white blood cells grow a ruffled front and a tail-like rear. Microtubules, the cell's rail-like fibers, are needed for steady directed movement. How they enforce the front-back layout was unknown.

Disturbing microtubules scrambled T cell polarity in their tests. The Rho and ROCK signaling route carried the microtubule effect. With that route mapped, the cell's steering system makes more sense. Immune cells must navigate well to reach infections quickly.
plos-pone-0008874:
Andrew Steptoe, Mark Hamer, Katie O'Donnell, and colleagues linked social rank to hidden heart disease in a famous British cohort. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The Whitehall II study follows civil servants across decades. Heart disease clearly falls harder on lower social grades. Whether that gap reflects vessel disease itself or its later complications was uncertain. Subclinical measures can catch disease before symptoms speak.

Scans and tests measured silent coronary disease across grades. A social gradient appeared already at this hidden stage. Prevention must therefore start earlier in lower-grade groups. The findings strengthen the case for tackling inequality in heart health.
plos-pone-0008974:
Jessica Schwarz and co-authors built a three-dimensional map of fullness signals in the mouse brainstem, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The lower brainstem decides when a meal should end. Signals from the gut arrive there by blood or along nerves. Two spots, the area postrema and the nucleus tractus solitarii, receive those signals.

The team fed mice different nutrients and marked active brain cells with the protein Fos. Fat, protein, and carbohydrate each lit up their own pattern across the brainstem. The 3D maps show the spots are not a single fullness switch. They form a detailed readout of what kind of meal was eaten.
plos-pone-0009074:
Franck Thuny and co-authors linked a strong antibiotic given for heart infection to later weight gain, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Vancomycin treats infective endocarditis, an infection of the heart's inner lining. Gut microbes help decide how much energy food yields. A vancomycin-like drug, avoparcin, was long used to fatten farm animals.

The team tested whether patients gained weight after vancomycin treatment. Recently acquired obesity appeared linked to the therapy. Wiping out gut bacteria may change how much energy patients harvest. The finding adds weight to worries about antibiotics' wider body effects.
plos-pone-0009174:
Sarah Straschewski and co-authors tagged a widespread herpesvirus with a yellow glow for drug screening, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Human cytomegalovirus infects most people and can endanger transplant patients badly. Viruses labelled with glowing proteins are handy tools in the lab. They reveal virus movement, protein location, and gene activity in living cells.

The team built three new viruses carrying yellow glowing fusion proteins. Each virus was checked for normal growth and for brightness in cells. A glowing virus turns drug screening into a simple light measurement. Faster screening matters because current drugs for this virus are few and harsh.
plos-pone-0009274:
Benjamin Geisler, Jeremiah Schuur, and Daniel Pallin published this health study in PLOS ONE in 2010. At the time, U.S. leaders were urging hospitals to switch to digital patient records. Cash rewards were offered for using the new systems well. Emergency rooms stood to gain a lot, but few counts of their uptake existed.

The authors used national data to gauge how many emergency rooms had gone digital. Their figures set a starting point for the years that followed. With that baseline, leaders could later judge whether the rewards worked. The study catches U.S. emergency care just as it began to go digital.
plos-pone-0009374:
Sarada Bulchand and co-authors published this fly muscle study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fly body muscles are built by fusion. A founder cell merges with streams of partner cells, growing into one large fiber with many nuclei. A surface protein called Dumbfounded sits on the founder cell and guides the process.

The team studied Dumbfounded's tail, the part inside the cell. That tail affects how efficiently myoblasts fuse. It also interacts with two other proteins, Rolling Pebbles and Loner. Mapping these contacts explains how a surface signal is converted into the mechanics of cells merging into muscle.
plos-pone-0009474:
Benjamin Schuster-Bockler, Donald Conrad, and Alex Bateman studied copy number changes in human DNA in PLOS ONE in 2010. People differ in how many copies of some DNA stretches they carry. Some genes suffer if their copy count changes at all. Others tolerate extra or missing copies with ease. The team used genome data to see how this plays out over time.

Genes that are hurt by dose changes tend to keep a stable copy count across people. Tolerant genes vary much more freely. The pattern shows that dose sensitivity shapes which parts of the genome can change. It helps explain why some copy changes cause disease while others cause no harm.
plos-pone-0009574:
Kevin Emerson, William Bradshaw, and Christina Holzapfel studied a winter sleeping mosquito in PLOS ONE in 2010. Wyeomyia smithii lives in pitcher plants and spends winter as a larva in diapause, a deep rest. Day length starts, keeps, and ends that rest. When days grow long, the larva wakes. The team used gene chips to catch the first gene changes at waking.

Genes switched on in waves as diapause ended. The study lists the early players in that waking program. Because populations differ in their timing, the work also speaks to adaptation. It reveals the alarm clock that times an insect's year to the light.
plos-pone-0009674:
Stephen Bottoms and co-authors separated the roles of related proteins in mouse asthma in PLOS ONE in 2010. Asthma involves airway inflammation and long term remodeling of the airway walls. Proteins of the TGF beta family are deeply involved in both processes. The family has several isoforms, near copies with distinct jobs. The team tested what each isoform does in a mouse model of asthma.

Different isoforms regulated inflammation and remodeling in different ways. Lumping them together had blurred the picture. Sorting out each one's role opens the way to more precise drugs. A treatment might block the harmful isoform while sparing a helpful one.
plos-pone-0009774:
Meritxell Genovart and co-authors published an ecology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study asks whether birds of prey take prey at random, or pick out weak targets. The team used a culling program for yellow-legged gulls, in which some birds were killed by raptors and others were shot at random.

Careful study of the bodies showed that raptors did not hunt at random. They took young birds, sick birds, and birds in poor muscle shape more often than chance predicts. Birds in oddly good muscle shape were also taken more than expected. The authors call this a clear case of selection at work in the wild.
plos-pone-0009874:
Stem cells meant for therapy can be killed by the patient's own immune guards. Anahid Jewett and colleagues looked for strategies to rescue stem cells from that attack. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dental pulp stem cells come from inside teeth.

The attackers are NK cells, natural killer cells that destroy abnormal cells on sight. The cells at risk were mesenchymal stem cells and dental pulp stem cells. Cytotoxicity is the killing power NK cells aim at their targets. Protecting grafted stem cells could make regenerative treatments last longer.
plos-pone-0009974:
Gene therapy vectors can switch genes on with a drug, but the switch itself may alarm the immune system. David Markusic and colleagues tested a timing trick to dodge that alarm in rats. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The switch is rtTA, a protein that turns genes on when given a trigger drug. The team separated lentiviral vector injection from induction of gene expression in time. That delay did not prevent an immune response to rtTA. The negative result steers gene therapy design away from a tempting fix.
plos-pone-0010174:
The authors were Katinka Vigh-Conrad, Donald Conrad, and Daphne Preuss. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study built a new allergy screening tool. Standard allergy tests, like skin pricks, cannot screen many allergens cheaply at once. Extracts for those tests also come from washed pollen, which loses surface material that may itself trigger allergies in patients.

The team built a protein allergen microarray holding many allergens on one chip. It detected specific IgE antibodies to pollen surface, cytoplasmic, and commercial extracts. One broad, cheap screen could change how clinics find a patient's true triggers.
plos-pone-0010274:
The authors were Antoine Popelut, Fabien Valet, Olivier Fromentin, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study asked whether industry sponsorship skews dental implant results. Dental implant treatment grows every year, with competing firms making the devices. In drug research, reviews show industry-funded trials more often report pro-industry results, raising concern for other device fields.

The team systematically related sponsorship to implant failure rates in the literature. If sponsored studies report fewer failures, patients and dentists deserve to know. Their approach gives clinics a way to weigh implant evidence with funding in view.
plos-pone-0010374:
Birgitte Forst and colleagues studied two proteins that may drive tumor spread together, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The tissue around a tumor shapes how it grows and moves. One protein, S100A4, is known to promote that spread in animals. It had also been seen in human breast cancer samples. The team asked how it works with a second signal, called RANTES.

In mice, the two together pushed tumors forward more than either alone. Their cooperation seems to help build a tumor-friendly neighborhood. Blocking such teamwork is a different strategy from attacking tumor cells directly. It aims at the soil rather than the seed, in the old phrase. The study gives that strategy two named targets to test.
plos-pone-0010474:
Lia Danelishvili and co-workers identified two tuberculosis proteins that help the bacterium spare its host cell for PLOS ONE in 2010. Macrophages are immune cells that swallow bacteria, then often kill themselves to help destroy them. TB bacteria block that suicide, staying alive inside the cell. Which bacterial proteins do the blocking was the question. The team pointed to two secreted proteins, Rv3654c and Rv3655c.

Released by the bacteria, these proteins take part in suppressing the host cell's death. A pathogen that disarms its jailer's last weapon gains a safe home. Blocking those proteins could restore the cell's defense. The study also clarifies how TB persists for years in people. It names specific tools in the bacterium's survival kit.
plos-pone-0010574:
Dan Stein and colleagues used survey data from many countries for a PLOS ONE study in 2010. The data came from the World Health Organization's World Mental Health Surveys. The team asked which kinds of traumatic events are most closely tied to suicidal thoughts, plans, and attempts.

Not every trauma carried the same risk. Some events predicted the first appearance of suicidal behavior better than others. The pattern also differed for moving from thoughts to actual attempts. Sorting out those differences helps health workers focus support on people whose history puts them at greatest risk.
plos-pone-0010674:
James Hunt and colleagues asked when paper wasps become set toward queen or worker life, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Polistes wasps live in small nests where caste is not fixed at birth. A well-fed female may become a queen, while others work. The species is a model for how insect societies first arose.

Genes and proteins already leaned toward one fate early in adult life. The lean showed before clear outward signs appeared. So caste bias starts inside the body well ahead of behavior. Finding that early lean helps explain how loose groups of equals could harden into queens and workers over time.
plos-pone-0010774:
Andy Fischer, Christopher Zelinka, and Melissa Scott compared support cells in bird and mammal eyes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Glia are the support crew of the nervous system, feeding and guarding neurons. The retina holds several glial types. A new type had just been found scattered through the bird retina, raising the question of how widespread such variety is.

Glial mixes differed between birds and mammals and between retina and optic nerve. Some types appeared in one group only. The bird retina also held glia that respond to growth signals by multiplying. Eye support systems, it turns out, evolved along separate paths even in close vertebrate kin.
plos-pone-0010874:
Qian Liu, Dae In Kim, Janet Syme and co-authors published this cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lamin A is a protein mesh that lines the inside of the cell nucleus, and it is built from a precursor that must be trimmed in several steps. A faulty trimming step causes Hutchinson-Gilford progeria, a disease of rapid aging in children.

Drugs that block the trimming steps are used in treatment trials, and some HIV drugs block the final step as a side effect.
