The team tracked how precursor protein built up and cleared when each drug was applied and then washed away. Recovery after the HIV-type block was fast, while other effects lingered. Liu and colleagues clarify the timing of these drug actions, useful knowledge for dosing progeria therapy safely.
plos-pone-0010974:
Dwain Irvin, Emmanuel Jouanneau, Gretchen Duvall and co-authors published this brain tumor study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Malignant gliomas contain a minority of stem-like cells that can regenerate the whole tumor, and most knowledge about them came from artificial lab settings. The team asked how immune activity inside a real tumor changes that stem-like character.

They defined stemness by gene pattern similarity, finding it stronger in lower-grade tumors, then compared human glioblastomas before and after a dendritic cell vaccine. Stemness rose after vaccination and tracked best with vaccine-altered genes and the patient's own anti-tumor T cell activity. Mouse tumors confirmed that immune pressure can enrich stem-like traits. Irvin and colleagues deliver a warning for immunotherapy: pushing a tumor with T cells may also make its most dangerous cells more stem-like.
plos-pone-0011074:
Weidong Xiong, Marianela Candolfi, Chunyan Liu and co-authors published this brain tumor therapy study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Glioblastoma is the commonest primary brain tumor in adults and one of the deadliest. The team is developing a gene therapy. It pairs an immune-stimulating cytokine, Flt3L, with a conditional cell-killing gene. They aim to test it in pet dogs with spontaneous tumors, as a bridge to human trials.

A key doubt was whether the human cytokine works on dog immune cells. Delivered by an adenovirus vector into dog blood cell cultures, human Flt3L generated dendritic cells closely matching those raised with dog immune factors in shape and surface markers. Xiong and colleagues clear a make-or-break checkpoint: the human ingredient can raise the canine immune instructors the therapy depends on, so a dog clinical trial can proceed.
plos-pone-0011174:
Bonte, De Roissart, Vandegehuchte and colleagues linked soil and plant eaters in PLOS ONE in 2010. Life in the soil changes how plants grow above ground. Insects and other herbivores that feed on those plants may then adapt locally to the plant forms the soil life creates.

The team tested whether such local adaptation really occurs in the herbivores. A proven link would tie the hidden half of ecosystems to the visible half. That matters for farming, where soil management shapes pests above ground. It also expands the idea of adaptation to span two linked habitats at once.
plos-pone-0011274:
Fukuda, Cao, Morita and colleagues profiled cloned mouse embryos in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cloning resets an adult cell's gene program, but the reset is often faulty. By reading all active genes in single early cloned embryos, the team identified genes that were reprogrammed wrongly.

Those mis-set genes mark the weak points of cloning. Fixing them could raise the low success rate of cloning and improve stem cell work based on it. Single embryo analysis matters because each clone fails in partly its own way. The catalogue of errors gives researchers a checklist for improving the reset.
plos-pone-0011374:
Carla Yuede and colleagues studied in 2010 how certain brain drugs given to infant mice affect later behavior. The drugs block a receptor that helps brain cells communicate, and they are used in anesthesia and some treatments. In very young animals, blocking that receptor can trigger widespread death of developing brain cells, a risk that worried doctors who treat infants.

The team linked that early cell death to lasting changes in how the mice behaved as they grew. Animals exposed as infants performed differently on behavior tests than unexposed animals. The work does not settle how the drugs should be used in children, but it sharpens the concern with direct evidence. It urges care in dosing the youngest patients and supports research into safer ways to sedate infant brains.
plos-pone-0011474:
Taras Oleksyk and co-authors mapped in 2010 the worldwide spread of kidney risk variants near the MYH9 gene. People of African ancestry suffer kidney disease at far higher rates than other groups, and much of that excess risk traces to this gene region. The team charted its risk forms and haplotypes, the sets of variants inherited together, across populations worldwide.

Risk forms proved common in Africa and rare elsewhere, with signs that natural selection had favored them in Africa in the past. A variant kept because it once protected against something, perhaps an infection, can exact a kidney price in modern life. That trade-off story matters for medicine and for fairness in genetics. Risk tests and donor screening built on other populations would miss the pattern entirely, so ancestry-aware research is a clinical need, not a courtesy.
plos-pone-0011574:
Benedikta Haflidadóttir and co-authors showed in 2010 that a small RNA dials down the master switch of pigment cells in melanoma. Mitf governs the identity of melanocytes, the pigment-making cells, and in melanoma, the deadliest skin cancer, its control goes awry, helping tumors grow and spread. The team tested microRNA-148, a tiny regulator, against Mitf in melanoma cells.

MiR-148 regulated Mitf levels, giving the cell, and potentially a drug, a handle on a cancer-driving switch. MicroRNAs are attractive handles because one small RNA can tune a whole program, not just one protein. Turning Mitf down will not cure melanoma alone, since its role shifts with tumor state, and the paper adds the knowledge needed to judge when the dial helps. A defined regulator of a defined switch is the kind of precise fact that later therapies are built from.
plos-pone-0011674:
Stanislaw Schastak and co-authors tested light-activated treatment against drug-resistant bacteria, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rising antibiotic resistance worldwide has created an urgent need for other ways to kill bacteria. Photodynamic therapy pairs a light-sensitive dye with illumination to produce a toxic burst that destroys germs.

Their dye, THPTS, is switched on by infrared light, which penetrates tissue more deeply than visible light. It proved effective against both major bacterial groups, Gram-positive and Gram-negative. A light-based method that works across both groups could treat stubborn infections that antibiotics can no longer touch.
plos-pone-0011774:
Davide Danovi and co-authors screened mammalian genes for a hallmark of cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Growth without anchorage is a hallmark of oncogenic transformation, letting cancer cells proliferate away from their site of origin. Earlier Schwann cell experiments had shown one viral protein alone was not fully sufficient to grant that ability.

Their genetic screen searched for genes that confer anchorage-independent proliferation. It identified a membrane-bound neuregulin, a growth signal fixed to the cell surface. Naming this driver gives cancer researchers a fresh lead on how tumour-like growth begins.
plos-pone-0011874:
Ami Schlesinger and co-workers described in 2010 the unusually flexible sex life of a sea anemone, Aiptasia diaphana. Questions about what shapes mating systems sit at the heart of evolutionary biology. Anemones are fixed in place as adults, so finding a mate of the right sex at the right time is not guaranteed.

Through experiments, the team showed that this species can shift its sex in response to conditions and can even fertilize itself. Such flexibility is a strong fallback for an animal that cannot go searching for partners. The study gives a concrete case of how the local setting can bend a trait as basic as whether an animal is male, female, or both at once.
plos-pone-0011974:
Jun Hong Xia and colleagues built in 2010 the first physical genome map of the Asian seabass, a major farmed food fish in Southeast Asia and Australia. Selective breeding had improved the species since the nineteen-nineties, and marker tools were accumulating. A physical map based on BAC clones, large stored DNA pieces, was the missing scaffold.

The map orders those clones along the chromosomes, giving researchers fixed addresses for genes. Breeders can then tie traits such as growth and disease resistance to map positions. For an industry species, that scaffold shortens the path from a good fish to a better breeding line.
plos-pone-0012074:
Tessa van Leeuwen, Karl Magnus Petersson, and Peter Hagoort scanned in 2010 the brains of synaesthetes, people whose letters automatically trigger colors. In synaesthesia, stimulation in one sense produces experiences in another, unstimulated sense. How the brain mediates that extra experience bears on how normal perception and awareness work.

Comparing synaesthetes with matched controls by fMRI, the team found synaesthetic color processing reaching beyond the brain's standard color areas. Extra areas joining in suggests the experience is built by a wider network, not a single mis-wired patch. That changes where researchers should look for the difference between synaesthetic and ordinary brains.
plos-pone-0012174:
Peter Lenting, Geertje Westerlaken, Cécile Denis, and co-authors studied a natural brake on platelet clumping, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Collagen, exposed when a vessel wall tears, is one of the strongest triggers for platelets to activate and stick. Immune cells carry a collagen receptor that calms them, and a loose, soluble relative of that receptor floats free and can interfere with its work.

The loose relative proved to block collagen-driven platelet activation and sticking quite well. A natural molecule that safely damps clotting at injury sites is a promising lead. It could inspire anti-clotting drugs that prevent harmful clots while leaving normal healing better intact than current drugs do.
plos-pone-0012274:
Edwin Jacox, Valer Gotea, Ivan Ovcharenko, and co-authors mapped the alternative starting points of human genes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many genes can begin transcription at more than one promoter, a choice that produces different message versions and helps each tissue build its own identity. Promoters near the gene's main start behave differently from those set farther away, and the team charted which styles serve single tissues and which serve all.

A map of promoter habits explains part of how one genome yields a brain cell and a liver cell. It also helps interpret disease variants that fall in promoter regions. Gene regulation studies lean on reference maps of exactly this kind.
plos-pone-0012374:
Patricia Mateo-Tomás and Pedro Olea mapped future habitat for the griffon vulture in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. This large scavenger crashed in numbers during past decades but is now spreading back into old range in Europe. Knowing where it can live next lets land managers plan protection before the birds arrive, rather than after conflicts start.

The authors combined sighting records with land and climate data to predict suitable areas across the region. Their maps show both the current range and the empty but suitable land the species is likely to fill. Such forecasts help place feeding stations, guard power lines, and ease tensions with farmers in the zones vultures will colonize next.
plos-pone-0012474:
Mark Chen, Ian Barr, Gerald Koh and colleagues measured antibody responses in patients with confirmed pandemic H1N1 flu, in a 2010 PLOS ONE observational study. All cases were verified by the genetic test RT-PCR during the 2009 pandemic. Knowing how antibody levels rise after real infection helps set the thresholds used to judge past infection in blood surveys.

The team ran two standard antibody assays, hemagglutination inhibition and virus neutralization, on patient samples over time. The two tests agreed in broad strokes but differed in detail. Their comparison tells labs what each assay can and cannot prove when tracking a pandemic through a population.
plos-pone-0012574:
John Soechting, Hrishikesh Rao and John Juveli refined models of how eyes track moving targets, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Smooth pursuit keeps a moving object centered on the retina, and the eye plainly predicts where the target goes next: it can follow slow wavy motion too well for pure reaction. How much prediction contributes to the command signal was the issue.

The authors built prediction into their two-dimensional pursuit models and checked them against eye recordings. Models with a predictive component matched human tracking far better. Better tracking models feed into neurology, where pursuit faults flag disease, and into robotics, where cameras must follow motion smoothly.
plos-pone-0012674:
Sato, Poynter, Huss and co-authors filmed blood vessels as they form inside quail embryos. How flat sheets of cells fold into tubes and organs is one of biology's deepest questions. Their 2010 study used quail carrying glowing tags in their vessel cells, so growth could be watched live.

Time-lapse views show vessel networks sprouting, joining and reshaping step by step. Watching the process beats guessing from still images, since wrong turns and repairs become visible. The method gives developmental biology a moving picture of a basic event. The quail model is now a shared tool for that work.
plos-pone-0012774:
Reece, Loh, Alcantara and co-authors linked the timing of viral escape to whether a vaccine works. A good HIV vaccine must hold the virus down hard enough that escape mutants never gain ground. Broad immunity is thought to be part of that answer, since it corners the virus on several sides.

Their 2010 study watched when escape mutations appeared in relation to vaccine success or failure. Early escape spelled failure, while delayed escape matched control. The timing itself becomes a useful early readout in vaccine trials, long before final outcomes are known.
plos-pone-0012874:
Hoving, Heeneman, Gijbels and co-authors tested aspirin variants against two kinds of artery disease in mice lacking ApoE. Earlier work showed radiation to neck arteries speeds up fatty, inflamed plaques in these mice. Their 2010 study compared NO-donating aspirin and plain aspirin across age-driven and radiation-driven disease.

The drugs partly slowed the age-related form but did not help the radiation-induced form. That split shows the two kinds of plaque are not the same disease underneath. Cancer survivors with radiation-linked artery risk need different protection.
plos-pone-0323074:
Jemina Villanen and Arve Vorland Pedersen compare elite men's and women's golf using season data from the two top professional tours. Women play shorter courses under much the same rules, yet body size and strength differ on average. Their 2026 study gathers scoring and course data from every event in one season on both tours to see where play diverges.

Women drove the ball more accurately than men but scored fewer very low rounds and rare hole-out feats. Course lengths for women ran about nine-tenths of the men's. The authors argue that scaling still falls short of matching body differences, leaving women's golf relatively more demanding. Fairer course setup, they suggest, would let skill show more cleanly.
plos-pone-0338874:
Md Khan and six colleagues mine a traditional Chinese herb for breast cancer compounds, entirely by computer. Their 2026 study starts with Scutellaria barbata, a plant with a long anticancer reputation. Thirty-four plant chemicals were profiled for drug-likeness and safety. Three flavonoids passed the filters. Network analysis then mapped their likely human targets. Three hub proteins emerged, all central to cancer signalling. Docking simulations tested how snugly each compound grips those targets.

One compound, apigenin, took the headline. It bound the master growth switch AKT1 strongly. Its simulated complex also proved the most stable over a long virtual run. A sister compound actually docked slightly tighter, but moved more. Nothing here has touched a cell, let alone a patient. The contribution is triage. From a whole herb's chemistry, the study picks one prioritised molecule and target. Laboratory testing can now confirm or kill the idea cheaply.
plos-pone-0341174:
Huagang Shan and colleagues combined drone photography with advanced rock mechanics modelling to judge the stability of a layered rock slope in Shaoxing, China. Slopes cut through tilted, cracked rock layers fail in complicated ways. Drone images became a detailed three-dimensional model, and a statistical rock-mass model captured how the layered material deforms unevenly under stress.

The simulated weak-plane direction matched the observed one within a degree. The analysis pinpointed pockets of poor rock with high failure probability needing extra support, while the slope as a whole held a comfortable safety margin. The authors present the workflow as a fast, visual route to targeted slope reinforcement.
plos-pone-0347574:
Hanbit Jin and colleagues describe a planned South Korean registry following homebound older adults who receive traditional Korean medicine home care. Many frail elders wish to age in place, yet evidence on home medical services is thin. The 2026 protocol sets up six home care centres to enrol about two hundred fifty patients over sixty-five with declining function.

Over one year the registry will track daily-living ability as its main outcome, plus frailty, pain, deaths, long hospital stays, and moves into care facilities. It will also ask which patients respond best. As a protocol, it reports design, not findings. The results should inform how home care for ageing in place is judged.
plos-pone-0347774:
Manisha Mangal and colleagues compared two resistant chilli lines with one susceptible line under attack by fruit rot fungi that devastate hot pepper crops. Leaves and fruit were challenged with two rot species, then defence enzymes, phenol build up, lesion size, and defence gene timing were measured in each line.

Resistant lines kept lesions small, ran defence enzymes hot, and switched defence genes on early and strongly, with one key gene rising near a thousandfold. The susceptible line answered late and weakly, with late surges that came too late to stop rot. Breeding for speed of defence, not just its presence, may be the trait that saves chilli harvests.
plos-pone-0347874:
Brendan Boyle and co-authors tested in 2026 how authentic leadership, leaders who act openly and by their values, affects team members' extra mile behaviour at work. Earlier results were mixed, and the team suspected belonging and professional identity hold the key.

Two recall experiments and a field survey of sixty healthcare teams supplied the data. Authentic leadership raised extra effort through stronger team identification, but only in mixed profession teams where members' own professional identity was weak. Where professional pride ran strong, the path faded. The conditional result explains past mixed findings and warns managers that one leadership style lands differently across team types.
plos-pone-0348074:
Rui Lu and colleagues compared five trauma scoring systems at four major trauma centres in China and Thailand, asking which best predicts death in injured patients over sixty-five. Nearly one thousand elderly patients treated during 2023 were scored by anatomical, physiological, and combined systems, and the results set against actual survival.

About eight percent died in hospital. The combined TRISS score predicted death best, followed by a geriatric-specific score and a physiology-based one, while pure anatomy scores trailed. Age, cancer history, clotting measures, transfusion, and consciousness level independently raised risk. The authors recommend the leading scores for early triage of elderly trauma patients in Asia.
plos-pone-0348174:
Alexandra DiGiacomo, Samantha Andrzejaczek, and Barbara Block measured white sharks in Monterey Bay without touching them, using drones and underwater cameras. Body size governs growth and maturity, yet measuring a free-swimming great white is nearly impossible by hand. Their computer vision pipeline extracts total length and a girth-based condition score from aerial images, checked against underwater footage.

Sharks of different sizes grouped in different parts of the bay along ocean temperature and depth gradients, suggesting the coast serves as a series of nurseries and staging areas as sharks age. Eastern Pacific whites carried proportionally more girth than other populations, especially females. Tracking size structure from the air lets scientists watch how a protected predator uses its habitat across its whole life.
plos-pone-0348274:
Zewei Wang and colleagues tested a drug already known to cancer researchers as a reliever of acute gout in rats. Gout flares when urate crystals ignite an immune alarm complex inside joints. The drug blocks a gene-silencing enzyme and, through that, the alarm. Rats with crystal-injected joints received the drug or the standard gout medicine colchicine, and their joints, blood, and tissues were examined closely.

Treated rats walked better, with less swelling and milder joint inflammation, and their blood carried far less of the inflammatory messengers gout releases. The joint alarm complex quieted, while the cells' internal recycling and energy recovered, shown by restored power levels and revived cleanup proteins. Kidney damage eased too. The authors trace the benefit to calming the alarm while boosting cellular cleanup, and propose the drug as a gout candidate.
plos-pone-0348574:
Ruxandra Malina Petrescu-Mag and co-authors named a neglected barrier to climate action: boredom with the climate topic itself. Fear and hope dominate research on climate psychology, yet sheer disengagement may quietly sap the will to act. Their 2026 survey of a representative sample of Romanian adults modeled what predicts climate boredom and whether boredom, in turn, dulls the intention to act.

Beliefs about climate change, commitment to climate goals, confidence in cooperating with others, perceived health effects, living environment, and age together explained about two thirds of the variation in boredom. Boredom then significantly weakened people's intention to act. The authors argue that climate communication must fight fatigue as well as denial, refreshing motivation before disengagement hardens into inaction.
plos-pone-0348674:
Minji Park and colleagues compared two virus shells for delivering anti-cancer genes into natural killer cells, a type of immune cell being engineered into cancer therapy. The gene package carries instructions for a chimeric antigen receptor that aims the cell at tumors. Getting the package into killer cells so it stays switched on has been a persistent problem.

The standard shell gave a brief burst of receptor expression that quickly faded, and its DNA broke down inside the cells. The baboon-virus shell, by contrast, kept the receptor expressed, integrated its DNA durably, and preserved the cells' tumor-killing power, in both a cell line and real donor cells. Delivery vehicles decide whether cell therapies are practical, so a sturdier shell is a meaningful advance.
plos-pone-0348774:
Kasiye Shiferaw and co-workers study the link between teenagers going hungry and common mental health problems in Ethiopia's Harari Region. Most earlier work measured hunger at the household level, not the teenager's own experience. Their 2026 study surveys more than three thousand three hundred school adolescents with checked scales for food insecurity, mood problems, self-esteem, and quality of life.

About one in seven teens faced moderate to severe food insecurity, and close to a quarter showed signs of common mental disorders. Hunger itself predicted more symptoms, as did substance use and frequent money trouble at home. Better quality of life, stronger self-esteem, and city living were protective. Feeding teens, the authors argue, is also mental health policy.
plos-pone-0348874:
Shabani and colleagues, in a 2026 study, audit how well Tanzania's routine health data system counts newborn deaths. Global goals call for cutting newborn death rates sharply by 2030, and Tanzania is off track; its survey rate implies tens of thousands of newborn deaths a year. The team pulled a decade of records from twenty-eight regional and seven top referral hospitals.

The system recorded only a fraction of the expected deaths, a few thousand a year rather than the survey-based figure. Hospitals filed monthly reports only a bit over half the time, and top hospitals reported less reliably than regional ones. Few hospitals were even internally consistent from year to year. The official system's newborn death rate for 2024 came out about four times lower than the household survey's. The authors say the missing babies are a data problem first: fix reporting, and planning can start from truth.
plos-pone-0349074:
Yusuke Haruna and colleagues built an artificial intelligence model that outlines the eye muscles on MRI scans of people with thyroid eye disease. The single-center study, from a hospital in Osaka, used scans from fifty-two patients whose muscles had been traced by hand. The model learned from those tracings and was tested against them.

Accuracy improved as the training set grew from twelve to fifty-two cases, and the model's brightness measures inside the muscles matched hand measures closely. Swollen eye muscles drive much of the harm in this disease, so fast and consistent outlining could help doctors stage it and follow treatment. The gains with more training cases show data size matters.
plos-pone-0349574:
Junyi Ren and colleagues catalogued seven families of phosphate transporter proteins, the gates that move phosphorus into and within plant cells, across forty species from bacteria to flowering plants. Phosphorus is essential for growth yet scarce in most soils, so these transporters decide how well a plant feeds. The team compared the proteins' sequences, structures, and shared motifs.

They counted more than two thousand transporters in total, some families numbering in the hundreds. They also mapped how active each family's genes are in roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and fruit in eight vegetable species, including under phosphorus starvation. The family portrait helps breeders and engineers target the right transporter when improving how crops use fertilizer.
plos-pone-0349674:
Yanfang Mo and colleagues put a new lab machine, the Molecision R8, through its paces. The machine does the whole gene test on its own: it pulls the gene strands out of a sample and then runs the search in one sealed box. Gene tests are strong but slow by hand, and a sealed, hands-off run cuts both time and mix-ups. The team checked each part and the whole box against trusted machines.

They used a hepatitis B test and a three-in-one test for three common infections spread through sex. Readings wobbled by less than five percent, tracked the trusted machines with only tiny gaps, and matched on the germ tests more than ninety-six times in a hundred. For busy labs, proof like this means same-day results they can trust.
plos-pone-0349774:
Mytien Nguyen and colleagues examined scores on the second big licensing exam for American medical students, sorted by disability status, race, and ethnicity. Since the first exam went pass-fail, this Step 2 score carries heavy weight in residency selection, raising fears it could deepen unfairness. The study drew on records from nine medical schools covering the classes of 2020 to 2023.

Students registered with disability offices were matched with similar peers by school, gender, class year, and entrance scores, so gaps could be read more cleanly. Students in groups underrepresented in medicine were analyzed alongside. Score gaps at this gate matter because they shape who becomes a specialist and who treats which communities.
plos-pone-0350274:
Boxuan Xu and colleagues in China published a trial plan in 2026 on mixing two sedatives for gut endoscopy. Each drug alone has drawbacks, from slowed breathing to muscle twitching and sickness after waking. No results are reported yet.

One hundred thirty-five adults will be split at random among one drug alone and two set mixtures. The main measure combines side effects such as low blood pressure, low oxygen, and pain at the injection site. Sleep success, waking times, and patient satisfaction count too. A safer mix would make a very common procedure gentler for patients and staff alike.
plos-pone-0351074:
Malak Mashaabi and Hend Al-Khalifa built an automatic checker for Arabic privacy policies under Saudi Arabias data protection law. Reading each policy by hand to judge compliance is slow and costly. Their system, called Mumtathil, labels which legal duties a policy covers. Training data joined an older Saudi set with newer policies and computer made examples to fix lopsided coverage.

A classic support vector method beat both other classic learners and two Arabic language transformers, reaching a top score in the low nineties. That result is striking, since transformers often win on text tasks. A simple, well fed classic model, the authors show, can give firms and regulators a fast, clear first pass on privacy compliance.
plos-pone-0351174:
Qingqing He, Jianhua Deng, and Guixin Yuan crushed cracked sandstone samples to see how water and crack angle jointly weaken rock. Water soaked rock fails more easily, which matters for tunnels, slopes, and dams. Samples were tested dry, natural, and soaked, with single cracks set at five angles from flat to upright, while energy flows during crushing were tracked.

Soaked samples lost roughly a third to over half their peak strength versus dry ones. Strength rose as crack angle steepened. Two new ratios captured how cracks weaken rock at first cracking and at spread. An energy based warning sign rose with wetness and peaked at two middle angles, which may help forecast rock failure in wet ground.
plos-pone-0351574:
Transplanting gut microbes from a healthy donor can ease irritable bowel syndrome, and Ying Fei and colleagues searched gene data for how the treatment works. Their 2026 PLOS One analysis reused colon tissue data from eight patients before and after transplant, plus single-cell data from healthy colons.

Ten genes stood out where changed genes overlapped a strongly linked gene network. Those genes pointed at switching on CD8 T cells, a class of immune killer cells, and immune mapping showed more of those cells after treatment. The team also screened drug databases for compounds touching the genes. The work is computational, offering targets for lab confirmation rather than proof.
plos-pone-0351774:
Chunxiang Li and three colleagues set out a plan, published as a protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026, for clarifying what dignity means for older people living in nursing homes. The idea is widely praised in care policy but rarely pinned down, and the authors give special weight to Chinese cultural views. Their planned review will gather earlier qualitative studies about residents' own experiences.

Under the plan, three reviewers will screen studies from seven databases and judge their quality with standard appraisal tools. Findings will then be merged to describe dignity's core features, from bodily needs to personal worth. A clearer concept could guide staff training and shape how homes are judged.
plos-pone-0351874:
Bernice Hoenderboom and colleagues asked Dutch young adults about a test that does not exist yet. The test would predict a person's risk of fertility harm from chlamydia. That infection is often silent, yet it can scar reproductive organs. The team ran focus groups first. A survey of over four hundred young adults followed, reached through sexual health centers and social media.

Nearly four in five said they would take such a test. Most expected relief from a low-risk result. Most also expected worry from a high-risk one, along with a chance to prepare. Accuracy, easy access, and good follow-up care ranked as firm demands. A few questioned the worth of knowing a risk they cannot change. Developers now know the demand is real.
plos-pone-0352174:
Serena Rossi and three colleagues examine this 2026 PLOS One psychometric study of a short questionnaire that measures anxiety about mathematics. The scale is used worldwide, but researchers had not checked whether its questions mean the same thing to students in different countries. The team analyzed answers from more than thirty-six hundred university students in the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy, and Poland.

The questionnaire worked nearly identically across the four countries, with only one of its items behaving differently, so average anxiety levels can fairly be compared between these groups. One caution stood out: the conclusions depended noticeably on which statistical estimator the analysts chose. The authors urge researchers to test measurement equivalence before comparing groups, and to choose their methods with care.
plos-pone-0352674: English ‘be going to’ — its grammaticalization revisited with corpora. This paper traced the future marker’s evolution. The findings illuminate how yesterday’s movement verb became tomorrow’s grammar — language change in action.
plos-pone-0352874:
Masahiro Hemmi and three co-authors study throat surgery for a paralyzed vocal fold in Japan. A paralyzed fold harms both voice and swallowing. Surgery that improves voice might also keep food and drink out of the lungs, and so prevent pneumonia. The team used a large insurance database of workers and their families. It covered diagnoses from 2013 to 2022. They matched operated and unoperated patients with similar profiles.

The two analyses disagreed. Matched comparisons hinted that operated patients got pneumonia slightly more often, but the hint was not certain. A second analysis compared each patient's own record before and after surgery. It showed pneumonia rates falling sharply after the operation. Given the conflict, the authors claim no firm protective effect. They call for studies designed to settle the question.
plos-pone-0352974:
Waithaka Huria Karugu and two colleagues examine this 2026 PLOS One study of what makes building projects in the Nairobi metropolitan area succeed or fail. Poor handling of risk and contracts is blamed for the cost overruns and delays common in Kenyan construction. The researchers surveyed sixty-four completed residential and non-residential projects about their management practices and the skills of their managers.

Both risk management and contract management practices significantly predicted better project performance, together explaining about three-fifths of the differences between projects. Managers' skills, surprisingly, added little and did not strengthen the effect of the formal practices. The authors conclude that solid systems for handling risk and contracts matter most, and they recommend firms invest there first.
plos-pone-0353174:
Kaiying Chen and six colleagues published this 2026 PLOS One study of the bacteria carried by chiggers, the tiny mite larvae that spread scrub typhus. The team collected free-living chiggers across North Carolina's mountain, piedmont, and coastal plain regions and used DNA sequencing to identify both the mite species and their bacterial communities. They also tested which chiggers carried Orientia, the scrub typhus agent.

Three chigger species turned up, and bacterial communities differed by collection site. In the most common species, infected and uninfected chiggers carried measurably different bacteria, with some genera more common in infected mites. Sequences from several potentially harmful bacterial genera also appeared. The authors suggest place and infection status together shape a chigger's microbes, which may in turn affect how well it transmits disease.
plos-pone-0353274:
Amin and colleagues created and checked a teaching booklet for people with scarring lung disease in India in a 2026 study. Late diagnosis and weak patient teaching worsen outcomes for this illness. The booklet was built in stages, starting with a review of key teaching themes, then expert review, then feedback from patients.

Expert agreement on the booklet's content rose to a perfect score after revisions. Ten patients who read it all judged it clear, relevant, and well designed. A version shaped by local culture and language can help patients grasp daily care, warning signs, and treatment choices. The team offers the booklet as a ready aid for clinics serving similar patients.
plos-pone-0353374:
Justin Hoffmann, Christopher Mai, and Ricardo Buettner build a deep-learning method that identifies diseases on radish leaves without being fooled by the leaf itself, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Field photographs are messy: veins, folds, and dirt can masquerade as disease spots to a neural network. Their approach was designed to weigh disease-specific signs against such surface distractions, and was tested on a peer-reviewed set of nearly three thousand leaf images in five classes.

Across repeated validation folds the method averaged accuracy just under one hundred percent — the best reported on this dataset. Reliable leaf diagnosis from photographs could speed crop scouting and post-harvest sorting, cutting both losses and waste.
plos-pone-0353474:
Butt and Handy tracked daily mood and self-rated thinking in young adults in a 2026 study. In older adults, wobbly day-to-day thinking can signal decline. Whether similar wobbles mean anything in healthy young people was unclear. More than two hundred volunteers reported mood and thinking three times daily for two weeks.

Baseline questionnaires on memory and thinking habits were used to adjust the daily data. Daily ups and downs in felt thinking tracked mood closely in these young adults. That warns against reading young people's daily wobbles as early decline. The study also gives a baseline for comparing groups where daily swings may truly carry meaning.
plos-pone-0353674:
Jaso-Vera and colleagues, in a 2026 study, identify a liver RNA that throttles how the body breaks down amino acids, the building blocks of protein. That breakdown, and the making of urea to clear its waste, keep nitrogen in balance. In fatty liver disease the process is repressed, for reasons that were unknown. The RNA, named hLMR1, is made only in liver cells and does not code for a protein.

In mice carrying human liver cells, silencing the RNA switched the breakdown and urea genes back on broadly. The RNA was found gripping the draft copies of those very genes, through a short matching stretch of its own letters; deleting that stretch killed its effect. In human liver data, more of this RNA went with quieter breakdown programs in fatty liver disease. The authors present hLMR1 as a newly found brake on liver nitrogen handling, and a possible drug target.
plos-pone-0353774:
Leila Ghazaleh and five colleagues ask how much the knee matters for simply standing still, in this 2026 PLOS ONE balance study. They compared twelve people who had undergone ligament reconstruction in the knee with twelve uninjured controls. Motion cameras and force plates tracked joint movements and sway while participants stood quietly, first with eyes open and then closed.

In the reconstructed group the knee took a larger share of the work of keeping the body steady, especially without vision to help. Their sway measures were also worse with eyes closed. The authors say rehabilitation after ligament surgery should train the knee's position sense directly, not just its strength.
plos-pone-0353974:
Seonju Lee and four colleagues feed broiler chickens a preparation of dead bacteria — a postbiotic — and watch their guts and immune systems, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The strain used is a lactic acid bacterium known to calm gut inflammation. Chicks drank water dosed with its culture fluid for twelve days, then received a routine vaccine against a poultry virus, with gut tissue and microbes sampled afterwards.

The treated birds grew no faster, but their gut lining genes for mucus and tight sealing ran higher, and anti-inflammatory signals rose. Their gut microbe mix shifted toward helpful genera, while vaccine antibody responses stayed normal. A calmer, better-sealed gut without growth penalties is exactly what poultry producers want from feed additives.
plos-pone-0354174:
Arvind Chandna and colleagues asked whether the subtle, higher-level vision problems of cerebral visual impairment, where the brain rather than the eyes fails to process sight, persist when affected children grow up. Their 2026 prospective study adapted a fifty-nine-item inventory for adults and compared adults with early-onset impairment against typical adults, adults with later brain injury, and previously studied children.

Deficits were plainly present in the early-onset adults, partly echoing the childhood pattern and partly distinct. The late-injury adults showed a broader, more variable spread, similar enough that the authors question the terminology separating the groups. The adapted inventory worked as a detection tool. Their conclusion is practical: visual brain injury is lifelong, and adult services should keep assessing it.
plos-pone-0354274:
Prasit Mahawongkajit, Porrawat Rodsa, and Saritphat Orrapin published this 2026 CT study measuring belly wall thickness in people with obesity. Surgeons need to know how deep they must reach, yet thickness is rarely measured before surgery. The team measured wall thickness at nine surgical landmark points in just over a hundred patients and compared simple body measurements.

Body mass index tracked thickness moderately and consistently everywhere on the belly, ahead of neck, arm, and waist measures. Mahawongkajit suggests such bedside numbers could one day feed prediction tools for safer surgical access in larger patients.
plos-pone-0354374:
Mohammad Eghbali and colleagues translated a fear-of-side-effects questionnaire into Persian and tested it with Iranian cancer patients. Fear of chemotherapy side effects can harm mental wellbeing and weaken commitment to treatment. Their 2026 study worked with several hundred patients at a Tehran cancer institute and put the translated scale through standard checks.

Patients and experts judged the questions clear and relevant. Analysis grouped the final eleven items into two themes: fear about body effects and fear felt in the mind. The structure held up under confirmatory testing, and scores behaved consistently. Eghbali and colleagues conclude the Persian scale is ready for use in clinics and research on treatment fears in Iran.
plos-pone-0354474:
Emadeldin M Elsokkary, a single author, published this 2026 validation study of an Arabic questionnaire measuring how young adults feel about their digital lives. Saudi adults aged eighteen to twenty-five, four hundred and fifty in total. They completed the Perceived Digital Well-Being Scale, and the sample was split so one half could test the structure and the other confirm it.

Three themes emerged: emotional, social, and thinking-related well-being. Scores lined up sensibly with life satisfaction and fear of missing out, and answered consistently. Elsokkary concludes the Arabic scale is ready for research on balanced smartphone use in Saudi youth.
plos-pone-0354674:
Haonan Yu and colleagues published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on a plant extract that kills the freshwater snail spreading schistosomiasis in Asia. The snail is the only intermediate host of the parasite Schistosoma japonicum, so killing snails is a fast way to break transmission. The team screened well over a hundred botanical extracts, then studied the most promising one, drawn from a hellebore species, in laboratory and field trials.

The extract proved strongly toxic to the snails at low concentrations, and a field dose killed more than four in five snails where it was applied. Examination of treated snails showed wide damage across the foot, gills, salivary glands, stomach, and digestive gland. Reassuringly, the same dose left zebrafish, water fleas, frogs, another snail species, and shrimp unharmed in the team's tests. The authors propose the extract as an effective, environmentally gentler snail killer for disease control programs.
plos-pone-0354874:
Zenia Taluja led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study testing survey questions about phone and internet access in rural North India. Measuring the digital gender gap requires questions people actually understand. The team ran about a hundred cognitive interviews in Hindi, asking men and women to think aloud over more than a hundred draft questions.

Nearly every question needed revision. Problems ranged from wrong terminology and tangled wording to digital ideas like privacy policies that meant little locally. Taluja shows that careful translation is not enough; questions must be tested in the respondent's own world.
plos-pone-0354974:
Dennis Gyasi Konadu led a team of eight authors on this 2026 pregnancy study in Ghana's middle belt. They enrolled women before the twentieth week of pregnancy, tested vaginal samples for bacterial vaginosis, an imbalance of vaginal bacteria, and followed the women through delivery and the baby's first year.

The imbalance proved common in early pregnancy, especially among younger and unmarried women. Yet it showed no clear link to bad birth outcomes in this group. Konadu suggests aiming screening at higher-risk women and using gene-based tests next, since finer types of the imbalance may carry the real risk.
plos-pone-0355174:
Serah Wanjiru Wachira leads a scoping review of what health systems in sub-Saharan Africa do to improve outcomes when childbirth turns into an emergency. Such emergencies still drive much maternal death in the region even as more women deliver in facilities. The review screened hundreds of records and kept several dozen recent studies, sorting their strategies into themes.

Strategies grouped into life-saving clinical and system fixes, workforce training and mentorship, and supporting themes around referral and readiness. Drugs, monitoring and triage tools, and service strengthening all appeared, alongside programs that coach front-line staff. Wachira and colleagues map where evidence clusters and where it stays thin, giving ministries and funders a clearer menu of proven moves and open questions.
plos-pone-0355374:
Sonia García-Merino and colleagues describe in 2026 a trial plan aimed at young women at university who study health subjects. The plan tests group teaching built on a theory of self driven motivation, paired with lessons that value what the body can do over how it looks. Participants will be split at random between the course and a waiting group.

Six face to face sessions form the course, with checks before, just after, and six months later. The main outcome is self driven motivation for exercise at the final check. Other measures cover activity, body image, and eating risk. No results are claimed yet.
plos-pone-0355474:
Alexandria Innes and Merili Pullerits gathered first-hand research on sexual violence faced by people migrating without state permission. Such journeys expose travellers to smugglers, officials, and fellow migrants with little legal protection. Their 2026 review searched for qualitative studies and kept those with enough detail for full analysis.

The synthesis describes sexual violence as widespread and built into unauthorised migration, not as rare bad luck. Findings group around agency, money, a climate of violence, normalisation, perpetrators, and gender. Women described planning around expected attacks, sometimes accepting unwanted sex to stay safe. Poverty raised risk, yet money could not prevent the worst cases. The authors present the evidence as structural, demanding structural responses.
plos-pone-0355674:
Suman Pande and co-authors asked what drives instructional leadership in public secondary schools in Kathmandu, Nepal. Instructional leadership means school heads who actively guide teaching and learning, not just paperwork. Their 2026 survey study adapted a well-known Western model to local conditions and tested it with factor analysis.

Three factors stood out. Heads plan, manage, and supervise teaching programmes. They motivate teachers and students and build their skills. They also involve parents in learning, a factor the authors note is new for Nepal. Because local student results stay low, Pande and colleagues offer the model as a practical guide for head teachers and policymakers who want leadership centred on learning.
plos-pone-0355874:
Patricia N Albers and a school health network team report pilot survey results. The topic is mental health and school belonging. The students were secondary pupils in southwest England in the early twenty twenties. Several thousand students in two year groups answered standard questionnaires. Topics ran from life satisfaction and low mood to anxiety, well-being, and loneliness. Students also rated how connected they felt to school. Results were weighted and broken down by gender, year, and family means.

Poor mental health was common: large shares reported low life satisfaction and severe depressive symptoms, and under half felt a real sense of belonging at school. Patterns differed across gender and background groups in the full analysis. Albers and colleagues present the pilot as a targeting tool, showing schools where need and weak belonging coincide.
plos-pone-0356074:
David Musoke and colleagues assessed how well health facility managers in Wakiso District, Uganda, lead and manage their services. These managers run lower-level government health centres, yet the topic is rarely studied locally. Their 2026 survey questioned sixty facility heads about skills ranging from supervision to handling staff, money, and supplies.

Only a quarter showed good leadership skill, and only a third showed good management skill. Most had never been inducted into their roles, and many reported low motivation. Managers rated monitoring, speaking, and listening as key thinking skills, and finance handling as a top business need. Musoke and colleagues argue structured induction and support could lift everyday management across the district.
plos-pone-0356174:
Boyan Yang, Guilin Zhou, and Jun Dai published a 2026 computational study in PLOS ONE on atopic dermatitis, the chronic itchy skin condition often called eczema. Instead of running wet-lab experiments, they combined several computer methods: mining drug-target data, machine learning, single-cell gene data, and three-dimensional modeling of molecules. Their goal was to find which skin-cell targets the plant compound baicalin might act on.

One enzyme, called CA2, kept surfacing across every method they tried. The signal sat mainly in keratinocytes, the cells that build the skin's outer barrier, and computer simulations suggested baicalin can bind CA2 strongly. The authors present the link between baicalin, CA2, and a particular keratinocyte state as a hypothesis for lab testing, not a proven treatment. It gives eczema researchers a focused starting point for experiments on the skin barrier.
plos-pone-0356374:
Jessica R Duke and Emily A Holt set out to define a phrase science education uses loosely: climate change acceptance. Their 2026 Delphi study built the definition in stages. It started from a scoping review of more than five hundred articles. It added a student pilot survey. It ran four rounds of consultation with 210 experts and stakeholders in biology, chemistry, and geoscience.

Consensus produced not one definition but two. The shorter holds that acceptance means believing climate change is happening and humans cause it. The longer adds understanding the greenhouse mechanism behind warming. Experts split along that line, suggesting the right bar depends on a student's level. Either way, teachers and researchers now have explicit definitions to aim instruments at.
plos-pone-0356474:
Brandon Mossop and Salimur Choudhury introduce a forecasting method for data series whose behavior keeps changing, in this 2026 paper. Most forecasting tools assume the rules stay fixed, which fails for things like disease spread, where relationships shift as conditions change. Their framework, called CaReBayes, first chops a series into stretches with stable behavior, which they call regimes.

Within each regime, the method maps which variables seem to drive which others, then fits a Bayesian forecasting model suited to that stretch. New data are assigned to the regime they best match before a forecast is made, complete with uncertainty estimates. Tested on synthetic data and on COVID-19 records from Ontario, the method beat standard benchmarks. As a bonus, its per-regime diagrams give users a readable picture of how the system's drivers change over time.
plos-pone-0356774:
Marcel Rainer and four colleagues compare how two neighboring countries handle reports of harmful drug interactions, in a 2026 study of safety registries. Switzerland and Austria have similar health systems but organize their drug safety monitoring differently. The team analyzed roughly fifteen hundred interaction reports filed in the two countries over a period of more than sixteen years.

Switzerland filed well over three times as many reports as Austria relative to its reporting rate, and most reports in both countries described serious outcomes. Taking many medicines at once was strongly tied to serious harm in both systems. The content differed too: Swiss reports more often described the mechanism of a problem, while Austrian ones more often described symptoms. The authors suggest that who processes the reports, including whether specialists are involved, shapes what a safety system learns.
plos-pone-0356874:
Yangyi Qu, Jie Tang, and Hailong Wang compared sixty villages across China and India. They tested whether the strength of village rule, not just wealth, drives rural progress. Their 2026 study scored each village on thirty-two signs. These spanned roads and services, public voice, the economy, and the local ecology. The team then modeled how governing strength turned into residents' life satisfaction and land-use gains.

Governing capacity mattered strongly. It worked mainly through public services and shared facilities. China's top-down model delivered more even results. India's looser villages varied wildly in how well they carried plans out. Villages near cities beat purely farm villages in both countries. The lesson across both nations is plain. Bodies that cut the cost of acting together beat raw economic scale.
plos-pone-0357174:
Gerald P Mwing'a and colleagues link clinic records with weather data to study seasonal diarrhea in Tanzanian children under five. Diarrhea remains a top killer of young children there, and weather may drive its timing, but short-term links across regions were little measured. The analysis covered about nine hundred children seen at ten facilities across seven regions over one year, joining health system records with national weather service data.

Diarrhea prevalence peaked in the dry season in regions with a single rainy season, and the modeling searched for short-lag ties to rainfall and temperature alongside family traits. Mwing'a and colleagues argue that if weather signals prove reliable, clinics could staff and stock ahead of predictable surges instead of reacting after children arrive.
plos-pone-0357274:
Alene G Pohly and colleagues genotype a tissue parasite found in California sea lions suffering a distinctive muscle disease. The illness, marked by repeating bouts of muscle inflammation, has appeared in both wild and managed sea lions, and its drivers are murky. Archived muscle from twenty-five affected free-ranging animals was screened for parasite DNA and typed at six variable gene spots, then compared with types recorded in otters and land hosts.

Fifteen distinct parasite types turned up in just this small sample. Six matched types already known from southern sea otters or other hosts, while nine had never been reported anywhere before. Pohly and colleagues say the sheer variety argues against one outbreak strain, and the sea-lion-only types hint at transmission routes science has yet to trace.
plos-pone-0357374:
Hyun Dong Yoo, Jae Guk Kim, and Seung Young Chung model a hard choice for patients over eighty with an unruptured brain aneurysm: watch it or coil it. Coiling through a blood vessel can prevent a deadly rupture, but the procedure itself carries risk at advanced age, and other causes of death compete. Their decision model compares watching against coiling at ages eighty, eighty-five, and ninety for Korean patients, counting a combined set of bad first events.

Answers swung with age and sex. Watching won in every panel at age ninety and for older men, while coiling won in selected panels at eighty and for some women at eighty-five. A quality-weighted recheck agreed with most of the original verdicts. Yoo and colleagues stress how tightly the answer binds to age, sex, and what outcomes a patient values most.
plos-pone-0357474:
Jozo Grgic, Vanessa Kristina Wazny, and Dorian Varovic track hand squeeze strength among teenagers in South Korea across nearly a decade of national health surveys. Grip strength is a quick marker of overall muscle health, and the team wanted both a trend line and normal ranges for each age and sex. Their data cover several thousand young people aged from ten to nineteen.

Strength stayed broadly steady across the survey years, with small dips and rises in some age groups that never formed a clear slide. Values rose with age and differed between boys and girls, as expected during growth. The published reference tables let doctors and teachers judge whether a given teenager's grip is low, typical, or high for Korean peers.
plos-pone-0357774:
Yimeng Liu and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on a fungus quietly eating the insulation of power cables. Surveying the living film on soiled substation cables, the team found one fungus, Curvularia lunata, dominant. They isolated a strain and grew it on fresh cable samples on purpose, watching the damage unfold over two months.

The growth scarred the surface with holes and furrows. The plastic turned less water-repellent, steadily absorbed more moisture, and chemically changed: chlorine bonds fell away and oxygen-bearing groups appeared, signs of oxidation and dechlorination driven by the fungus. Electrically, the material weakened clearly, its resistance dropping as it degraded. The authors piece these steps into a full mechanism, surface growth, moisture retention, chemical attack, electrical failure. Power firms, they argue, should treat fungal growth as an aging factor for cables in humid substations, not mere dirt, when planning inspection and protection.
plos-pone-0358074:
Christian Anker-Hansen and colleagues published a 2026 nationwide family study in PLOS ONE on whether osteoporosis and fractures run in families in Sweden. Linking national registers, they followed over six and a half million people and compared risks across twins, full siblings, half-siblings, and cousins, adjusting for birth year, sex, education, and other illnesses.

Risk climbed steadily with genetic closeness. Having an affected twin nearly tripled a person's risk of hospital-treated osteoporosis, full siblings more than doubled it, and half-siblings and cousins still carried clearly raised risk. Fractures showed the same graded pattern. The family effect was strongest in the young: among full siblings under twenty, the osteoporosis risk linked to an affected sibling was extraordinarily high, though from a very small base. The authors conclude heredity is a real, measurable force in bone fragility, and that a close relative's early disease should put clinicians on alert.
plos-pone-0358274:
Subhanwita Manna led a team of eight authors setting out a study protocol on abortion care in rural India, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Full abortion care in rural areas faces blocks at many levels, from clinic capacity to local culture. The planned multicenter study will map the current state of services, what blocks them, and what helps.

Manna's protocol pairs numbers with qualitative work across several centers. Publishing the plan ahead of the study helps ensure the findings can guide policy rather than gather dust. Rural women's access to safe care is the stake: delays and gaps can turn a legal service into a dangerous one. A clear map of barriers is the first step to removing them.
plos-pone-0358574:
Jingjin Gong led a team of eight authors studying a natural compound and pregnancy-related vessel damage, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The compound, ergothioneine, is an antioxidant found in foods such as mushrooms. The condition in view was preeclampsia, which harms the lining of a mother's blood vessels.

Gong's team traced how the compound eases that vessel damage through a chain of signals in the cell. Their results name a path by which a dietary substance might protect the vessel lining. Much more work would be needed before any treatment use, but the study gives drug researchers a defined route to test in mothers at risk of this serious condition.
plos-pone-0358774: Gao and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on modeling how people and light interact indoors. Their network uses graph attention across space and time to capture that interplay. Rooms lit in step with where people are and what they do could save power and feel better. The work joins building physics with modern neural network design.
plos-pone-0359074:
Raquel Cervigón and Evangelos Kontopantelis analyzed in 2026 whether older people who care for others outside their own household pay for it with their heart health. Their cross-sectional analysis draws on SHARE, a large European study of aging. Informal care by older adults is a pillar of European welfare that budgets rarely count, and caregivers are themselves an aging, medically vulnerable group.

The authors compare the cardiovascular health of these caregivers with that of similar older people who do not provide such care. If helping others outside the home carries a measurable cost to the helper's heart, support services should count caregivers as people needing care too. The study adds European evidence to a question usually asked only about family caregivers.
plos-pone-0359274: Zhang and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE pooled analysis of exercise for Parkinson's disease. The team combined past trials on how exercise affects walking, movement, and balance. As a meta-analysis, it weighs the trials together for a clearer verdict. Their paper also draws out what the results mean for clinical care. Exercise is one of the few tools that may slow daily decline.
plos-pone-0359574: Zhang and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on light inside college teaching buildings in China's Changsha-Zhuzhou-Xiangtan area. They worked on mixing daylight with electric light so rooms stay bright without waste. Their aim was a lighting setup that suits study and teaching through the day. Smarter light design can cut power bills and ease eye strain for students and staff.
plos-pone-0359974:
Arkadipta Bakshi, Vipsa Patel, Andrew Ward, Mahbuba Ferdous, and Brad Binder wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on plant growth. It studies Arabidopsis thaliana, the standard laboratory plant, grown in the dark. The response measured is the rapid growth reaction to ethylene, a gas that acts as a plant hormone.

Three kinds of factors are compared: environmental, developmental, and genetic, and the title notes they affect the response kinetics differently, meaning the speed and shape of growth change. Separating these influences helps explain why seedlings respond unevenly to the same gas. Plant biologists studying hormone signaling are the core audience.
pmc-13236774: Reid and colleagues publish a correction to their study of sleep after psilocybin treatment. The original paper reported early evidence that sleep improved following a dose of psilocybin, the active compound in magic mushrooms. It also examined whether those sleep gains played a part in the drug's antidepressant effect, a question of wide interest in mental health research. The notice records that the original article has been corrected, and carries the publisher's standard notes on maps and affiliations.
pmc-13236974:
Bi and colleagues present an expert consensus on treating condylar hyperplasia and the face deformities it causes. In this condition, one jaw joint knob keeps growing, pushing the face sideways over time. It distorts the bite, strains the jaw joint, and unbalances the whole face, so no single operation fixes it.

The consensus sets out combined care: trimming the overgrown joint, jaw surgery to realign the bite, contour surgery for facial balance, and orthodontics. Sequencing those steps across specialists is the hard part. A shared expert plan helps surgical teams across China offer the same careful pathway instead of improvising case by case.
pmc-13238774:
Dema, Choden, and Wangmo report a case where meningitis was complicated by a stroke that clot-busting treatment failed to fix. Their patient, a man of fifty-two, arrived with fever, headache, vomiting, and dulled awareness, and his neck was stiff on examination. Those signs point to meningitis, infection of the membranes around the brain.

A stroke followed, one of the rarest and gravest turns meningitis can take. Thrombolysis, the drug treatment that dissolves clots, was tried and failed. Whether such drugs help infection-driven strokes is unsettled, since the clots and vessels differ from ordinary strokes. This case adds a sober data point for emergency teams facing the same double crisis.
pmc-13241374:
Lepot and colleagues at UCLouvain Brussels tested whether deep learning reconstruction sharpens MRI hunting for myeloma bone lesions. Ten patients underwent whole-body scans with three sequence types. CT scans served as the reference standard. Three readers, from resident to twenty-six-year veteran, scored ten bone regions. They counted lesions region by region against CT.

The enhanced zero-echo-time images beat the native sequence on every reliability measure. Accuracy reached eighty to ninety-three percent across readers. Junior readers gained the most, and the enhanced scans found about thirty percent more lesions. Fewer false alarms accompanied the extra detections.
pmc-13242674:
Junnan Zhang, Mingyue Gao, and Congjiao Sun reviewed the mechanisms of female reproductive aging and made the case for an unlikely model animal: the laying hen. Their review appeared in the Journal of Animal Science and Biotechnology in 2026. Ovarian aging shrinks the egg supply, lowers egg quality, and disturbs hormones, yet animal models that mirror the human course are scarce. Hens, by contrast, lay on a predictable schedule with clear peak and decline phases.

The review walks through the interlocking drivers of decline: signaling pathways, cell senescence, epigenetic change, hormonal drift, and failing mitochondria with oxidative stress. Together they deplete the ovarian reserve and erode egg competence. Because a hen's laying life is short and easy to measure, tests that would take decades in women can run in a few years. The authors propose the hen as an underused bridge between basic mechanisms and treatments for human fertility loss.
pmc-13243174:
Sunil Jaiswal, Shraddha Uprety, and Pratichya Thapa present a diagnostic puzzle built around a painful lump under a fingernail. Their case report appeared in Clinical Case Reports in 2026. A fifty-eight-year-old woman arrived with a tender nodule beneath the nail of her right middle finger that had grown over one month. The nail's far edge had yellowed and lifted, and she recalled no injury beforehand.

The report walks readers through rival explanations first: a wart under the nail, a glomus tumor, a fungal infection, or a fleshy growth called pyogenic granuloma. Dermoscopy showed thickened skin and nail separation, but the X-ray settled it by revealing a well-defined bony growth on the fingertip bone. The diagnosis was subungual exostosis, a benign bone spur that appears on toes in the young, making this finger case in an older woman unusual. She was referred to orthopedics for removal.
pmc-13243874:
Sutapa Bhowmik, Sangita Ahmed, and Fatema Hasan Kaifa reviewed the science on Cronobacter sakazakii, a bacterium that contaminates powdered infant formula. Their systematic review appeared in the International Journal of Microbiology in 2026. The germ causes meningitis, blood poisoning, and gut destruction in newborns, and it survives drying, salt stress, and heat that kill most rivals. The team screened studies from 2009 to 2024.

Eighty-two papers fed the synthesis. Virulence rests on surface proteins that help the bacterium invade cells, iron-gathering systems, and stubborn biofilms on factory surfaces. Two sequence types, ST4 and ST1, dominate newborn infections and form biofilms especially well. The review compares slow culture tests with faster molecular detection and weighs defenses from plant compounds to stricter plant hygiene. Most strains still yield to common antibiotics, but resistance genes are accumulating. Powdered formula, the authors stress, is not sterile and must be handled as such.
pmc-13244074:
Virginie Kreutzinger and colleagues used combined PET and MRI scanning to probe the conversation between spinal disks and the bone plates that cap them. Their study appeared in JOR Spine in 2026. Nine patients with low back pain underwent hybrid scans measuring disk hydration and degeneration alongside bone remodeling activity in the vertebral endplates, using a radioactive fluoride tracer. Eighty-six endplates entered the analysis, adjusted for age, sex, and body size.

One pattern stood out: the more water-rich the disk's outer ring, the more active the neighboring endplate bone. The link grew stronger where Modic changes, a type of endplate lesion, were present. Bone remodeling showed no tie to disk dehydration itself. That decoupling points the authors toward biology over mechanics: the endplate changes look like chemical crosstalk with the disk, not wear from load. If confirmed, treatments might target those signals rather than just bracing the spine.
pmc-13245774:
Block Ngaybe and co-authors asked Ugandans at highest HIV risk what prevention products they actually want, in this 2026 PLOS One qualitative study. Long-acting injectable PrEP, which protects for months per shot, has been approved but not yet rolled out in Uganda, and a future vaccine would face the same uptake question. The team interviewed ten HIV-prevention experts and ten peer leaders from key populations in English and Luganda.

Condoms and daily PrEP pills were the practices people knew best. Barriers to the injectable options included how long protection lasts, how easily clinics can be reached, and practical access issues that surfaced across the interviews. The authors say rollout plans for injectables, and any eventual vaccine, should be built around these stated preferences of the communities expected to use them, not around supply alone.
pmc-13247074:
Best, Braunschädel, Bethke, and co-authors probed the sense of upright in Parkinson's patients who lean sideways, in this 2026 Scientific Reports study. About a tenth of Parkinson's patients develop Pisa syndrome, a sustained sideways tilt of the trunk. The team tested twenty Parkinson's patients, eight with the syndrome, plus patients with isolated neck dystonia and healthy controls, using visual-vertical judgments and a line-orientation test before and after electrical vestibular stimulation.

Only the Pisa group judged vertical abnormally, and stimulation made their errors worse, the fingerprint of faulty central processing of balance signals rather than a simple muscle problem. Neck dystonia patients, by contrast, kept a normal sense of vertical and improved with botulinum toxin treatment. The findings point rehabilitation for Pisa syndrome toward the brain's vestibular processing.
pmc-13248974:
Wang and colleagues tested a plant compound against depression after stroke, in a 2026 mouse study. About a third of stroke survivors develop depression, which slows recovery. Echinocystic acid, drawn from medicinal herbs, calms inflammation, so the team modeled the condition by combining a blocked brain artery with weeks of mild, unpredictable stress.

Treated mice showed less depressive behavior, less neuron death in the hippocampus, and lower levels of three inflammatory messengers. A signaling pathway called JNK/NF-kappaB quieted under treatment. When the team forced that pathway back on with another drug, the benefits vanished, supporting the proposed mechanism. The work is early and animal-only, a lead rather than a treatment.
pmc-13250074:
Ibrahim and colleagues tested a muscle relaxant drug as a rust shield for steel, in a 2026 study. Carbon steel in strong acid corrodes fast, and cyclobenzaprine hydrochloride was a candidate protective additive. The team weighed samples, ran electrical tests, photographed surfaces, and modeled the molecule on a computer, varying dose and temperature.

The drug formed a surface film that slowed corrosion on every measure. At the best dose it blocked about ninety-six percent of the attack. It clings mainly by physical attraction, in a classic adsorption pattern, and lost strength as the temperature rose. Computer modeling pointed to its ring systems and heteroatoms as the gripping parts of the molecule.
pmc-13250174:
Haut, editor-in-chief of Trauma Surgery and Acute Care Open, marks the journal's tenth anniversary in this 2026 editorial. The open-access journal published its first manuscript a decade ago, founded under editor Timothy Fabian. Haut took over at the start of 2023 and describes settling into the role with a strong team.

He lists the decade's milestones: two thousand manuscript submissions, a thousandth published article, and a first impact factor. Formal partnerships grew from one to ten, linking the journal to major trauma meetings and societies. New article types include a patient education series written for families and the public. Haut thanks his editorial team and publisher and points to steady growth in reach and relevance.
pmc-13250874:
Zhang and Zheng interview Chinese parents who lost their only child and cope by living life on the child's behalf. Their 2026 European Journal of Psychotraumatology study concerns shidu parents, a group shaped by China's one-child era. Ten parents who use this strategy described it in phone or face-to-face interviews.

Living for the child means doing what the child did, finishing what the child hoped to do, and keeping ties with the child's friends. Parents said the practice restored purpose, steadied emotions, and widened their support circles. It also added life stress for some parents, so balance mattered. The authors describe the strategy as a culturally distinct way of rebuilding meaning after a devastating loss.
pmc-13251074:
Mollon and a large team test whether genes shape thinking skills differently in girls and boys. Their 2026 Biology of Sex Differences study uses the Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort, nearly forty-seven hundred young people aged eight to twenty-one. Each completed a computerized battery covering memory, reasoning, social reading, and speed.

Score differences between the sexes were small across most tests. Genetic influence ran stronger in males for executive and complex reasoning accuracy, and stronger in females for complex and social speed. Yet the underlying genetic factors were essentially the same in both sexes; only their strength differed. The authors say environment and genes must be studied together to explain the small gaps that appear.
pmc-13251274:
Aline Delva and a large team ask why certain brain areas shrink in Lewy body dementia in this 2026 study. The condition shares features with both Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease, but what makes particular regions fragile was unclear.

Brain scans from 89 patients and 89 matched controls were mapped against gene activity data from healthy brains. Shrinking was worst in regions rich in genes for energy production and signal passing between nerve cells. Much of the pattern overlapped with Parkinson's and Alzheimer's pathways, yet 90 genes stood apart, tied to a calming signal system. Thinning also followed the brain's wiring, hinting it spreads along networks.
pmc-13251774:
Xinliang Cai and colleagues fine-tune glowing molecules for screens in this 2026 chemistry paper. The molecules, called MR-TADF emitters, promise pure colours and high efficiency for organic light-emitting diodes, but designers have lacked basic rules linking structure to glow behaviour.

Instead of chasing new shapes, the team compared twin versions of the same skeleton that differ only in how parts connect. Those small changes revealed what sets the emission colour and how long the excited state lasts, and theory backed the explanation. Two of the molecules then performed strongly in test devices, with high efficiency and clean colour. The authors offer the isomer trick as a design guide.
pmc-13253974:
Josué Louokdom Simo and colleagues study liver signs in sickle cell disease in a 2026 study in Cameroon. Sickle cell disease is an inherited blood disorder that can harm many organs, including the liver. Over four months at Bafoussam Regional Hospital, the team compared 94 patients with the disease to 73 healthy controls.

Liver enzyme levels were higher in patients across the board. One enzyme, AST, was raised in 72.3 percent of patients and in no controls. Albumin, a blood protein made by the liver, was low in 38.3 percent of patients. The authors link the pattern to red blood cell breakdown.
pmc-13255474:
Izabela Plumbom, Benedikt Obermayer, and a large team introduce a cheaper way to profile T cells in a 2026 methods paper. Reading T cell receptor codes from single-cell and spatial data is normally costly or needs special equipment. Their method, circVDJ-seq, recovers that receptor information from standard 3-prime workflows, including single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics.

The team applied it to freshly removed neuroblastomas, childhood nerve tumors, and to lymph nodes from people who died with pneumonia or COVID-19. The method revealed distinct immune environments and T cell clonality patterns. The authors present it as a broad, cost-saving tool for immune studies.
pmc-13259174:
Hiroki Ito and colleagues gather every sensor method used to measure ankle lifting after stroke. Dorsiflexion, raising the foot toward the shin, keeps walking safe, yet clinics grade it crudely by hand. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis spans studies from two thousand to twenty twenty-five.

Eighteen studies covering seven hundred eighty-three survivors used dynamometers, load cells, or proprioception devices instead of hand grades. Stronger ankle lifters generally walked faster and farther, though some studies disagreed. The link's strength swung with the device, the exact measure, and how long ago the stroke occurred. Standard sensor protocols are the field's clear next need.
pmc-13260974:
Meraj Sharifi and co-authors present a 2026 cross-sectional study of non-glaucomatous optic atrophy, wasting of the optic nerve not caused by glaucoma, at a referral center in southeastern Iran.
