All 155 patients had a confirmed cause established through clinical evaluation, additional tests, and record review. Causes were grouped into categories including ischemic, meaning reduced blood flow, traumatic, toxic, inflammatory, compressive, and hereditary. The team also analyzed which factors predicted current visual sharpness.

Ischemic causes were most common, in forty-six patients or 29.7 percent, almost all from one condition called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Trauma was second, in thirty-seven patients. Nearly half the patients had vision of counting fingers or worse. Toxic optic neuropathy had the poorest outcomes, with five of six cases at that severe level. Longer time since symptom onset was the only independent predictor of worse vision.
pmc-13262574:
Hang-Yu Zhao and colleagues map chest infections in Shenyang children after pandemic rules lifted. Nearly twenty-seven thousand children in hospital with acute lower respiratory infections were tested for twelve pathogens. Their 2026 study covers three years of stays at two hospitals in northeast China.

By gene testing, rhinovirus led, trailed by influenza A and respiratory syncytial virus. Antibody testing instead crowned Mycoplasma pneumoniae, which sat mostly in six to fourteen-year-olds. Infants carried the RSV burden, and several pathogens struck girls more often. Age, season, and sex each on its own shaped infection odds. Their atlas guides local testing and timing of preventive care.
pmc-13262674:
Edson Munanura and colleagues audit how three Ugandan referral hospitals use a workhorse antibiotic. Ceftriaxone treats infections and guards surgical patients, but misuse breeds resistance. Their 2026 study reviews seven hundred fifty-three patients across the three hospitals, plus talks with staff.

About two-thirds of use matched national rules, mostly as surgical prevention in once-daily doses. Blood cultures, the test that should steer therapy, happened in barely one percent of cases. Long treatment courses hurt fit, while surgery wards helped it. Staff blamed missing limits, stockouts, crushing workloads, and patchy checking. A national use plan is the authors' call.
pmc-13263274:
Fatema Mohamed Ali Abdulla Aljufairi leads the first Gulf region study of thyroid eye disease in children in a 2026 journal article. Graves' disease is an immune condition that overactivates the thyroid; its eye form inflames tissues around the eye. Doctors in Bahrain screened all known child Graves' patients in late 2025 and compared those with eye disease to an adult group.

Among 22 children, half had thyroid eye disease, most of it mild and often affecting both eyes. None had sight-threatening disease or double vision. Eye bulging or swelling was the most common symptom, and lid retraction the leading sign. Children had milder disease than the 81 adults, who more often showed lid lag. Parents being blood relatives was more common in children with eye disease.
pmc-13263674:
Stacy Schmidt and colleagues write the missing rulebook for obesity medicine fellowship training in the United States. Programs existed without shared rules, unlike other fields. Their 2026 project drafts standards for adult and children's programs through an expert council process.

Drafts went through many rounds of expert edits, with input from the specialty's board and every known program's leaders. All thirty-one programs then voted section by section, with a section kept only on three-quarters of votes. Every single item cleared the bar for both adult and pediatric tracks. The agreed rules give a young field shared standards for curriculum and bedside training.
pmc-13264274:
Nastaran Ansari and colleagues published a 2026 study of gut viruses in the water supply of Hamadan, Iran. Such viruses spread through water and can harm health, yet local data were scarce. The team checked raw source water, treated water, and well water across the city system.

They took 100 samples in summer and autumn and tested each with five methods. Adenoviruses, one virus group, showed up in 24 percent of samples. Source water was much more polluted than well water, and summer samples were worse than autumn ones. The authors say virus traces in treated water call for more checks on amount, spread risk, and public exposure.
pmc-13264574:
Eleni Papachristodoulou and a large team wrote a 2026 study on stress before diagnosis in systemic lupus erythematosus, an illness where the immune system attacks the body. Stress has been tied to such diseases, but its link to later lupus course was unclear. The team measured major life stress in the two years before diagnosis.

They studied 140 patients at one large hospital, most of them women, with a median diagnosis age of 35.5 years. About 46 percent reported moderate to high stress before diagnosis. The high stress group had more depression, high blood pressure, obesity, and fatigue than the low stress group. High stress also linked to a clotting syndrome tied to lupus and to fewer long quiet periods of disease. The authors call for studies that follow patients forward in time.
pmc-13264974:
Remzi Çetinkaya and colleagues published a 2026 study of the HALP score as a death warning in pneumonia caught outside hospital. The score blends four routine blood values: haemoglobin, albumin, lymphocytes, and platelets. Older pneumonia scores have limits, so the team tested whether this simple blend predicts death within 30 days.

They reviewed 467 adults admitted with pneumonia at one center. The 30-day death rate was 21.4 percent. Patients who died were older, more often male, and had lower HALP scores. The score predicted death well on standard tests. Further analysis showed its link to death ran largely through illness severity: standard severity scores, confusion, oxygen levels, and scan findings carried much of the effect. The authors offer HALP as a support tool beside the standard scores, not a replacement.
pmc-13266474:
Ece Bayram wrote a 2026 commentary arguing that sleep deserves more focus in Alzheimer's disease in women. Alzheimer's is the most common cause of dementia, and women carry the higher risk. Poor sleep is common in the disease yet is left out of its formal diagnostic rules.

Bayram discusses a study of women over 65 with mild memory loss and high genetic risk. In the higher-risk group, worse sleep was linked to weaker visual memory and more tau protein build-up in limb regions of the brain. No such links appeared for word memory. Bayram urges more research and better sleep care for women at risk.
pmc-13267574:
Sheng Huang and colleagues wrote a 2026 study of steel for bridge cables under fast loading. Bridge cables face shaking from wind, traffic, and quakes, so their steel must behave in a known way when stretched quickly. The Book of Jubilees retells Genesis and the start of Exodus as a secret account given to Moses by angels. It was written in Hebrew in the second century BC, most likely. R. H. Charles edited and translated the surviving text, which came down whole in Ethiopic.

The story is divided into blocks of forty-nine years, the jubilees that give the book its name. It adds detail on angels, the calendar, and laws it says the patriarchs already kept. The Ethiopian church counts it as scripture, while other churches treat it as apocrypha. It helps show how Jews of its age read the Bible.
tob-13329-15474:
Books one to three of the Mahabharata open Ganguli's translation in its Vyasa-titled copy. The Kuru kings rise, marry, and quarrel. A dice game in the royal hall, played with loaded stakes, costs the Pandava brothers their kingdom and sends them into the forest.

Thirteen years of exile follow, full of demons, pilgrimages, and stories nested inside stories. The brothers gather allies and grievances in equal measure. Ganguli, the first to render the whole epic into English prose, keeps the huge cast straight. Every feud that drives the later war is planted here, in the longest story ever told.
tob-4074:
L. W. de Laurence's 1916 Chicago edition presents the Goetia, the famous first book of the Lesser Key of Solomon, under the subtitle The Book of Evil Spirits. Seventy-two spirits are listed with their seals, ranks, and legions, alongside the ceremonies prescribed for calling and binding them. De Laurence's no-frills printing put ritual magic into mail-order reach.

His editions spread occult texts across America to readers far from metropolitan bookshops, a genuine landmark of occult publishing. The grimoire itself is medieval in origin, whatever its Solomonic branding claims. V1 evidence calls the volume a landmark whatever one makes of its contents; historians of American occultism would agree.
tob-4146-15474:
Kisari Mohan Ganguli spent years turning the Mahabharata, India's great Sanskrit epic, into English prose. Volume one covers the first three books. They tell of the Bharata clan's origins, the feud between the Pandava and Kaurava cousins, and the rigged dice game that ruins the Pandavas.

Losers in the game, the five Pandava brothers accept thirteen years of exile. Stories within stories fill the long forest years, since the epic pauses for tales of gods, kings, and lovers. Ganguli's Victorian prose moves steadily through it all. The longest poem in world literature opens here, with every thread of the coming war in place.
tob-4174:
The 1902 edition of Julian of Norwich's Revelations of Divine Love presents, in modernized spelling, the sixteen showings the anchoress received during a near-fatal illness. Julian, walled into a cell at Norwich, pondered the visions for twenty years. Their recurring promise, that all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well, anchors the whole work.

Julian's theology is tender and daring at once: God as mother, sin as somehow answered by love, and a hazelnut held in the palm standing for all creation loved by its maker. The first book in English known to be written by a woman, the Revelations reward the 1902 edition's easier spelling with immediate intimacy.
tob-9052-15474:
Ganguli's complete English Mahabharata begins, in this copy, with the epic's opening movement. Two branches of the Kuru house grow up rivals. A dice game, fixed against the honest Pandava brothers, strips them of kingdom, wealth, and freedom in one disastrous hall scene.

Sentenced to thirteen years of exile, the brothers withdraw to the forest. The long banishment fills with adventures, disguises, and tales told to pass the years. Every insult stays remembered; every debt will be called in. Readers meet the vast cast slowly, which suits a poem of this scale. The fuse for the great war is lit here, and it burns through the whole epic.
tob-9174:
Budge compiled his Egyptian Hieroglyphic Dictionary as the key to the carved and painted writings of ancient Egypt. Sign lists and vast word lists fill its volumes, the fruit of his decades at the British Museum. Generations of pupils learned to read the glyphs from Budge's pages.

The dictionary's learning is very much of the 1800s, and later Egyptology corrected it in many places. Its scale, though, commands respect: thousands of words gathered before modern corpora existed. Checked from the 1919 printing, the work stands as a high point of early Egypt lore and a tool that opened tombs and temples to readers.
un-ga-res-a-69-74: Africa's regional hub for peace and disarmament work is backed in Resolution A/69/74, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The United Nations Regional Centre for Peace and Disarmament in Africa gives staff support, on request, to the states of the region. The text recalls the chain of votes on the centre since 1985, and the Assembly's 2012 nod to the role of women in arms work. The centre's part in regional arms steps is restated with force.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014, Resolution 69/74 of the General Assembly deals with the United Nations Regional Centre for Peace and Disarmament in Africa. It describes the Centre's cooperation with the African Union. That includes help in drafting the Union's small arms strategy and a common African position on the Arms Trade Treaty. It includes support for the Pelindaba Treaty through the African Commission on Nuclear Energy. It includes work behind the Kinshasa Convention. It urges African Union member states to fund its trust fund.
un-sc-res-1374:
Angola occupied the Council on 19 October 2001, when it unanimously adopted Resolution 1374 on Angola. Sanctions had targeted the UNITA rebel movement for years. A team of experts tracked how the rebels sold diamonds and got arms. The war's cost to civilians stayed severe.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the expert monitoring team for six more months, to 19 April 2002. Four experts will serve on it. The team must file an action plan within sixty days. Its focus is rebel diamonds, arms-ban breaches, and rebel finances. The sanctions committee will review the team's past reports by year's end and guide its next steps.
un-sc-res-1474:
Somalia's arms embargo gained a new panel of experts under a Security Council decision of 8 April 2003. The embargo set in 1992 had been broken without pause, even after the Eldoret peace declaration of October 2002. Weapons and ammunition kept flowing in from abroad.

The Council stressed that every state had to obey resolution 733 (1992) in full, and that defiance breached the Charter. It welcomed the Panel of Experts' report of 25 March 2003 and re-established the panel for six months. Up to four experts, skilled in arms and related fields, would serve. Somali and regional parties had to cooperate with the panel fully. The panel owed a mid-term briefing and a final report. The Council also decided to send its sanctions committee on a mission to the region as soon as the panel was in place.
un-sc-res-1574:
A Council decision on Sudan took shape as Resolution 1574, adopted in Nairobi on 19 November 2004. The Council met away from New York to push the north-south peace talks to a close. The two sides signed a pledge that same day to finish their deal by 31 December. War in Darfur, though, kept spreading.

The text strongly backs a final Comprehensive Peace Agreement by that year-end date. Once signed, the Council stands ready to send a peace support operation. It extends the advance mission in Sudan by three months, until 10 March 2005. It also backs the African Union plan to grow its Darfur force to 3,320 staff.
un-sc-res-1674:
Protection of civilians in armed conflict was restated as doctrine on 28 April 2006. The Council built on resolutions 1265 (1999) and 1296 (2000) and its texts on children and on women, peace and security. It voiced deep regret that civilians form the vast majority of war's casualties. Illegal resource trading, small arms flows, and child recruitment drew its concern.

The Council stressed that preventing armed conflict comes first and that attacks aimed at civilians are grave breaches. It reaffirmed the 2005 World Summit's words on the responsibility to protect populations from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing, and crimes against humanity. All parties were told to obey the law of armed conflict strictly. Ending impunity was named essential, and states bore the duty to comply with their obligations and prosecute offenders. Regional bodies such as the African Union won praise for their protection work.
un-sc-res-1774:
The Rwanda war crimes tribunal needed its prosecutor renewed in 2007. On 14 September 2007 the Security Council reappointed Hassan Bubacar Jallow to the post. The Secretary-General had nominated him. His new term ran from 15 September 2007 for four years. The Council could end it early once the tribunal finished its work. The tribunal statute allows this way of filling the office.

The reappointment came as the tribunal raced a deadline. Resolution 1503 had told it to finish first-instance trials by the end of 2008. Jallow had led the prosecution since 2003. Keeping him in place avoided a change of leadership mid-stream. The court sat in Arusha, Tanzania.
un-sc-res-1874:
The matter of North Korea was settled for the Council in Resolution 1874, adopted on 12 June 2009. North Korea had set off a nuclear test on 25 May 2009. The test broke earlier Council orders and defied the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. The country had also announced its exit from that treaty and kept firing missiles.

The Council condemns the test in the strongest terms and bans any further test or missile launch. The arms embargo widens to cover nearly all weapons, not just heavy arms. States must inspect suspect cargo at their ports and airports, and may seize banned goods. Banks must block funds tied to the nuclear and missile work. A panel of up to seven experts will watch for breaches for one year.
un-sc-res-274:
Improvements in Cyprus had held through the autumn of 1969, and the peacekeeping force was still required to protect them. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 3 December, said the force was still needed to maintain peace. It also noted that the situation on the island had kept improving. Cyprus's government agreed the force should stay beyond 15 December. Resolution 274 was adopted unanimously on 11 December 1969.

The Council reaffirmed its Cyprus resolutions, from Resolution 186 of 1964 onward. The parties were urged to act with the utmost restraint and to press on with their joint efforts. The force's stationing was extended for a further period, ending on 15 June 1970. The Council expected that progress toward a final settlement would be made by then. Renewals of this kind had become the rhythm of the Cyprus mission, term after term.
un-sc-res-2774: The Security Council's Resolution 2774 on the war between Russia and Ukraine was adopted on 24 February 2025. The short text mourns the tragic loss of life across the conflict. It recalls that the United Nations exists to keep peace and settle disputes without force. The Council implores a swift end to the fighting. It urges a lasting peace between Ukraine and the Russian Federation. The resolution came three years into the full-scale war, and its brevity itself marked a shift in the Council's stance.
un-sc-res-674:
Iraq's treatment of Kuwaitis and foreign nationals was condemned in October 1990. Baghdad's forces had taken third-state nationals hostage and seized diplomatic staff. Kuwaiti records were being destroyed, Kuwaitis forced out, and settlers moved in. Public and private property, hospital supplies among it, was looted or wrecked.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council demanded that Iraq stop at once the taking of hostages and the abuse of Kuwaiti and foreign nationals. States were invited to gather solid evidence of Iraq's grave breaches for later use. Iraq had to let every foreign national who wished leave Kuwait and Iraq at once. Food, water, and basic services for Kuwaitis and foreigners had to be secured. Diplomatic staff and premises were to be protected. Iraq was reminded that it bears liability under the Convention for grave breaches, as do the persons who commit or order them.
un-sc-res-74: The Atomic Energy Commission sent the Council a letter in the summer of 1949. It carried two resolutions on atomic control, adopted that July. On 16 September 1949 the Security Council told the Secretary-General to pass the package on. The General Assembly and all member states would receive it. The record of the commission's debate went along with the papers. The one-sentence act kept atomic diplomacy in the open as the arms race began.
un-sc-res-874:
Nagorno-Karabakh received the Council's formal attention in Resolution 874, adopted on 14 October 1993. A cease-fire had been reached through direct talks backed by Russia. Leaders from the region had met in Moscow on 8 October. Still, the fighting had caused deep suffering and driven many civilians from their homes.

The Council calls on the parties to make the cease-fire firm and lasting. It commends the Minsk Group's adjusted timetable for carrying out its earlier resolutions. Forces must leave land taken in recent fighting, and blocks on transport and communications must go. The text backs a monitoring mission and asks for urgent aid so refugees can return home in safety and dignity.
un-sc-res-974: Readers meet Resolution 974 here as a Security Council record, catalogued with a date of 1995. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Ukraine fills the agenda of the Security Council's 8974th meeting, held on the night of February 23, 2022, and kept in this verbatim record. Russia's ambassador chaired the session while Russian forces massed on Ukraine's borders. The Secretary-General, António Guterres, opened with a direct plea to President Putin to stop his troops from attacking Ukraine and to give peace a chance.

As the meeting ran, word arrived that the attack was beginning. Delegates condemned the move in turn while the chair insisted Russia was acting in defense. The record captures, hour by hour, the moment diplomacy failed and a major war began.

Angola's civil war was still raging in the autumn of 2001. Resolution 1374, adopted unanimously on 19 October 2001, kept a team of outside investigators on the case. Their job was watching whether sanctions against the UNITA rebel movement were being obeyed or quietly broken.

The monitoring group's mandate grew by six months, ending on 19 April 2002. Four experts were to serve on it. Members demanded a detailed work plan within sixty days. The plan had to focus on UNITA's diamond trade, arms deals, and money. A review of earlier expert reports was also ordered by the end of 2001.

Resolution 1474, adopted unanimously on 8 April 2003, tries to give the Somalia arms embargo some teeth. The embargo, dating from 1992, had been violated continuously, even after Somali factions signed a ceasefire declaration at Eldoret the previous October. The Council worried about the money channels that paid for illegal weapons and military activity.

It backed the Somali reconciliation conference hosted in Kenya and insisted that states, especially in the region, stay out of Somalia's affairs. Its practical step was to set up a panel of experts to investigate embargo violations and report on how the ban could be enforced. The panel model, documenting routes, brokers, and financing, shaped UN monitoring of Somalia for years afterward.

Sudan's north-south peace deal nears completion in Resolution 1574, adopted on 19 November 2004 at a meeting in Nairobi. The six protocols between the government and the SPLM/A formed the core of a Comprehensive Peace Agreement. A memorandum signed that day set a deadline of 31 December 2004 for the final deal. In Darfur, insecurity and ceasefire breaches were growing.

The Council strongly backs the peace effort. It promises, once the agreement is signed, to help build a peaceful, united Sudan. It also promises to consider a UN peace support operation to back it. It extends the UN Advance Mission in Sudan, UNAMIS, by three months to 10 March 2005, with more staff. It urges fast preparation of a reconstruction package, including possible debt relief. It strongly supports expanding the African Union mission in Darfur to 3,320 personnel and demands an end to all violence.

Resolution 1674, adopted on 28 April 2006, renews and deepens the Council's doctrine on protecting civilians in armed conflict. It builds on the two earlier civilians resolutions of 1999 and 2000, and on its texts about children, women, and cooperation with regional bodies. The preamble regrets that civilians make up the vast majority of casualties in today's wars.

The resolution treats protection as a core Council task rather than a humanitarian afterthought. It condemns deliberate attacks on civilians, presses all parties to obey humanitarian law, and links civilian safety to the traffic in small arms and the looting of natural resources. Peacekeeping mandates written after 2006 routinely cite it when authorizing troops to shield civilians under threat.

Jamaica danced out of British rule on 6 August 1962. The isle was the first of Britain's Caribbean lands to go free. Its bid for a UN seat came on the heels of the fete. Resolution 174 passed with no dissent on 12 September 1962. The meet was the Council's 1018th.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit Jamaica. The Assembly did so in days. A twin text for Rwanda and Burundi had passed weeks past; now the Caribbean took its turn. Jamaica's voice at the UN grew fast past its size. Its chiefs spoke for small isles and poor lands in trade talks for years. The seat dates from this calm vote, a legal seal on a week of flags, song, and street dance in Kingston.

The Rwanda court's chief prosecutor kept his post by this vote of 2007. On 14 September, the Council adopted Resolution 1774. The prosecutor serves a four-year term under the court's statute. The Secretary-General had put the incumbent forward again. Hassan Bubacar Jallow had held the job since 2003. The court was then working to a tight finish plan.

The text reappoints Jallow from 15 September 2007 for four years. The term can end early once the court's work is done. The finish plan aimed to close trials by the end of 2008. All work was to wrap up in 2010. Those dates slipped in practice. Steady leadership at the top kept the genocide cases on track.

North Korea is sanctioned harder after a nuclear test in Resolution 1874, adopted unanimously on 12 June 2009. The DPRK had tested a nuclear device on 25 May 2009 in defiance of Resolution 1718 (2006) and announced withdrawal from the Non-Proliferation Treaty. The Council said Pyongyang could never have nuclear-weapon state status under the treaty.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council condemns the test in the strongest terms and demands no further tests or missile launches. It extends the 1718 arms embargo to all arms and related services, except small arms notified in advance. States are called on to inspect suspect cargo in their ports and, with flag-state consent, on the high seas, and to seize banned items; bunkering services to suspect DPRK vessels are prohibited. Financial services that could fund nuclear or missile programmes must be blocked. A Panel of Experts of seven is created for one year.

Resolution 274 is a UN Security Council renewal of the Cyprus peacekeeping force, adopted unanimously on 11 December 1969. The Secretary-General reported the force was still needed, noted that the island's situation had continued to improve, and recorded Cyprus's agreement to the force staying beyond mid-December.

The resolution reaffirms the full chain of earlier Cyprus texts, urges restraint and cooperative effort in the favorable climate, and extends the force to 15 June 1970. It voices the now-routine expectation that sufficient progress toward a final solution would then allow withdrawal or substantial reduction, closing out the mission's first six years of rolling renewals.

Resolution 2774, adopted by the Security Council on 24 February 2025, three years into the war, addresses the Russia-Ukraine conflict in a single operative paragraph. The Council mourns the tragic loss of life throughout the conflict and recalls that the United Nations' principal purpose is to maintain international peace and security and to settle disputes peacefully. It implores a swift end to the conflict and urges a lasting peace between Ukraine and the Russian Federation. The text names no aggressor, demands no withdrawal, and sets no conditions or deadlines.

Mozambique's admission is recommended in Resolution 374, adopted unanimously on 18 August 1975. Mozambique had applied under its formal state name. The country had won independence from Portugal in June of that year after a long liberation war. Several African states freed from Portuguese rule applied to the UN in the same season.

The resolution asks the General Assembly to admit Mozambique to membership, in the standard single-sentence form. Behind the formula sat a major change: another large African territory had left colonial rule, and the FRELIMO government now spoke for it in world forums. Mozambique's seat also strengthened the bloc pressing the Council on Rhodesia and apartheid South Africa.

Iraq's occupation of Kuwait in 1990 is the crisis behind Resolution 674. The Council condemned Iraqi forces for taking foreign nationals hostage, abusing Kuwaitis and foreigners, wrecking population records, forcing Kuwaitis out, and seizing public and private property, including hospital supplies. It said the Fourth Geneva Convention applied to Kuwait and that Iraq had to answer for grave breaches of it.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council demands that Iraq stop the hostage-taking and abuse at once. It demands that foreign nationals, including embassy staff, be free to leave and that food, water, and basic services reach people in Kuwait and Iraq. It reminds Iraq that it must pay for loss and harm caused by the invasion and asks states to gather records of claims. It warns that more steps will follow if Iraq does not comply.

Atomic energy talks hit the Council's desk in September 1949. The Atomic Energy Commission's chair had sent a letter on 29 July. Two of the body's own texts came with it. Resolution 74 passed on 16 September 1949. Nine members voted yes. The Ukrainian and Soviet teams held back.

The Secretary-General was told to pass the file along. The letter, the two texts, and the full debate record went to the General Assembly. Member states got copies too. The commission was the UN's first try at ruling the atom. By 1949 its work was stuck fast. The great powers could not agree on checks or bans. This text is a clerk's note on a dying effort, sent on for the record.

Nagorny Karabakh's war is addressed in Resolution 874, adopted on 14 October 1993. Fighting between Armenia and Azerbaijan had displaced large numbers of civilians and created a humanitarian emergency. Russian-assisted direct contacts had produced a ceasefire. The CSCE Minsk Group had drawn up an adjusted timetable of urgent steps. The steps were to carry out the Council's earlier resolutions 822 and 853.

The Council calls on the parties to make the ceasefire effective and permanent and to accept the Minsk Group's adjusted timetable. It demands the reciprocal steps at once: withdrawal of forces from recently occupied territories and removal of all obstacles to communications and transport. It backs an early Minsk Conference for a negotiated settlement. It supports the CSCE monitoring mission. It asks for urgent aid to the affected population. It also asks for help for refugees and displaced people to return home in safety and dignity.

Lebanon asked for more time for the United Nations force in its south in January 1995. Its request came in a letter dated 16 January. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 23 January, was also before the Council. The force, UNIFIL, had stood in southern Lebanon since 1978. Resolution 974 was adopted unanimously on 30 January 1995.

The Council extended UNIFIL's mandate for a further interim period of six months, until 31 July 1995. It restated its strong support for Lebanon's territorial integrity, sovereignty, and independence, within its recognized borders. The force was to carry out its original 1978 mandate in full. That mandate covered confirming Israel's withdrawal and helping Lebanon's government restore its authority in the south. The Council also backed the Secretary-General's plans to streamline the force's maintenance and supply work, in order to save money.
valera-pepita-jimenez-1874:
Juan Valera published Pepita Jimenez in 1874, a Spanish novel told mostly in letters. Luis de Vargas is a young man training for the priesthood. He returns to his village and meets Pepita, a young and charming widow. His letters to his uncle trace a growing love he feels he must resist.

The clash between duty and desire drives the whole story. Valera writes with warmth and gentle humor about faith, family, and small-town life. Pepita is no mere temptress but a strong and thoughtful woman. The English text here dates from 1886. The novel remains Valera's best-known work in any language.
verne-mysterious-island-1874:
Jules Verne published The Mysterious Island in 1874, a novel about five men cast away during the American Civil War. They escape by balloon and land on an unknown island in the Pacific. Led by the engineer Cyrus Smith, they build tools, a home, and even a telegraph. Almost nothing on the island is wasted.

Strange help arrives at key moments, and the men sense a hidden presence. Late in the book the source of that help is revealed, linking this story to Captain Nemo. The Kingston translation is the text given here. Readers value the novel as a hymn to skill, science, and teamwork.
wallace-defence-modern-spiritualism-1874:
Alfred Russel Wallace first spoke out for the faith in A Defence of Modern Spiritualism, a brief tract of 1874. Foes had mocked his faith in the dark room in the press. Wallace, a famed man of science, replies in calm print. He sums the proof as he sees it and asks for a fair test, not scorn.

The tract is short, clear, and brave for its day. It came ere his fat book of 1878 on the same theme. Here is the first time a top name in science stood up in print for the seance.
walras-elements-vol1-1874:
Léon Walras published the first part of his Elements of Pure Political Economy in French in 1874. Walras, teaching at Lausanne, aimed to do for economics what Newton had done for physics: state the whole system in exact, mathematical form. The first part lays the foundation with his theory of exchange.

He shows how prices form when many traders, each seeking the most satisfaction, meet in one market. From two traders and two goods he builds toward the general case, the whole economy balanced in a system of equations. Value, on his account, comes from scarcity joined to usefulness. The book founded general equilibrium theory, the idea that all markets clear together. Economics became a mathematical science in these pages, though the world took decades to notice.
walras-elements-vol2-1874:
The second part of Walras's Elements of Pure Political Economy followed the first in French in 1874. Part 1 had built the theory of exchange between traders. Part 2 works out the system in full, extending the equations to production, capital, and money.

Walras treats capital goods as sources of services that earn rent, and money as the good in which accounts are kept. His famous device of an auctioneer crying prices until supply meets demand shows how equilibrium could be found in practice. The mathematics scared off many early readers, and the book's fame grew slowly. By the mid-twentieth century it was honored as the most exact statement of the marginal revolution. The Lausanne master's complete theory stands in these two parts.
wundt-artzney-buchel-leonhart-bagasser-a: Wundt Artzney Büchel Leonhart Bagasser, 1570. The wound medicine book. This book preserves that work. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
zola-conquest-plassans-1874:
Chatto and Windus issued The Conquest of Plassans at London in 1917, in Vizetelly's English version. Twenty-two chapters carry the tale in the fourth Rougon-Macquart volume. The scene returns to Plassans, the small town where the family saga began.

A smiling young priest, Abbe Faujas, arrives and slowly takes hold of the town. His grip tightens on the sound Mouret household, which becomes his tool. Faith curdles into fanatic drive as ambition conquers from within. The tale ends in madness and fire, by the v1 account. Dark and tense, it ranks among the most gripping volumes of the whole cycle.
